entries.name: Adversarial Test Hardening
entries.summary: Point an agent at your checks and tell it to cheat. A second agent patches every exploit it finds, a third confirms legitimate solutions still pass, and you repeat. On one benchmark this took attack success from 62% to 0%.
entries.whenToUse: Use it before any high-autonomy setup, because [[Dark Factory]] and unattended [[Goal Loop]] runs make the oracle the only control. Use it when you evaluate agents rather than ship their work. That is the paper's setting, and the incentive to game is strongest there. Use it on the few checks that gate merges, not a whole suite. Use it after a run where an agent passed the checks and produced something wrong. That is a vulnerability report, and this is how you find its siblings.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it on a suite nobody gates on. Hardening a check that decides nothing is wasted effort. Do not run it without the validator role. You will harden the oracle by rejecting correct solutions, and you will not notice until real work starts failing. Do not use it where the tests are already the specification and there is nothing to exploit—a pure property-based suite has a different failure mode. And do not treat a hardened verifier as a correct one. Resisting exploits is not the same as testing the right behavior.
entries.drawbacks: It is three agent roles and a loop. It costs real compute, and you must repeat it as the suite changes. Without the validator it hardens into rejecting correct work. Exploits it does not find remain. "The hacker stopped finding things" is a statement about the hacker, not the verifier. The evidence comes from benchmark settings where the verifier is a discrete scoring function. A repository test suite is messier, and the transfer is untested. A hardened verifier can also test the wrong behavior with great rigor, and no adversarial pressure detects that.

entries.name: Agent Handoff
entries.summary: A handoff transfers control. It is not a function call. A triage agent routes the conversation to a specialist, and the specialist becomes the active agent for the rest of the turn. A manager, by contrast, calls specialists as tools and keeps control.
entries.whenToUse: Use handoffs when routing is the workflow—a triage step whose whole job is deciding which specialist should own the conversation. Use them when the specialist needs its own instructions rather than a paragraph inside a larger prompt. Switching the active instructions is the mechanism's distinguishing feature. Use them when the specialist should answer the user directly and a manager restating the answer would only add distortion. Use agents-as-tools for everything else, which is most cases: bounded subtasks whose results the caller needs to combine.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use a handoff when the caller must combine several specialists' outputs. After a transfer there is no caller to combine them. Do not use one when shared guardrails must apply to the final answer. Those live with the manager, and a transfer leaves them behind. Do not use one where the conversation must return to a general agent afterwards, unless the framework supports transferring back. And do not transfer control without deciding what permissions transfer with it.
entries.drawbacks: Control does not come back, so anything needing synthesis across specialists has to be a tool call instead. Guardrails enforced by the manager stop applying at the transfer. This is easy to miss because nothing fails. The answer just leaves by a different door. Routing errors are expensive. A misrouted conversation is owned by the wrong specialist for the rest of the turn, with no manager to notice. And authority transfers along with control unless something stops it. That is the [[Delegation Chain]] failure, and the reason this pattern belongs in a security conversation as well as an architecture one.

entries.name: Agent Instructions as Testing Contract
entries.summary: Write the exact build and test commands, in order, with expected results, into the instructions file the agent reads every session. In a large real repository this single change tracked a jump in pull request success from 38.1% to 69%.
entries.whenToUse: Use it on any repository whose build is not a single obvious command, which is most real ones. Use it wherever the agent has repeatedly run the wrong thing. That repetition is the signal, and it does not fix itself. Use it before blaming a model: the measured jump here came from setup, not a better model. Use it especially for monorepos, multi-target builds, and anything with an inner-loop versus full-build distinction. Guessing is most expensive there.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it to document the whole build system. The file competes for attention, and a long one gets ignored, as [[Context File]] documents. Do not write commands you have not verified. A wrong command in the instructions file is worse than none, because the agent will trust it and stop reasoning. Do not use it for things that change frequently, since a stale command is a confident failure. And do not treat it as a substitute for a working `init.sh` or task runner, a better place for the commands to live ([[Initializer Agent]]).
entries.drawbacks: Stale commands are the main risk, and they fail confidently. An agent following a documented command that no longer works has no reason to doubt it. That is worse than an agent reasoning from scratch. The file competes for attention with everything else in it, so this content has to displace something rather than be added to it. The reported number is a correlation from one repository with two changes made together: the instructions file and firewall access to package feeds. Attributing it to instructions alone is Toub's reading, not an isolated variable. And documenting commands does not make them work. A fragile build stays fragile.

entries.name: Agent OS
entries.summary: Agent OS keeps durable standards and feature context in a small Markdown tree, then injects only the standards that match the task. It leaves planning and execution to the host agent.
entries.whenToUse: Agent OS fits when your real problem is convention drift rather than planning. Picture an established codebase (often Rails, given its origins) with tribal knowledge that agents keep violating. You want standards written once, discovered from the code rather than authored from scratch, and injected only when relevant. It suits developers who already like Claude Code's plan mode and want a light layer on top, not a replacement. HN user dchuk described the loop that works: ideate a PRD with Claude and ChatGPT, "go through agent os to bootstrap the core artifacts and then it's just a loop of shaping specs, break into tasks, implement, then I manually test it out… this agent os thing adds just enough structure to tame complexity and variability" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46570793)).
entries.whenNotToUse: If you want the framework to own verification, parallel execution or context isolation, use [[GSD]] or [[Superpowers]]. Agent OS v3 explicitly does not. If you have no standards worth encoding (a throwaway prototype), the discovery step is wasted work. If you are outside Claude Code or Cursor's plan-mode world, v3's central assumption (that the host agent handles planning and task tracking) does not hold. You would be on the older v2 workflow.
entries.drawbacks: The v3 refocus is also its main limitation. There is no verification stage, no fresh-context execution and no orchestration, so implementation quality depends entirely on the host agent. dchuk's own report notes he "haven't looked at a line of code" and that "sometimes I have to nudge the model after my smoke testing to clean up some stuff". That is the review-debt risk every spec-driven flow carries. Command churn is a real cost. v2.1 replaced the four-phase flow with six, retired roles, and renamed agents. v3 replaced the commands again ("Commands and scripts are new"), so tutorials from 2025 no longer apply. The changelog for 2026 shows install-script bugs (`set -e` with `((var++))`, GNU `tac` on macOS) that silently broke installs. Standards can rot like any documentation, and nothing checks them against the code after discovery. Evidence of adoption is thin. HN threads on it drew two points each, and the one comment on the 2026 submission was dismissive ("just a bunch of prompts in Markdown. Looks great on a resume though" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46613073))). I found no arXiv paper and no independent large-scale experience report.

entries.name: Agent Teams
entries.summary: Peers, not workers. Each teammate is a full independent session. It claims work from a shared task list and messages other teammates directly, instead of reporting to a parent that does all the coordinating.
entries.whenToUse: The documentation names four cases. They share a shape: work that decomposes into pieces that benefit from talking to each other. Research and review, where teammates "share and challenge each other's findings." New modules or features, where each owns a separate piece. Debugging with competing hypotheses. Cross-layer coordination spanning frontend, backend, and tests. Start with three to five teammates, keep five or six tasks per teammate, and begin with read-only work—"reviewing a PR, researching a library, or investigating a bug"—before attempting parallel implementation.
entries.whenNotToUse: The documentation is direct: teams "add coordination overhead and use significantly more tokens than a single session," and "for sequential tasks, same-file edits, or work with many dependencies, a single session or subagents are more effective." Do not use teams when only the result matters. Subagents do that for less. Do not use them for work whose pieces touch the same files, since "two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites." Do not use them unattended: "letting a team run unattended for too long increases the risk of wasted effort." And do not use them in headless or non-interactive mode, where teammates are not spawned at all.
entries.drawbacks: Cost scales linearly with teammates, each a full session, and the documentation says so plainly. Permission inheritance is the sharpest risk. Teammates start with the lead's permission mode, and "if the lead runs with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, all teammates do too," which is [[Delegation Chain]] by default. Coordination fails in documented ways. Task status lags when teammates forget to mark work complete, which blocks dependents. The lead sometimes starts implementing instead of waiting. Teammates stop early on errors rather than recovering. Shutdown is slow because each finishes its current call. File conflicts are a design responsibility, not a solved problem. The feature is experimental with named limitations—no session resumption for in-process teammates, one team per session, no nested teams, and a fixed lead—so treat it as a capability under development.

entries.name: Agent-Computer Interface
entries.summary: An agent-computer interface is the tool surface designed for a model: bounded reads, precise edits, useful errors, and safe defaults. The interface becomes part of the agent’s capability.
entries.whenToUse: Apply ACI thinking whenever you expose a capability to an agent: writing an MCP server, wiring a CLI into Claude Code, or building a custom harness. When an agent keeps failing on the same tool (malformed edits, unbounded output, wrong flag), the fix is usually in the tool, not the prompt. It is also the lens for evaluating third-party tools. Does the output fit in a few hundred tokens? Does the error message say what to do next? Does the tool refuse obviously broken input?
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not over-scaffold a strong model. mini-swe-agent's result shows that for current frontier models a plain shell plus good defaults is competitive. Heavy custom command sets add surface for the agent to misuse and for you to maintain. Do not add guardrails that hide information: an edit command that silently reformats or a search that silently drops hits will produce confident wrong behavior. And do not design tools in the abstract. SWE-agent's and Anthropic's method is evaluation-driven, so without an eval you cannot tell whether an interface change helped.
entries.drawbacks: Guardrails can fight the model. An edit rejected for a lint rule the agent does not understand can trigger repeated retries. Custom command sets must be taught in the system prompt, which costs tokens every turn, and models trained on bash may use it badly. Interfaces that pre-digest too much (for example returning a summary instead of the file) prevent the agent from noticing details. The HN discussion of Cursor-style automatic indexing versus Aider's manual file selection raised this critique ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44108042)). Finally, the ACI is a security boundary in disguise. Anthropic's skills post warns that "malicious skills may introduce vulnerabilities," and the same holds for any tool an agent can call.

entries.name: Agentic Project Management
entries.summary: Planner, Manager, Workers. State lives in files outside any context window. Workers accumulate domain expertise across assignments instead of restarting fresh. A handover command transfers a worker's knowledge to a new instance when it runs out of room.
entries.whenToUse: Use it on projects long enough that a single conversation degrades. That is the problem it names. Use it when the work splits cleanly by domain, since persistent domain workers pay off only when each has a stable area. Use it when you want state in files, not in a tool's database. Borrow the handover protocol whether or not you adopt the rest. Most setups answer "what do we do when a context fills" badly and ad hoc.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for short projects. Three roles and a document set are more process than a week of work can repay. Do not use it if you disagree with the persistent-worker premise. The fresh-context position ([[Ralph Loop]], [[Research Plan Implement]]) is at least as well supported, and this library's research holds more evidence for it. Do not use it where an existing tracker already coordinates work. Be honest about maturity: the project is maintained and documented, but no independent evaluation or adoption data was found.
entries.drawbacks: The persistent-worker premise is a contested bet, not a settled finding. Accumulated context is also accumulated noise, and this library's [[Context Compaction]] note collects the evidence that long contexts degrade. Handover is lossy by construction. A handover that drops a constraint reproduces the failure documented in [[Constraint Pinning]]. Three roles multiply token cost against a single session. The Manager is a bottleneck and a second translation layer between your intent and the work. That is the intent-loss problem described in [[Delegation Chain]]. And the evidence base is a single project's self-description.

entries.name: Agentless Pipeline
entries.summary: Agentless fixes repository issues in stages. It narrows the search space, generates several patches, filters them with tests, and selects a candidate. The simple pipeline also makes a useful baseline for agentic systems.
entries.whenToUse: Use an Agentless pipeline when you process many similar tasks in batch, such as an issue backlog, a dependency bump across repositories, or a lint-rule migration. Use it when cost per task must be predictable. Use it when you need to audit exactly what the model saw at each stage. It also suits a weak or small model. Agentless and Kimi-Dev both show that fixed stages extract more from a limited model than an open loop does. And it is the natural CI shape, because each stage is a deterministic script with an LLM call inside.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it when the task needs exploration the pipeline did not anticipate. Examples: an issue that requires running the app, reading logs, or finding a configuration file the tree skeleton hides. The paper's own limitation notes list dependence on code search for hard cases and a suboptimal majority-vote selector. Do not use it interactively. Developers want to redirect mid-task, and a pipeline does not allow that. And the SWE-bench numbers cover single-issue bug fixes. There is no evidence here for multi-file feature work, where [[Plan-and-Execute]] or an agent loop fits better.
entries.drawbacks: Localization is one-shot. If the top-N files are wrong, nothing downstream can recover. An agent could grep again. The reproduction test is LLM-written and can be wrong in the same direction as the patch, so a patch and its test can agree while both miss the issue. The paper mitigates this by requiring the test to fail on the original code. That does not catch a test that fails for the wrong reason. Majority voting among K patches prefers the *common* fix, not the *correct* one. The benchmark-audit part of the paper (SWE-bench Lite-S) also warns that headline numbers include problems whose issue text contains the exact patch.

entries.name: AGENTS.md Convention
entries.summary: AGENTS.md gives an agent the few repository facts it cannot cheaply infer. Keep it short, testable, and specific. Treat it as context that needs evaluation, not a policy engine.
entries.whenToUse: Always, but sparingly. Use the file for anything an agent cannot cheaply infer from the code and would otherwise get wrong. That means build and test commands, non-standard conventions ("use this assert library", "never write comments", "structured logging", as tptacek listed), forbidden actions, and required workflows such as running the linter before finishing. It helps most on fresh projects "without much code," where conventions exist only in someone's head. It also helps with framework knowledge newer than the model's training data, which is Vercel's case. Nested files earn their keep in monorepos with divergent conventions per package.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it as a wiki. The ETH study's negative result for repository overviews, Augment's "12+ document reads on simple tasks", and the BMAD test all say the same thing. Prose the agent could derive from the code costs tokens on every turn and can hurt. Do not stack warnings without fixes. Do not expect the file to replace verification. HN's darkbatman found Claude Code "often doesn't follow instructions from claude.md or forget things mid-way" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45323477)). Instructions decay over a long context. Hooks, tests and reviewers enforce rules. The file does not.
entries.drawbacks: Extra instructions can increase exploration and testing without improving the requested result. Redundant descriptions, stale rules, and contradictory requirements each fail differently. A line-count limit alone does not tell you which instructions help. Tool-specific loading behavior also differs. Verify that guidance loads and that it changes the intended behavior. See [[Research Experiments#E1 Evaluate repository guidance]].
