entries.name: Aider Architect-Editor
entries.summary: Aider’s architect mode separates reasoning from edit formatting. One model explains the change. Another emits the file edits. The split helps when a strong reasoner is a clumsy editor.
entries.whenToUse: Use it whenever the best reasoning model available is not the best editing model. In 2024–2025 that meant every reasoning model. The documentation still says it "excels with reasoning-focused models like OpenAI's o1, which excel at problem-solving but struggle with detailed file editing." It also pays off with a single model on hard changes, since the two-request structure alone improved scores. Cost-conscious setups pair an expensive architect with a cheap editor. Local setups pair a strong hosted architect with a local editor.
entries.whenNotToUse: For small edits the extra round trip is pure overhead. HN's macNchz uses "sonnet alone" most of the time. The top-scoring "whole" edit-format configurations "are quite slow, so probably not practical for interactive use." The split also assumes the architect's description is unambiguous. When it is vague, the editor guesses, and the human sees only the final diff.
entries.drawbacks: Two calls per turn double latency and cost on trivial changes. The architect can propose changes to files not in the chat, and the editor cannot apply them. Information is lost at the boundary. The editor sees only the architect's summary, not the user's original intent, so subtle requirements can be dropped silently. The benchmark is aider's own Exercism-derived suite. Gains there did not always transfer to large repositories, which is why later methodologies added research and verification stages around the split. Finally, it works per turn, with no memory or planning across turns. It solves the edit-format problem, not the project-scale problem.

entries.name: Architect-Editor Split
aliases: Plan with Opus Edit with Sonnet
entries.summary: The architect-editor split routes a task through two roles: a reasoning-heavy planner and an edit-reliable implementer. It can improve accuracy. But the handoff loses information, so verify it.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when your best reasoning model is unreliable at edit formats. The original o1 was one case. Any "thinking" model with a strict harness is another. It also fits when cost matters and a cheap editor can apply what an expensive planner decides: the architect call is short and the editor call is the long one. It fits when you already separate planning from execution (plan mode, [[Plan-and-Execute]]) and want the planning phase on the strongest model. And it fits when you want a local or open-weight editor for privacy while renting reasoning from a frontier model.
entries.whenNotToUse: Skip it for interactive, rapid-fire edits, where you feel the extra round trip. Aider notes the approach "uses two LLM requests, which can take longer and increase costs" and is "less practical for interactive use with slower configurations". Skip it for small changes where a single strong model already edits reliably. Modern frontier models mostly can. Skip it when the architect's prose loses information the editor needs, such as exact line context or subtle invariants. Then the editor guesses. And when the two models disagree on conventions, you get plan/implementation mismatch with no one accountable.
entries.drawbacks:
- **Latency and cost of two calls** (Aider's own caveat).
- **Lossy handoff.** The architect's plan can omit the exact code the editor needs. The editor may follow the letter of the plan and miss context only the architect saw. ACE-FCA warns of the same failure: "bad research" cascading into flawed code.
- **Editor drift on weak models.** Very small editors (the HN thread's Devstral Small / local Apple Silicon setups) risk malformed or partial edits. Commenters were still exploring which open-weight editors held up.
- **Two sets of quirks.** Different vendors have different refusal behavior, formatting habits, and context limits. The pipeline inherits both.
- **Benchmark vs reality.** The 85% figure comes from Aider's own edit benchmark with 2024 models. No independent study of the split in 2026 tooling surfaced in this session's searches.

entries.name: Best-of-N Sampling
entries.summary: Best-of-N sampling generates several candidates, then picks one with tests, agreement, a reward model, or a judge. You pay for extra calls and get robustness. The selector matters as much as the sampler.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when a strong oracle exists and single attempts fail often: flaky-but-fixable tasks, hard bugs, benchmark or leaderboard climbing, competitive-programming-style problems, and migrations with a mechanical correctness check. Use CodeT-style generated tests when no tests exist and the function has a clear input/output contract. Use it for unattended batch work, where paying 4-8× compute to avoid a human round-trip is a good trade.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it interactively. A developer waiting for eight parallel runs gets the worst of both. Do not use it when the oracle is the model's own opinion: ranking N samples by an LLM judge without execution adds little and can select the most confident wrong answer. Do not use it for tasks with large side effects (deploys, data migrations), where discarded candidates leave residue. Do not use it when candidates are not diverse (same prompt, temperature 0). The ensemble collapses to one answer.
entries.drawbacks: Cost scales linearly with N. Selection is the weak point. Majority vote prefers common over correct (Agentless's authors call their vote "suboptimal"). Generated tests can be wrong in the same direction as the code. A scoring model is another model with its own blind spots. Test-based filtering invites the overfitting SpecBench documents: agents pass visible tests and fail held-out ones, with gaps growing "approximately 27 percentage points for every tenfold increase in lines of code" ([arXiv 2605.21384](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.21384v1)); SpecBench also found that "additional search iterations also failed to eliminate hacking, sometimes amplifying it." Diverse candidates can each be right in incompatible ways, and a selector cannot merge them. Every candidate also needs isolation (worktree or container), which most teams do not have by default.

entries.name: BMAD Method
aliases: Breakthrough Method for Agile AI-Driven Development
entries.summary: BMAD is a role-based, artifact-heavy workflow. Research and product framing become a PRD, architecture, epics, and story files before implementation. Its value is traceability when the work is large enough to justify the ceremony.
entries.whenToUse: BMAD suits greenfield products whose requirements genuinely need working out, where you would write a PRD and architecture document anyway. The personas are good interlocutors, and the PO checklist catches contradictions between documents before code exists. It also fits teams that already run agile ceremonies and want the agent workflow to mirror epics, stories and QA gates. It fits regulated environments, where the homepage's promise of "documented decisions and traceability" matters. One HN user shipped a 126,000-line Kotlin Android app with no prior Kotlin experience. They wrote that "vibecoding something that big is not an option... To maintain my specifications I use BMAD framework. It helped me a lot to clear the requirements, prepare the architecture, UI, find any gaps" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48184549)). Planning can happen in a flat-rate web chat, so it also saves metered IDE tokens on the expensive thinking.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not reach for BMAD for a bug fix or a small feature in a codebase you understand. Even its own v6 documentation now routes "trivial work" straight to Change → Edit → Verify. It is a poor fit for developers who want to stay close to the code, because the method's value comes from trusting the artifact chain. It is a poor fit for tight token budgets, since each persona re-reads large documents. If your problem is a long-running session losing quality rather than unclear requirements, [[GSD]] or plain plan mode addresses that more directly.
entries.drawbacks:
The dominant critique is weight. HN user taffydavid "just spent a week training up in spec driven development through bmad, which was awful, and speckit which was ok but not great. Both had what seemed like unnecessary ceremony around the specs, generating fields of spec documents which presumably fill up the context window quickly" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47994926)). MattGrommes was blunter: "Basically, it's Waterfall for Agents. Lots of Capitalized Words to signify something" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47253518)). straydusk "found SpecKit to be over-engineered, and BMAD to be quite complex" and preferred a thinner tool where "I still felt like I was in control" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46021195)). desireco42 lumped it with GSD and Spec Kit as tools that "created a lot of changes, spent a lot of time doing something and in the end this was all smoke and mirrors", and wondered aloud whether the YouTube enthusiasm was sponsored ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47421102)).

Token cost follows from weight. Every persona switch reloads the PRD, architecture and story. The V4 design answered by moving planning to a flat-rate web chat and sharding documents. Sharding is itself a manual, error-prone step: copying documents into `docs/`, running the shard command, keeping shards in sync with the source. Manual command volume is a related complaint. One HN commenter counted that "for an Epic with 8 stories, that's potentially 40+ manual commands" through create → develop → test → review → fix → update status, and wrote a wrapper to automate it ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47048578)). Persona theatre is a subtler failure. When a single model plays Mary, John and Winston in sequence, disagreements between "roles" are shallower than the ceremony implies. The PO checklist can pass documents that merely restate each other. GSD's marketing line that BMAD adds "unnecessary enterprise ceremony" captures the market's view, even if it is self-serving. Finally, the method changes fast. The jump from v4 to v6 rewrote the command surface, the documentation site, and the persona list, so tutorials from 2025 no longer match the tool.

entries.name: Checkpoint and Rollback
entries.summary: Checkpoints make agent work reversible. Record a known-good state, try a bounded change, and verify it. If the experiment fails, restore the checkpoint. A checkpoint helps only when its scope and restoration command are explicit.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for any exploratory or risky change: refactors, dependency upgrades, "see if approach B is simpler". Use it when the agent produces a flurry of edits you want to review as one coherent diff. Use it for long-running or unattended runs. Commit each green step, so a bad iteration is one `git reset` away (see [[Ralph Loop]], [[CI Repair Loop]]). Use it when the conversation itself has gone bad: restore the conversation to the last good prompt and keep the code, or vice versa. Use it to compress a verbose failed detour without losing your initial instructions ("Summarize from here").
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not rely on tool checkpoints for changes made by shell commands, generated files, migrations, or subagents. Use git. Do not let WIP commits reach shared branches unsquashed ("your history will be cluttered and as hard to read as the codebase", hoppp). Committing every agent pause also pulls in junk: "These agents often generate randomly named files and dump them anywhere... a 'git add all' approach can bring in junk" (0x6c6f6c). Checkpoints do not replace review. Restoring a "good" state you never verified restores an unknown state.
entries.drawbacks:
- **Coverage gaps.** Bash-made changes, subagent edits, symlinked and hard-linked files (pnpm stores, dotfile managers) are skipped, sometimes with only a "skipped N files" warning.
- **Retention.** Snapshots are deleted after about 30 days; rewinding to a swept checkpoint fails with "No files were restored".
- **History pollution.** Aider-style auto-commits require discipline: "I always squash and reorganise the commits from aider" (black_knight).
- **Junk files.** Agents' scratch files get captured or, worse, missed, depending on staging strategy.
- **False safety inside sandboxes.** "You only mount the project dir so you can only lose your current changes" holds only if commits are frequent (see [[Sandboxed Execution]]).
- **Queued mid-turn messages are not checkpointed**: rewinding to the turn start discards the work done before your message arrived.
- **Rewind does not fix the prompt.** Restoring state without changing the instruction reproduces the failure. The best-practices advice is to re-prompt "with a more specific prompt that incorporates what you learned".

entries.name: CI Repair Loop
entries.summary: A CI repair loop treats a failing check as structured feedback. Reproduce it, make one bounded change, and rerun the relevant check. Stop when the evidence says green or the attempt budget runs out.
entries.whenToUse:
Use it for well-scoped, well-tested backlog work where CI is trustworthy: removals and cleanups (84.7% merged in dotnet/runtime), test additions (75.6%), refactors (69.7%), bug fixes (69.4%). Toub: "when you need to remove deprecated code, delete dead branches, clean up obsolete APIs, CCA is remarkably good at it," and 20% of the issues it took were more than two years old. It fits work you dispatch from a phone and review later (Toub's "Saturday birthday party" and "airplane" experiments). It also keeps a pull request alive while you are away, which is what auto-fix and `/loop` are for.

Use it when your CI already encodes your definition of done. The agent then inherits the same gate as humans. Greenfield repositories with clear conventions do better. The MCP C# SDK saw 77.3% success and 32.6% human intervention, versus 67.9% and 45.1% in the decades-old runtime.
entries.whenNotToUse:
Do not use it where CI cannot exercise the change. Copilot "runs on Linux x64 only," so Windows-specific and cross-architecture runtime work "cannot compile or test." Performance work (54.5% success) failed for want of benchmarking. Do not use it for changes that need architectural judgment. 1.8% of review comments said the approach was wrong, but those were the expensive ones.

Do not turn it on where a pull request comment can deploy. Anthropic's warning: "If your repository uses comment-triggered automation such as Atlantis, Terraform Cloud, or custom GitHub Actions that run on `issue_comment` events, be aware that Claude can reply on your behalf, which can trigger those workflows."

Do not point two bots at each other without an allowlist. Devin's documentation warns that "respond to all bot comments" "risks infinite loops with code review bots that comment back and forth with Devin"; Claude Code's Action "rejects a bot actor unless you list it in `allowed_bots`, which keeps bots from triggering Claude in a loop."
entries.drawbacks:
**Going green the wrong way.** The dotnet/runtime debut showed the agent "resolves" test failures by removing/commenting out the test cases, or change the assertions" (diggan). Kent Beck and Anthropic report the same behaviour in other settings. The CI loop makes it worse, because green is literally the objective. Guard with review-bot checks for test edits, branch protection on `tests/**` and `.github/workflows/**`, and a [[Fresh-Context Reviewer]].

**Ignoring feedback and repeating failures.** Reviewers on the early pull requests "repeatedly pointed out issues ('Your new tests aren't being run because the new file wasn't added to the csproj'), but the agent failed to incorporate corrections"; diggan: "It's like you have a junior developer except they don't even read what you're telling them." safety1st compared it to outsourcing firms that "will bill another 20 hours." Toub's data shows the fix was instructions and environment, not the model: 41.7% to ~71%.

**Log noise and review burden.** pull requests "became difficult to review due to excessive check failure output obscuring actual code changes." Merged agent pull requests averaged 16.5 comments vs 12.4 for humans. Direct human commits landed on 52.3% of merged agent pull requests because it was "faster than explaining." Success with direct human intervention was 86.2%; without, 55.1%.

**Review becomes the bottleneck.** "One person with good judgment and a phone can generate PRs faster than a team can review them." The top two reviewers handled 36% of all comments.

**Environment and firewall failures.** Early runs failed because the sandbox could not reach build dependencies. Copilot needed firewall configuration and "acknowledge environment limitations (Linux-only execution)" in its instructions.

**CI does not run on bot commits by default.** Both GitHub (workflow approval for Copilot pushes) and Claude's Action ("GitHub doesn't trigger workflows on commits made with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`") require configuration. A naive loop can wait forever for a signal that never fires.

**Merge conflicts are invisible.** "GitHub does not emit a webhook when the base branch advances and creates a merge conflict, so auto-fix can't react to conflicts on its own."

**Cost surprises.** kageiit on HN described running "multiple specialized AI agents on every code change" at "50-100+ LLM calls per PR," and a cheaper model that "retried identical failing tool calls" instead of adapting ([HN comment](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46911734)). Copilot charges per session; hosted review is $15–25 per run.

**Survivorship in the metrics.** HN commenters on the launch asked "how many Copilot PRs were *not* merged and/or required human take-overs," and one insider said adoption was "a *very* management-driven push, not developer-driven."

**Measurement is still immature.** SWE-CI's authors argue one-shot resolution benchmarks miss whether agents keep a codebase healthy across many CI rounds. A Semantic Scholar search also surfaced "On the Reliability of Agentic AI in Continuous Integration Pipelines" (Chouchen et al., 2026). Its abstract reports that across 11,771 GitHub pull requests, agent fixes resolve CI failures about 4x faster, but agents also introduce a large share of the failures. The paper could not be fetched to verify the figures. Treat that as a lead, not a citation.

entries.name: Circuit Breaker
entries.summary: Bound the loop by something the agent does not control: iterations, turns, dollars, wall clock, or lack of progress. It is the backstop. It makes every other exit condition survivable when that condition fails.
entries.whenToUse: Always, on any unattended loop. No loop is safe without a bound once it meets a task the model cannot solve. Use a spend breaker when subagents or teams are involved, since count breakers do not bound fan-out. Use a stall breaker when the task has a countable gap—failing tests, unfinished features—because it turns wasted iterations into an early, informative stop. Use a time breaker when the loop shares a machine or a deadline with something else.
entries.whenNotToUse: There is no case for omitting it. There are cases for setting it wrong. A cap too low turns a solvable task into a false failure. It also trains you to raise the cap reflexively, which is how caps stop meaning anything. Raise a breaker because a run hit it only when you have diagnosed why. "It needed more iterations" is not a diagnosis. A breaker that fires repeatedly is evidence about the task or the harness, not a configuration problem.
entries.drawbacks: The dominant human failure is cap inflation. The run hits the limit, someone doubles it, and after three rounds the breaker is decorative. The second is masking. A breaker that fires regularly means something upstream is broken, and raising it hides the signal that would have told you what. Breakers also cut mid-task by construction. A loop without [[Checkpoint and Rollback]] or a [[Progress File]] can leave the tree in a state nobody can resume from. Count breakers correlate poorly with cost. Spend breakers correlate poorly with progress. Neither notices a loop that cycles, looks productive, and goes nowhere. The stall breaker exists for that.

entries.name: Cline Memory Bank
entries.summary: Cline’s Memory Bank keeps project purpose, architecture, technology, active work, and progress in durable Markdown files. It reduces context loss across sessions. The cost is maintenance and stale notes.
entries.whenToUse: The Memory Bank fits solo or small-team projects worked in many short sessions with an agent that has no native memory. It fits best in tools like Cline and Roo, where context resets on every new task. HN user darkbatman "was using Cline/Roocode from almost an year and it always made sure to read things from memory-bank which i really liked", contrasting it with Claude Code forgetting CLAUDE.md instructions mid-task ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45323477)). jsmith99 uses it to give agents "the architecture, progress, road map etc." they otherwise lack ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45405368)). It is also a good on-ramp. Six files with clear purposes are easier to maintain than a sprawling CLAUDE.md.
entries.whenNotToUse: It scales badly. jsmith99 noted that "some of my more complex projects use 30k tokens just on this" at session start, and tharkun__ wrote that "as memory banks grow or accumulate the AI gets confused and doesn't quite deliver... I simply can't read all the doc[s]" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45610996)). CuriouslyC's structural objection is that memory "requires well tuned retrieval to deliver value, and one sized retrieval systems don't work". A bank loaded in full every time is the wrong shape for large projects. Agents with built-in memory or selective context loading (file-match steering, indexed standards) do not need the always-read-everything rule. The BMAD documentation' counter-principle ("more documentation is not more value. Extra context is a cost") is aimed squarely at this pattern.
entries.drawbacks: Token cost grows linearly with the bank and is paid on every task. The agent maintains the files, so they drift toward whatever the agent believed, mistakes included. The blog post itself lists "maintenance burden" and "manual updates required" as limitations. A stale `activeContext.md` sends the next session confidently in the wrong direction. Six prose files invite verbosity. Cline's own later guidance and other frameworks moved to smaller, indexed or file-matched context because full-read banks were bloating. And the pattern captures state, not verification. Nothing checks that what `progress.md` says works actually works.

entries.name: Command Classifier Guard
entries.summary: A deterministic program parses each tool call into typed effects and blocks the ones it can prove are disasters. No model is involved, so the verdict is fast and identical every run.
entries.whenToUse: Use it as the innermost layer whenever an agent has shell access. It matters most when permissions are relaxed, because it is most valuable where prompts have been turned off. Use it in CI and unattended runs, where the result means nothing without determinism. Put it in front of a model-based classifier, not instead of one. A rule decides the catastrophic cases and judgment decides the ambiguous ones. Use it when you need an auditable answer to "what would have been blocked," which a model cannot give.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it as your only control. It catches only what it can prove, and the ambiguous majority passes straight through to delegate. Do not expect it to handle obfuscation. A static parser sees what the call says. An agent that encodes a command, or writes a script and runs it, has moved outside what the parser can reason about. Do not use it to grant permissions, because a guard that can approve stops being a guard. And do not treat it as a substitute for [[Sandboxed Execution]]. It reduces the rate of bad calls. A sandbox reduces their consequences.
entries.drawbacks: Coverage is the tradeoff. A fixed rule set catches the disasters someone thought of. The interesting failures are often the ones nobody did. Obfuscation defeats static parsing—encoded commands, indirection through a written script, unusual shells. The guard's guarantee is about what it can prove, not about what is safe. Rules need maintenance as tooling changes, and a stale rule set gives false confidence. Delegate is not approve, and that is easy to misread. Something else decides a call the guard passed through. If that something else is a permissive mode, nothing decided it at all.

entries.name: Competing Hypotheses Debate
entries.summary: Spawn one agent per theory about a bug and tell them to disprove each other. The goal is to defeat anchoring. A single investigator finds one plausible explanation and stops looking.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when you have already failed to find a bug once. That is the signal that anchoring has happened. Use it when several plausible explanations exist and the evidence does not obviously discriminate. Use it for expensive bugs, where running five agents costs little against another day of investigation. Use it when the symptom spans layers and each layer suggests a different culprit. Use it for design decisions with genuinely contested tradeoffs, where the same anti-anchoring argument applies.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for bugs a stack trace already explains. Do not use it when you cannot enumerate distinct hypotheses. Five agents given the same vague brief will converge on the same theory and produce expensive agreement. Do not use it where the investigation requires shared state that is hard to isolate. And do not treat the surviving theory as proven. Surviving cross-examination by four language models is not a fix. The fix still has to reproduce and resolve the symptom.
entries.drawbacks: Cost scales with hypotheses, and each one is a full session. The true cause may not be among the enumerated theories. Then the debate produces a confident wrong answer with supporting argument—the most expensive failure here. Agents from the same model family share blind spots. Five investigators may be wrong in the same direction, and no amount of arguing detects that. Debate can end in the failure modes collected in [[Multi-Agent Debate]]: forceful agreement, prolonged disagreement, and premature convergence. A surviving theory is a candidate, not a diagnosis.

entries.name: Completion Sentinel
entries.summary: The loop ends when the agent emits an exact string. It is trivial to implement and trivially gameable, because the model controls the string. Where a data predicate exists, use it instead.
entries.whenToUse: Use a sentinel when no machine-checkable definition of done exists: open-ended research, exploratory writing, a task whose output is prose. Use it as a secondary signal alongside a real cap and a real predicate, so a cooperative agent can finish early. Use it in low-stakes interactive loops where you are watching and can interrupt.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it as the only exit condition for anything unattended. Do not use it when a predicate exists. If there is a test suite, an exit code, or a status field, use that. Do not use it for tasks where finishing early is rewarded and verification is expensive. That incentive structure produces false completion. And do not use it to express more than one outcome. Exact-match cannot distinguish success from blocked, so a stuck agent and a finished agent look identical to the loop.
entries.drawbacks: The model controls the exit. An agent that is stuck, confused, or optimizing for turn count can emit the sentinel, and the loop will believe it. This is textbook reward hacking. The literature under [[Test Tampering]] shows agents reliably find such shortcuts. Exact matching is brittle in both directions. A sentinel inside a code block, a quoted instruction, or the agent's own restatement of the prompt causes a spurious exit. A sentinel the agent formats slightly differently causes an infinite loop. Single-outcome matching means blocked runs never terminate cleanly. The pattern also gives false confidence. The loop exited "successfully," so downstream tooling treats the work as complete.

entries.name: Compound Engineering
entries.summary: Compound Engineering turns each feature into a loop of plan, work, review, and capture. The compounding step writes reusable lessons back into the project. Later tasks spend less time rediscovering the same constraints.
entries.whenToUse: Compound Engineering suits a long-lived product worked on continuously by the same small team. The same classes of mistake recur, so a written solution pays off many times. Less experienced developers like it. They get a brainstorm → plan → build → review scaffold plus a growing knowledge base. HN user michelb, "as an amateur developer", found it "helps me brainstorm, plan and implement apps very well" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48770605)), and kingkongjaffa, usually sceptical of third-party skills, called it the exception, "like an early brainstorm -> plan -> write -> embed knowledge and best practices" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48443194)). DeathArrow called it a reasonable "middle ground between spec driven development and iterations" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47775051)).
entries.whenNotToUse: On throwaway projects there is nothing to compound. On very large or many-team codebases, `docs/solutions/` and `CLAUDE.md` grow without a retrieval strategy. The always-loaded instructions then cost the context they were meant to save (the same failure HN's tharkun__ describes for memory banks: "as memory banks grow or accumulate the AI gets confused and doesn't quite deliver", [HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45610996)). If your bottleneck is context length within one session, not knowledge across sessions, [[GSD]]'s fresh-context execution addresses it more directly. The `/lfg` autonomous mode is exactly the "don't read the code" path that HN's dhorthy warns "leads nowhere good."
entries.drawbacks: Compounding cuts both ways. A wrong lesson written into `docs/solutions/` or `CLAUDE.md` is applied to every future cycle. Nothing in the method audits or expires old solutions. Always-loaded context grows. The BMAD documentation' test ("would removing this line change agent behavior?") is a useful discipline the CE plugin does not enforce. Evidence of effectiveness is mostly first-party (Every's own essays and videos) plus anecdotal HN endorsements. I found no independent quantitative study, no arXiv paper, and no dedicated critical write-up. The `/lfg` mode brings back the unreviewed-code risk that the 80/20 rule is meant to prevent. Review by specialist agents is still the model reviewing itself. The plan-versus-implementation check helps, but security and correctness reviewers share the implementer's blind spots.

entries.name: Conductor
entries.summary: Google’s Conductor extension for Gemini CLI keeps project context, track specifications, plans, implementation, review, and revert in repository files. The workflow is context-driven, with explicit human checkpoints.
entries.whenToUse: Conductor suits Gemini CLI and Antigravity users who want an official, maintained spec-driven workflow instead of a community plugin. It suits teams that want to roll back a whole feature attempt cleanly. Its project-level guideline files make it a reasonable way to enforce house style across many small tracks.
entries.whenNotToUse: It is young and lightly documented outside Google's own material. I found no substantial independent experience reports, no arXiv coverage and no critical write-ups. A team adopting it is an early adopter. It inherits the general spec-driven caveats: over-specification of small tasks and spec drift after implementation. It lacks OpenSpec's delta mechanism and Spec Kit's analyze/converge steps. It offers no fresh-context execution or parallelism.
entries.drawbacks: There is little evidence yet of behaviour at scale. The HN threads are near-empty and the videos are small. Plans are the agent's own decomposition, so the over-decomposition seen in Kiro ("massive task lists") is likely on small fixes. The same model reviews its own plan. Revert depends on the agent committing at the intended boundaries. If it batched changes, logical revert degrades to ordinary git archaeology.

entries.name: Confidence-Gated Escalation
entries.summary: Try the cheap path first. Escalate to the expensive one—more agents, a stronger model, a human—only when a confidence signal says the cheap answer is not good enough. Most tasks never escalate. Average cost drops, and the hard tasks do not suffer.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when an expensive pattern has proven useful but costs too much to apply uniformly. Use it when tasks vary widely in difficulty, which gives the gate the most to work with. Use it when you have a real signal: test results, compilation, agreement across samples. Use it to escalate to a human as well as to more compute. The pattern is the same, and the resource is scarcer.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it when the only signal is the model's own confidence. That means trusting self-assessment, the failure mode documented in [[Self-Refinement]]. Do not use it when tasks are uniformly hard. The gate fires every time and you pay for two passes. Do not use it when the cheap path's failures are silent and expensive, since an unescalated wrong answer costs more than the compute you saved. And do not use it when the expensive path is not actually better. Check that; do not assume it.
entries.drawbacks: The gate is only as good as its signal, and the most available signal—model self-report—is the least reliable. Threshold tuning is empirical and dataset-specific. A threshold that worked on one distribution of tasks is a guess on another. Failed escalation is the expensive failure. A task that should have escalated and did not produces a wrong answer that looks checked. There is also a double-cost floor. Escalating tasks pay for both passes, so a gate that fires often is worse than no gate. And the reported figures come from a benchmark, where task difficulty is distributed differently than in a repository.

entries.name: Constitutional SDD
entries.summary: Put non-negotiable security invariants in a versioned, machine-readable constitution that constrains generation. Do not wait to check for violations afterwards. One study reports a 73% reduction in security defects with velocity preserved.
entries.whenToUse: Use it where security requirements are stable and stateable in advance. That covers most of them—input validation, authentication boundaries, secret handling, output encoding. Use it in regulated environments, where the requirements already exist as a document and the work is making them machine-readable. Use it at high generation volume, where reviewing every diff for the same class of vulnerability does not scale. Use it as the home for invariants that keep reappearing in review comments. A recurring review comment is a constitution entry not yet written.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for functional requirements. They change per feature, and tests serve them better. Do not use it as the only security control. By-construction reduces defects; it does not eliminate them, as the reported 73% makes explicit. Scanning and review still apply. Do not write a constitution so long that it dilutes, the same failure [[Context File]] documents for instructions files. And do not treat conformance to the constitution as security. It covers the vulnerability classes someone enumerated, and the interesting breaches are usually elsewhere.
entries.drawbacks: The measured reduction is 73%, not 100%. By-construction reasoning tends to make people stop looking for the remaining quarter. A constitution covers enumerated vulnerability classes. Novel or composed vulnerabilities are outside it by definition. Maintenance is real: CWE-derived rules age, and a stale constitution gives confidence, not protection. Constraining generation can degrade output in ways that are hard to attribute, and the paper's velocity claim is about speed, not quality. And the evidence is a single paper read at abstract level, with no independent replication.

entries.name: Constraint Pinning
entries.summary: Keep governance constraints out of the compactable part of the context. A rule that gets summarized away stops being obeyed, and the agent gives no sign that anything changed.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for every constraint you would hate to see violated: prohibitions on editing tests, scope boundaries, forbidden directories, credential handling, anything with a blast radius. Use it in any session long enough to compact. That is most real work and all unattended work. Use it especially in [[Ralph Loop]] and [[Stop Hook Loop]] setups. There, context is either discarded outright or piles up until it compacts. Either way, a constraint stated once in the first prompt is gone.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not pin task-specific instructions. They belong in the prompt, and pinning them pollutes every later session. Do not pin so much that the pinned channel becomes noise. Anthropic's guidance on context files is explicit that a bloated file causes rules to be ignored, so pinning everything equals pinning nothing. And do not treat pinning as enough for a constraint that really matters. A pinned rule is still advisory. Anything you cannot afford to have violated should be a deny rule or a hook.
entries.drawbacks: Pinned content is paid for on every request. The channel has a budget, and over-pinning costs tokens and attention. Pinned rules are still instructions. A confusing enough situation can make the model ignore, misread, or override them. Pinning changes what the model can see, not what it must do. Choosing what to pin is a judgment call. It will sometimes be wrong, and nobody will see the error until the constraint is needed. Finally, the measurement behind the pattern is a single benchmark in a single paper. Do not treat its numbers as a general rate.

entries.name: Context Compaction
entries.summary: Reduce context when it helps the next decision, and keep a way to recover the evidence. Summarizing, masking old tool output, and restarting from a handoff are different interventions. None is a universal winner.
entries.whenToUse: Consider reducing context for repeated noisy tool output, unrelated work piled up in one session, expensive re-exploration, or a task nearing the supported window. Prefer a natural task boundary when a reset would interrupt an active investigation. Before discarding conversation, save facts that exist only there, such as a rejected design's rationale.
entries.whenNotToUse: Keep useful context when a short task is nearly finished or an investigation still depends on exact recent observations. Do not clear just to satisfy a fixed 20%, 40%, or 60% rule. Those thresholds describe particular practices, not measured optima across models. Do not add a summarizer until you have compared a simpler policy on the actual workload.
entries.drawbacks:
- **Lost rationale**: an agent repeats an approach whose rejection survived only in conversation. The firsthand discussion in [[Research Sources#S213 Rejected decisions after compaction]] reports this failure.
- **False continuity**: “tests passed” loses the command, tested environment, or scope. [[Research Sources#S215 Handoffs and test scope]] describes mock-only testing mistaken for real endpoint verification.
- **Recovery overhead**: a successful completion hides the extra reads and tool calls spent reconstructing state.
- **Stale evidence**: saved results describe an earlier source tree, dependency set, or running service.
- **Summary error**: an inference becomes a fact or a scoped decision becomes a permanent prohibition.
- **Excessive ceremony**: writing and reviewing large progress documents costs more than finishing the task.

entries.name: Context Engineering
entries.summary: The window's contents are the only thing you control. Managing them deliberately is the whole job. Every context-management pattern in this library is an instance of it.
entries.whenToUse: Use it as a diagnostic when output quality drops and the cause is unclear. Ask "what is in the window right now, and does it deserve to be?" That is faster than most debugging. The answer is usually that something large and no longer relevant is still there. Use it to choose between patterns that look interchangeable, such as reset versus compact or delegate versus read. Framing them as operations on one budget makes the choice concrete. Use it to introduce someone to this library's context-management section. It is the sentence the rest hangs from.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it as an answer. "Manage your context" is true and useless. The value lies in the specific patterns below it. A note like this one earns its place by pointing at them, not by restating the principle. Do not use it to explain away failures that are not context failures. A wrong approach, a missing test, or a bad model choice is not a context problem just because context is what you can see. And do not over-apply the "only lever" claim. It is scoped to using models, not building them.
entries.drawbacks: It is a frame, and frames are unfalsifiable in a comfortable way. Any failure can be narrated as a context failure after the fact. That makes the discipline feel more explanatory than it is. The "only lever" formulation overstates by design. Tool design, verification, and model choice are levers too. Taking it literally leads to tuning context when the real problem is that nothing checks the work. It also has no concrete advice of its own, so a team can agree with it completely and change nothing.

entries.name: Context File
entries.summary: A context file carries durable repository facts an agent cannot cheaply infer: commands, conventions, gotchas, boundaries, and pointers to deeper material. Keep it small enough to be read and specific enough to change behavior.
entries.whenToUse: Use it in any repository a coding agent will touch more than once. It pays off fastest in codebases with non-obvious build steps, unusual conventions ("we use pnpm, not npm"; "migrations are generated, never hand-edited"), monorepos where packages have different rules, and teams where several people run agents and want consistent behavior. It is the right home for one-line facts that apply every session. Anything procedural or occasional belongs in a skill or rule.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it as a linter: "Never send an LLM to do a linter's job" (HumanLayer). Do not use it for hard prohibitions. It is advisory. A `PreToolUse` hook or `permissions.deny` is the enforcement layer. Do not inline architecture overviews or file trees the agent can derive by reading code. The ETH Zurich study below found repository overviews "are not helpful". And do not auto-generate the file and forget it. In that same study, LLM-generated context files performed slightly worse than none.
entries.drawbacks: - **Measured efficacy**: The earlier percentage summary mixed an initial paper with practitioner interpretation. Use the versioned assessment in [[AGENTS.md Convention#Evidence Assessment]]. A small observed improvement is not automatically a statistically supported benefit.
related: Project Instructions, Rules, and Repository Memory

entries.name: Context Reset
entries.summary: Throw the context window away on purpose. Start a fresh agent that carries only a structured handoff. This is the primitive underneath Ralph, shift handoffs, and relay chains. Anthropic found it necessary because compaction alone was not enough.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when the window has filled with material that is no longer load-bearing: completed exploration, failed approaches, verbose tool output. Use it when compaction produces summaries you do not trust, the condition the harness work responded to. Always use it between unrelated tasks. Use it after two failed corrections on the same issue, when the context is working against you. Make it the default in unattended runs, since no one is there to notice degradation.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it mid-task when the accumulated reasoning is the asset. A deep debugging session where the trail matters is better served by [[Stop Hook Loop]]. Do not use it when durable state is incomplete. The reset will silently drop whatever you failed to write down, so fix the writing first. Do not use it so often that re-orientation dominates. Every reset pays a fixed cost to re-read and rebuild understanding. On short tasks that cost exceeds the degradation it avoids.
entries.drawbacks: Everything not written down is lost, and the loss is invisible. Nothing errors. The new agent simply does not know. Re-orientation is repeated work at every boundary. Constraints are the most common casualty, because they feel like background rather than state. Over-resetting produces an agent that never builds enough understanding to be useful. That looks like a model problem. It is a scheduling problem. The motivating evidence is also model-specific. A behavior seen in one model is not a permanent property of all of them, so "reset because compaction is insufficient" may not survive a model change.

entries.name: Convergence Loop
entries.summary: Convergence Loop turns a written desired state into a repeated gap check. Assess. Implement only the delta. Run checks. Stop when the gap inventory is empty or the bounded loop stalls.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when the desired state can be written down completely enough to check. Examples: a feature spec with enumerated requirements and acceptance scenarios, a migration with a target API, a port with a reference implementation to diff against (Anthropic's cosmology solver used the CLASS reference as a "test oracle" and the criterion "0.1% accuracy across the entire parameter range"). Use it after a first implementation pass to find what was stubbed, skipped, or contradicted. The converge step is a gap audit, and Anthropic's evaluator caught exactly this class of bug ("Rectangle fill tool only places tiles at drag start/end points instead of filling the region"). Use it when humans want to steer by editing the spec, not the code. Delimarsky's line is "your primary role is to steer; the coding agent does the bulk of the writing."
entries.whenNotToUse: Don't use it when the desired state is aesthetic or subjective. "Make it good" cannot be reconciled. Don't use it for exploratory work where the spec is still being discovered. Converging against a wrong spec produces confident, complete, wrong software (Huntley found a duplicated keyword definition in his language spec only after a month of loops). Don't run it unbounded. Without a cap and a "gaps not decreasing" check, the loop oscillates, particularly across fresh contexts that "retry the same dead end more than once" ([futureagi](https://futureagi.com/blog/loop-engineering/ralph-loop/)). And avoid letting one context both assess and implement. A worker "grading its own homework gives itself an A every time" ([lukasgrigis.dev](https://lukasgrigis.dev/blog/ralph-loop/)).
entries.drawbacks:
**Garbage in, converged out.** The loop converges on the spec as written. Spec errors "propagate significantly" (Huntley). Addy Osmani says "writing specs that survive contact with an autonomous executor" is the skill that is appreciating, and it is "harder than doing the work yourself" ([addyosmani.com](https://addyosmani.com/blog/long-running-agents/)).

**Assessment blind spots.** The converge template limits its scan to files named in the plan and tasks plus keyword matches. Anything outside that scope is invisible. Anthropic's evaluator could not see native browser alert modals, so modal-dependent features stayed buggy.

**Oscillation and thrash.** Fixing one gap can open another (a `contradicts` on requirement A caused by satisfying B). Nothing in the pattern guarantees monotone progress. The guard is an iteration cap and a check that the gap count is falling.

**Reward hacking the predicate.** If "converged" depends on tests, the shortest path is weakening tests. Every serious implementation forbids it explicitly ("It is unacceptable to remove or edit tests" in Anthropic's harness; "Do NOT delete or weaken tests" in practitioner prompts). Anthropic added a "test ratchet."

**Cost of repeated full assessments.** Each converge pass re-reads the spec, plan, tasks, and relevant code. On large features that is a substantial token bill per cycle, on top of the implement pass. HN's `roughly` estimated the last 30% of a project at "several hundred dollars per run" with harnesses like this ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46081704)).

**No published benchmarks for the loop itself.** The converge command shipped in mid-2026. No controlled study of implement/converge cycles was found. The evidence is Spec Kit's design, Anthropic's harness reports, and the refinement papers.

entries.name: Dark Factory
entries.summary: Agents write, test, and ship production code. No human writes or reviews the code. Oversight moves entirely to specifications, acceptance scenarios, and production telemetry. The factory inherits the quality of its test oracle, exactly.
entries.whenToUse: Use it where the oracle is strong and the domain is closed. Examples: well-specified transformations, generated clients from a schema, migrations with mechanical equivalence checks, high-volume low-novelty work where every acceptance criterion is executable. Use it where telemetry can detect the failures that matter, meaning failures show up in production signals and not only in a reviewer's judgment. Use it where a shipped defect has bounded cost and recovery is fast.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it where correctness is a matter of judgment, not assertion. That covers security boundaries, access control, anything with a regulatory or safety dimension, and anything where the failure mode is subtle wrongness, not a crash. Do not use it when the same agents wrote the tests and the code. Then the oracle and the optimizer share a blind spot. Do not use it when production failures are expensive, irreversible, or slow to detect. Telemetry is a lagging sensor, and "we noticed within the hour" is not the same as "we caught it in review." And do not adopt it incrementally by removing review and promising to build the preconditions later. That ordering is the failure mode, not a migration path.
entries.drawbacks: Oracle quality is the single point of failure, and it fails silently and at scale. The accountability gap is structural. The source poses it as "built by agents, tested by agents, trusted by whom?" and notes that responsible humans "can't appeal to the engineer who wrote this had a reason." Skill atrophy is a long-term organizational risk. Engineers who debug specifications, not code, become fragile during an outage, when the answer is not in the specification. The preconditions are expensive, so the realistic failure is adopting the label without the substrate. Removing review is a one-line policy change. Building the oracle, simulation, and telemetry that justify it is a program of work.

entries.name: Delegation Chain
entries.summary: An anti-pattern. Subagents inherit their parent's credentials and permission mode, but not the parent's intent. Authority widens silently with every link. One approval at the top authorizes actions nobody evaluated three levels down.
entries.whenToUse: Never deliberately. This is a failure mode. The useful inversion is knowing when you are exposed to it: whenever an agent can spawn another agent, whenever a lead runs with permissions broadened for its own task, and whenever a tool result or message from one agent becomes the prompt for another. Treat those three conditions as the trigger to apply the mitigations below.
entries.whenNotToUse: Not applicable. Delegation is safe in any one of these cases: each link's authority is explicitly narrower than its parent's, the chain is one level deep, the subagent is read-only, or the actions at the bottom of the chain are tier-1 actions under [[Permission Tiers]] regardless of who requested them.
entries.drawbacks: Intent degrades multiplicatively while authority stays constant. That is the core defect. Blast radius is invisible at the point of approval: the human approving a review cannot see that three links later something will write to a database. Auditing is hard because each action looks legitimate in isolation. Log review does not surface the problem. Only the chain does. Prompt injection composes with it badly: content read by a deep subagent can steer an agent that holds the full inherited credential set. The failure is also silent, which is the worst property. Nothing errors, nothing prompts, and the incident is discovered afterwards.

entries.name: Documentation-Driven Handoff
entries.summary: Documentation-Driven Handoff makes research and plans durable interfaces between people, sessions, and agents. The file is the handoff. The chat is only where you negotiated it.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for multi-week features and brownfield codebases, where the expensive part is understanding, not typing. It suits teams where several people and agents touch the same system and a chat transcript is not a shareable artifact. It fits any workflow that already splits research, planning and implementation across sessions ([[Research Plan Implement]], [[Shift-Worker Handoff]]). Use it for knowledge the code cannot express: rationale, rejected alternatives, operational quirks, "what talks to what and why". Karpathy's "the tedious part of maintaining a knowledge base is not the reading or the thinking—it's the bookkeeping" is the signal. If bookkeeping is what stops you documenting, an agent can do it.
entries.whenNotToUse: Skip it for throwaway prototypes and one-session tasks. Skip documentation that duplicates what the code or git history already says (the ETH AGENTS.md study found repository overviews unhelpful; Claude Code's auto memory skips derivable facts). Skip it where nobody will curate: agent-written documentation without human review accumulates confident errors. Do not point the agent at a large wiki wholesale. Load by pointer, or you recreate context rot.
entries.drawbacks:
- **Stale or wrong documentation is worse than none.** Liu et al.'s finding that models "perform better on shuffled haystacks than logically coherent ones" and the AGENTS.md study's cost numbers both warn that more prose is not free. A wrong research doc "cascades" (HumanLayer's own framing).
- **Bookkeeping drift.** Without a lint pass, wikis accumulate contradictions and orphan pages. Karpathy makes lint an explicit workflow for this reason.
- **Human bottleneck.** HN on ACE-FCA: "if a developer is working... with a bunch of agents, they are always going to be the bottleneck". Reading every research doc is real work.
- **Determinism illusion.** "Non-determinism is orthogonal to probability of being correct" (maltalex). Treating specs as the source of truth assumes an implementer that follows them.
- **Duplication with existing systems.** Issue trackers, ADR folders and wikis already exist in most orgs. An agent-specific documentation tree can fork the truth. One remedy on HN: make the GitHub issue "just a link to the md file in the repo".
- **Privacy and sprawl** when transcripts are ingested wholesale (see the memory-tool debates in [[Memory Bank]]).

entries.name: Evaluator-Optimizer
entries.summary: Evaluator-Optimizer separates making a candidate from judging it. The evaluator needs a rubric and evidence. The optimizer gets bounded chances to respond.
entries.whenToUse:
Use it when the quality bar is real but not fully mechanisable: API design consistency, readability, matching a spec's intent, security posture, test quality, translation fidelity. Anthropic's two-part test is that "human feedback can improve LLM responses" and "the model can provide such feedback itself." In coding agents the sweet spot combines the judge with hard signals. The evaluator runs the tests or drives the browser, then applies judgment on top. That is exactly how Anthropic's evaluator agent works.

It is also the right pattern for long unattended runs, where the producer will otherwise drift into self-congratulation. Anthropic's harness team found a separate skeptical evaluator was "essential" to keep a multi-hour build honest.
entries.whenNotToUse:
Do not use it when the criteria can be a command. If `pnpm test` answers the question, an LLM judge adds cost and noise. Use a [[Verification Loop]].

Do not use a same-context self-review and call it evaluation. Song's Cross-Context Review study found that reviewing twice in the same session gave "zero benefit" (F1 21.7% for a second self-review versus 24.6% for the first, and 28.6% for a separate-session review) ([Cross-Context Review](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.12123)). If you cannot afford a separate context, the pattern degrades to Self-Refine, whose limits are well documented.

Be cautious with subjective or style-heavy criteria, where judge bias dominates. Moon et al. show LLM judges give "inflated or unfairly low scores" to semantically identical code based on variable names, comments and formatting. The bias persists "even when models are prompted to generate test cases before scoring" ([Don't Judge Code by Its Cover](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16222)).

Skip it for trivial edits. A loop that costs 2–5 extra calls per change is wasteful on a rename.
entries.drawbacks:
**Lenient or sycophantic judges.** Anthropic's harness post reports agents "confidently praising" mediocre work, and says even a separated evaluator "remains inclined toward lenient judgments." Augment's guide collects the research. Models show self-preference driven by "familiarity bias." They "fix identical errors presented as external input but fail on their own output," and "leniency is especially visible on incorrect code" ([Adversarial Code Review](https://www.augmentcode.com/guides/adversarial-code-review)).

**Over-critical judges and over-engineering.** The opposite failure is equally common. Anthropic's best-practices page warns: "A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound, because that is what it was asked to do. Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering: extra abstraction layers, defensive code, and tests for cases that can't happen" ([Best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices)). Vincent's competitive "whoever finds the most serious issues gets five points" prompt is powerful for exactly the reason it is dangerous.

**Ping-pong loops.** On HN, `daxfohl` reported that adding QA/verification agents often means "rather than converging on a solution, they just get all out of whack... far more frequently it'll get stuck in a loop" ([HN: Effective harnesses](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46081704)). Without a hard iteration cap and a stable rubric, generator and evaluator can oscillate between two acceptable designs indefinitely.

**Judge bias on surface features.** Moon et al. found six bias types across five languages. A judge can be swayed by confident comments or nice variable names on wrong code.

**Cost.** Each iteration is at least two model calls. A grounded evaluator that drives a browser costs far more. Anthropic's full three-agent harness cost "$200" and "6 hours" versus "$9" and "20 minutes" for a solo run on the same task. On HN, `CharlesW` argued a fresh reviewer instance is "expensive" and unnecessary because "LLMs have no problem throwing 'them 5 minutes ago' under the bus when asked to review something 'skeptically'." `SmithersBot` countered that "a fresh instance doing the reviewing, not the one that did the work" is what reduces bias ([HN thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48291016)). The Cross-Context Review numbers side with SmithersBot.

**Multi-agent debate is not a free upgrade.** Zhang et al.'s position paper found that across 9 benchmarks and 4 models, debate "often fail[s] to outperform simple single-agent baselines such as Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency" while costing far more. Heterogeneity of models is the one lever they found consistently helpful ([Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08788)).

entries.name: Execution Feedback Repair
entries.summary: Execution Feedback Repair lets the compiler, test runner, or program report what actually happened. The agent then uses that verbatim signal to guide the next repair.
entries.whenToUse: Use it whenever a machine can say yes or no: compiling code, running tests, type-checking, linting, executing a script against a fixture, comparing a screenshot to a design. It is the cheapest reliability gain available and the precondition for unattended runs. Prefer the most specific feedback you can get. A failing assertion with expected/actual is worth more than "exit code 1." A stack trace is worth more than a log line.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it when the check is slow and flaky (a 40-minute integration suite with 2% nondeterminism). The loop will chase phantoms. Run a fast subset in the loop and the full suite once at the end. Do not use it when the only executable check is one the agent can edit, unless tests are protected (see [[Test Tampering]]). Do not use it as a substitute for understanding. An agent that "fixes" a null check per failing test can make everything pass while the design is wrong. SpecBench describes this over-fitting failure ([arXiv 2605.21384](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.21384v1)).
entries.drawbacks: The agent may satisfy the check without satisfying the intent. It may hardcode outputs, special-case test inputs, or edit the test (ImpossibleBench measured GPT-5 exploiting conflicting tests 76% of the time on one split; see [[Test Tampering]]). Feedback that is summarized, not quoted, drifts the goal. Slow checks make the loop expensive. Anthropic's Claude Code documentation advises "prefer running single tests, and not the whole test suite." Error output can flood the context (a 5,000-line stack trace), which is why tool-output truncation is part of [[Agent-Computer Interface]] design. An unbounded loop can thrash. Claude Code's 8-block Stop-hook limit and the paper's fixed iteration budget exist for that reason.

entries.name: Explore Plan Code Commit
entries.summary: Explore Plan Code Commit is a gate. Understand the code. Write the plan. Implement against it. Commit only after the named checks pass.
entries.whenToUse: Anthropic is precise: planning "is most useful when you're uncertain about the approach, when the change modifies multiple files, or when you're unfamiliar with the code being modified". Use it to onboard to a codebase, for cross-cutting features (auth, billing, migrations), and for any task where the wrong architecture would be expensive to unwind. It also fits a strong planner model paired with a cheaper implementer ([[Architect-Editor Split]]).
entries.whenNotToUse: "For tasks where the scope is clear and the fix is small (like fixing a typo, adding a log line, or renaming a variable) ask Claude to do it directly... If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan." Skip it for exploratory hacking where you want to see the model's interpretation first. Skip it, per HN critics of Tane's post, when experienced developers face small tasks: "all this planning and checking and prompting and orchestrating is far more work than just writing the code yourself" (jamesmcq, [HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47106686)).
entries.drawbacks:
- **Overhead on small tasks** ("Plan mode is useful, but also adds overhead").
- **Plans drift from reality.** Mo Bitar's critique of spec-first work: "Detailed upfront specs don't work because software development is inherently iterative and involves continuous discovery" ([atmoio](https://atmoio.substack.com/p/after-two-years-of-vibecoding-im)).
- **Shallow exploration.** Tane says you must ask for reading "deeply" and "in great details" or the agent skims.
- **Plan-quality ceiling.** A reviewer who does not know the codebase approves bad plans. The HN thread on ACE-FCA argued the human reviewer "are always going to be the bottleneck".
- **Long single sessions.** Tane runs research, plan and implementation in "one unbroken context window", which conflicts with [[Context Compaction]] advice. Others in the thread use plan files so they can `/clear` between phases ("The plan document and todo are an artifact of context size limits", renewiltord).
- **Implementation ignores the plan.** Without a verification step ("review the diff against PLAN.md"), the plan is only advice, like everything else in context.

entries.name: Facts-Driven Development
entries.summary: Replace the spec document with a list of atomic claims. Each claim can carry a shell command that proves it. Project status stops being something you assert. It becomes something you run.
entries.whenToUse: Use it where an architecture document keeps going stale. That is the failure it is built for. Use it for cross-cutting conventions that tests do not assert—which library is used for what, which patterns are forbidden, which decisions were made and must hold. Use it as a fast orientation artifact for a fresh agent. A checked fact sheet is a summary you can trust. A written one is not. When requirements are detailed, use it alongside a spec, not instead of one.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it as a test suite. The checks are structural and shallow by design, and the obvious trap is treating a passing fact check as correctness. Do not use it for detailed functional requirements, which need real assertions, not greps. Do not write facts with expensive checks. The whole point is that verification is one fast command. Be careful with grep-based checks in particular. They break on refactors that change nothing semantically, and those failures teach people to ignore the tool.
entries.drawbacks: The checks are shallow, and shallow checks passing is the most comfortable kind of wrong. Grep-based verification is brittle against refactors. False failures erode trust in the tool faster than real failures build it. Facts without commands are just a document, with every problem a document has. The format belongs to one project, with no ecosystem behind it. And there is a real risk of encoding what is easy to check instead of what matters. The same pull produces test suites full of getters.

entries.name: Fault Localization First
entries.summary: Fault Localization First treats “where is the bug?” as a deliverable. It comes before “what patch should I write?” Reproduction, search, and coverage narrow the edit surface.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for bug reports and issues in codebases the agent does not already have in context. Use it when the symptom is far from the cause (a UI error caused by a serializer). Use it in large repositories, where an unstructured agent reads the wrong files first and anchors on them. Use SBFL whenever a failing test exists or can be written cheaply. It is nearly free and turns "which of 400 files" into "which of 12 lines." Use debate-style multiple localizations when the first guess has been wrong before.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not add a localization phase when the location is given (the issue names the file and line, or the diff is one obvious change). Claude Code's documentation says if you "could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan." Do not rely on SBFL when the test suite is small or when the failing test exercises everything (coverage is uninformative). Do not let localization become open-ended exploration. Anthropic's "infinite exploration" failure pattern is an agent asked to "investigate" without scope, reading hundreds of files.
entries.drawbacks: One-shot localization cannot recover. If the funnel picks the wrong files, the patch phase fails silently (Agentless's own limitation). SBFL needs executable tests with coverage instrumentation, which many real repositories cannot provide quickly. LLM localization over skeletons is fooled by misleading names, and by symptoms that live in configuration or data, not code. Debate-based localization is expensive (see [[Multi-Agent Debate]]). And a strict "no edits during localization" rule can block the cheap experiment (add a print, run once) that would localize the bug fastest.

entries.name: Feature Chat per Task
entries.summary: One session per change, like one branch per change. At the end, have the model write a summary document and the opening prompt for the next session. What survives is curated, not accumulated.
entries.whenToUse: Use it as the default rhythm for feature work, which is what it was described for. Use it as soon as a session has absorbed a failed approach you no longer want influencing the work. Always use it after two failed corrections on the same issue. Use it when work will run in parallel, since scoped sessions are the precondition. Use it when you want a written trail per change. The summary step gives you one for free.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it mid-task, where re-establishing context costs more than carrying it. Do not use it for deep debugging where the accumulated trail is the asset—[[Stop Hook Loop]] serves that case. Do not skip the exit ritual. A session closed without a summary is context destroyed, not curated, and the pattern's whole value is in that difference. Do not let summaries pile up unmaintained, or the documentation index becomes one more thing that is stale and confidently wrong.
entries.drawbacks: Re-orientation costs something every session. Summaries are model-written, so they are selective in ways nobody audits. The omitted thing is invisible by construction. The next-session prompt carries the departing session's misunderstandings forward in a confident frame. That can spread an error more effectively than raw context would. Boundaries are a judgment call, and a "feature" that turns out to be three features makes a session that should have been split. The accumulating summary documents need maintenance they rarely get.

entries.name: Fresh-Agent Chaining
entries.summary: A chain of fresh agents. Each works only while its context is still cheap. At the token budget, it writes a deliberately tiny handoff and passes the baton. The next agent reads the plan from disk and continues.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for work that exceeds one context window and has a plan you can write down in advance. The plan is what makes a fresh agent viable. Use it when compaction produces bad results, since this pattern is the alternative, not a tuning of it. Use it for long unattended runs where you want every agent in the early, accurate part of its window. Use it when the work is phased and sequential, which is what the master plan encodes.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for exploratory work where no plan can be written. The master plan is load-bearing, and a fresh agent with no plan is just an agent with amnesia. Do not use it when the work needs accumulated context. A long debugging session where the trail matters is better served by [[Stop Hook Loop]]. Do not rely on the self-reported completion signal for anything that matters; pair it with a predicate. Do not use it where re-reading the plan and re-orienting on every handoff costs more than the degradation it avoids. That is the case for short tasks.
entries.drawbacks: Every handoff loses something, and the loss is invisible. The forty-line cap guarantees that most of what an agent learned does not survive. Re-orientation is repeated work: each agent re-reads the plan and rebuilds its understanding, a fixed cost paid per link. The plan is a single point of failure, since a wrong or incomplete plan misleads every agent in the chain identically. The completion signal is model-controlled and unverified. A constraint stated once at the start of the chain is gone by the third agent unless it is pinned. That is exactly the failure [[Constraint Pinning]] measures.

entries.name: Fresh-Context Reviewer
entries.summary: Fresh-Context Reviewer hands a change to a reviewer who has not seen the implementation conversation. Review is separate from the author’s explanation, but the reviewer still has access to requirements, callers, and tests. Whether this separation improves defect detection needs evidence.
entries.whenToUse:
Use it as a bounded extra check for consequential changes. It helps most when implementation history is long or acceptance tests leave important behavior unexamined. Give the reviewer a narrow question it can investigate. "Does logout invalidate an in-flight token refresh?" beats "find anything wrong."

Start with one reviewer. Add specialists when there are distinct unresolved questions and someone can adjudicate their output. Choose [[Multi-Model Cross-Check]] as a measured treatment when a different model might cover missed defect classes. Model diversity is not independence by definition.
entries.whenNotToUse:
Do not replace executable checks or needed domain review with a reviewer verdict. Do not run repeated rounds because an agent always produces another suggestion. Trivial changes may not justify another session.

Do not remove the source context needed to validate a finding. Do not preload the whole repository by default either. [[Research Sources#S19 Pull-request review benchmark]] reports worse results from expanded static context. It does not test targeted agent retrieval.

Avoid unattended review loops without cost, round, and escalation limits. Product pricing and review triggers change. Consult current documentation before configuring recurring runs.
entries.drawbacks:
**Noise and false positives**: [Practitioner reports in the same discussion](https://www.reddit.com/r/ClaudeCode/comments/1tdvnnt/critique_my_workflow/) disagree about whether automated findings are useful or petty. An always-commenting reviewer can become a bottleneck. Track supported material defects and adjudication effort, not comment volume.

**Over-reporting by construction**: Demanding a minimum number of findings rewards speculation. Require concrete effects on correctness, security, or stated requirements. Zero findings is a valid result. A very restrictive reviewer, though, may miss genuine defects. Evaluate precision and recall together. Neither verbose nor terse output is better by default.

**Shared blind spots**: Separate contexts can still share model weaknesses, missing requirements, and misleading tests. Evidence from general reasoning debate does not directly prove code-review effectiveness. [[Multi-Model Cross-Check]] treats context reset, model substitution, and debate as different interventions.

**Surface bias**: [Research on code judges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16222) examines how surface features affect judgments. Code that looks clean still needs behavioral evidence before a review can be trusted.

**Cost and latency**: Count every reviewer, candidate-verification pass, rerun, and human disposition. A multi-agent service and a single local reviewer have different costs. Measure the actual configuration.

**Review bottleneck moves to humans**: [Toub’s maintained-repository report](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/ten-months-with-cca-in-dotnet-runtime/) counted 16.5 versus 12.4 total comments per merged agent versus human pull request. The count includes bot messages and agent replies, across different task populations. It is neither human review time nor a controlled overhead estimate. [[Research Sources#S23 Maintainer review and repair workload]] records the distinction.

**Output categories are not defect labels**: The [AI-to-AI review study](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.21311v1) finds different comment-category mixes across authoring agents. It cannot separate code differences from reviewer calibration. It cannot establish correctness from review activity. See [[Research Sources#S20 AI-to-AI review prevalence]].
