entries.name: Git Context Controller
entries.summary: Treat the agent's memory like a git repository: COMMIT milestones, BRANCH to explore an alternative, MERGE what worked, and retrieve history hierarchically. Reported over 80% on SWE-bench Verified.
entries.whenToUse: As shipped practice, not yet. The paper describes a research system with a planned release. Apply the idea by hand in two situations. When exploring alternatives, branch the durable state, not the context: commit, copy the plan and progress files, explore on a git branch, and discard or merge based on the outcome. When memory must be reused across agents or sessions, prefer a structured, addressable store over a transcript. [[Issue-Tracker-as-Memory]] makes the same argument from the practitioner side.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not assume the reported numbers transfer to your setup. SWE-bench tasks are bounded and well-specified in ways real work is not. Do not build this yourself for linear work, where branching buys nothing over a [[Progress File]]. Do not assume merge is easy. Combining divergent reasoning trajectories is harder than merging text, and this note did not examine the paper's treatment of it.
entries.drawbacks: It is a research system, and the practitioner ecosystem has nothing equivalent. Merging reasoning trajectories is the hard operation and the likeliest to go wrong, since two branches can each be coherent and jointly contradictory. Versioned memory is more machinery than most work needs. Benchmark results on bounded tasks are weak evidence for open-ended work. Branching also invites a specific failure: branches never merged or discarded, which leave state that looks authoritative and describes an abandoned path.

entries.name: Goal Loop
entries.summary: You state a success condition. A separate evaluator re-checks it after every turn. The agent keeps working until the condition resolves or a try cap fires. The actor does not decide when it is finished.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when done is verifiable and you can state it: the suite is green, the migration reports zero remaining rows, the endpoint returns the expected shape, the screenshot matches. Use it for unattended runs. The documentation names it as one of two mechanisms that let a run finish correctly without you. Use it when you would otherwise have to watch. That is most of the value: the evaluator does the attention you were spending.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it when you cannot state the goal verifiably. A vague goal gives the evaluator nothing to check, so it approximates. That is [[LLM-as-Judge]] with extra cost. Do not use it for exploratory work with no fixed target. Do not use it without a try cap. The documented guidance pairs the goal with a maximum, and a goal loop on an impossible task is an expensive infinite loop. Prefer a deterministic gate where one exists. If `npm test` decides the question, a `Stop` hook is cheaper and cannot be talked into anything.
entries.drawbacks: An evaluator is a model, so it can be wrong in both directions. It can declare success on work that does not satisfy the condition. It can also refuse to resolve a goal that has been met, which burns the entire try budget. Per-turn evaluation costs tokens every turn, real overhead on long runs. Compaction is a documented hazard. This library's research records "compaction amnesia" reports for a goal that outlives the context needed to judge it, leaving an evaluator checking the condition against a summary. A vaguely stated goal turns the whole mechanism into an opinion poll. That is worse than no gate, because it looks like one.

entries.name: GSD
entries.summary: GSD is a compact spec-to-task workflow. It turns a vague feature into written intent, an executable plan, and a sequence of small verified changes.
entries.whenToUse: GSD works best on multi-file projects that span days or weeks. The main danger there is that a single long session slowly forgets what it decided and starts producing worse code. The Pulumi comparison of Superpowers, GSD and GSTACK concluded that GSD "shines" on work "spanning days/weeks" and "marathon sessions", precisely because "the orchestrator's context window grows slowly and predictably" while every spawned agent starts fresh and scoped to one task ([Pulumi](https://www.pulumi.com/blog/claude-code-orchestration-frameworks/)). It also fits greenfield projects, where the interview and research waves produce a roadmap you would otherwise write by hand. And it fits developers who want an audit trail: every decision lands in a Markdown file and every task in its own commit.
entries.whenNotToUse: It is overkill for small changes. The same Pulumi comparison lists "small, quick changes" as where GSD struggles, since the overhead "feels excessive". The beginner guide's own caveats say tiny tasks are better served by a direct prompt. It is a poor fit on a low-tier plan. Users report roughly four tokens of orchestration for every token of code written, and the guide recommends Pro/Max tiers. Finally, an HN commenter with long experience of the tool reported that as projects get large "GSD can't manage to deliver working code reliably" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47420059)). For large brownfield systems, expect to supplement its verification with real integration tests.
entries.drawbacks:
Token cost is the most common complaint. The beginner guide records a reported 4:1 ratio of orchestration tokens to code tokens and warns that the $20 tier is not enough ([dev.to](https://dev.to/alikazmidev/the-complete-beginners-guide-to-gsd-get-shit-done-framework-for-claude-code-24h0)). In the 473-point HN thread of March 2026, MeetingsBrowser wrote that GSD "absolutely tore through tokens... I don't normally hit my session limits, but hit the 5-hour limits in ~30 minutes and my weekly limits by Tuesday", gtirloni estimated "they burn 10x more tokens" versus plain Plan mode "for no discernable benefit", and yolonir called it "a highly overengineered piece of software that unfortunately does not get shit done, burns limits and takes ages while doing so" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47417804)). The same thread has the opposite testimony. yoaviram had "been using GSD extensively over the past 3 months... GSD consistently gets me 95% of the way there on complex tasks" and shipped a SaaS with it. Sceptics repeatedly say the volume claims ("250K lines of code in less than a month") are a cost, not a result. dhorthy said it is "very hard... to take seriously any system that is not proven for shipping production code in complex codebases", and CuriouslyC argued "your code quality is a function of validation time... which isn't increased by better orchestration." Verbosity is a related gripe. One HN user noted they "actually like the verbosity" but framed it as something others complain about.

Verification is weaker than it looks. HN user DIVx0 reported that on a project that grew large, agents left orphaned code and "won't wire them up properly because verification stages use simple lexical tools." They abandoned Markdown as the source of truth for a property-graph-based system ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47420059)). The codecentric review reached a similar conclusion from the design side. GSD "might not go deep enough in some places and lack detail in others" and is best suited to "small to medium-sized projects".

Skipping `/gsd:discuss-phase` produces assumption-driven plans and long fix cycles. Running on an existing codebase without `/gsd:map-codebase` leads to pattern conflicts with the existing code ([dev.to](https://dev.to/alikazmidev/the-complete-beginners-guide-to-gsd-get-shit-done-framework-for-claude-code-24h0)). GSD also concentrates all decision-making in Markdown files that the agents write themselves. Documentation drift is a real risk on long projects.

Governance risk turned out to be the biggest failure mode of all. The original repository is archived. The npm packages under the original name went unmaintained. Users have had to migrate to GSD Core or community forks. An HN user asked of a GSD-built project, "did you test it properly or just shrug?" It is a reminder that a heavy process does not by itself guarantee quality ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46746231)).

entries.name: Gstack
entries.summary: Gstack packages a product sprint as specialist skills: clarify, plan, build, review, test in a browser, ship, and reflect. Artifacts connect the stages.
entries.whenToUse: gstack fits founders and small product teams shipping web products. The browser-based `/qa` and the deploy/canary skills close the loop that code-only frameworks leave open. Pulumi's verdict is that it "shines when building products with multi-perspective needs; browser-based QA" and is the pick "if shipping a product (not just infrastructure)". The plan-review skills are useful even alone, as a structured way to settle scope before building.
entries.whenNotToUse: It is "overkill for pure provisioning" and infrastructure work, where "extra roles add overhead" (Pulumi). Backend-only or library projects get little from `/qa`, `/design-*` and `/canary`. Teams uneasy with telemetry or with a YC-branded toolkit in their workflow should read the egress log design before adopting. dmppch's caution also applies: the "git-clone-and-copy install model works great solo," but keeping 23 skills composable and in sync across many projects and people is real maintenance.
entries.drawbacks: Twenty-three roles is a lot of ceremony. The same "enterprise theatre" critique aimed at [[BMAD Method]] applies, and it is easy to skip stages quietly. Autonomy across ship and deploy magnifies mistakes. An HN commenter recounted a Claude Code agent stuck "in a 70-minute loop, repeatedly injecting a staging URL into a production config file" with "exit code 0 (all green)", and argued that "velocity without constraints is terrifying" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47355173)). gstack's `/land-and-deploy` is exactly the kind of skill that needs hard guardrails. The productivity claims are self-reported and contested in the LOC-inflation debate. Independent critical reviews are scarce. Most coverage is enthusiastic YouTube walkthroughs.

entries.name: Hooks and Guardrails
entries.summary: Hooks and Guardrails move repeatable safety rules from memory into lifecycle events. A hook should make the safe path automatic and the unsafe path observable.
entries.whenToUse: "Use hooks for actions that must happen every time with zero exceptions" (Anthropic). Concretely: formatting and linting after every edit; blocking writes to secrets, lockfiles, migrations and generated code; forcing tests before commit or before the turn ends; logging every tool call for audit; injecting context after compaction; desktop notifications when the agent needs input; classifying dangerous shell commands when running with broad permissions. Any rule you have written in CLAUDE.md more than once and still see violated is a hook candidate.
entries.whenNotToUse: Judgment calls that depend on intent ("is this refactor in scope?") belong in prompts, plan review or an agent-based hook, not a shell script. Blocking mid-plan has a cost. Shankar found "Blocking an agent mid-plan confuses or even 'frustrates' it," so he blocks at submit time, not on every edit. Slow hooks on hot events (a full test suite on every `Edit`) make sessions crawl. Hooks also run with your privileges. The same HN thread that praised them noted the security and complexity trade-off. Anthropic warns that multiple PreToolUse hooks rewriting the same input race non-deterministically.
entries.drawbacks:
- **Stop hooks are not absolute.** Claude Code caps consecutive blocks at 8, then "Claude keeps working instead of stopping, then ends the turn with a warning." A "Tell HN: Claude 4.7 is ignoring stop hooks" thread (109 points) described a test-gating stop hook being bypassed. One commenter found the actual bug ("The 'cat' command always exits with code 0. You need to exit with code 2"). Another argued that if the hook result arrives as a tool result, the model may be trained to discount it. An Anthropic engineer asked for `/feedback` reports ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47895029)). Silent misconfiguration (wrong exit code, non-executable script, JSON with no effect) is the most common failure.
- **Bypass mode breaks blocking.** The author of `nah` warns that with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, "hooks fire asynchronously—commands execute before nah can block them" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47343927), citing claude-code issue #20946).
- **Deny lists are a losing game.** "Even when you curate permissions, 200 IQ Opus can find a way around it. Maintaining a deny list is a fool's errand" (nah's README); a critic replied that a PreToolUse classifier "feels a bit like bolting the door and leaving all the windows open," because the model can write and execute a script.
- **Hook output is context.** Text a hook injects is "Summarized with the rest of the conversation" at compaction; only `SessionStart(compact)` hooks re-run.
- **Agent frustration / thrashing** when blocked repeatedly mid-task (Shankar).
- **Maintenance burden**: a growing pile of hooks becomes an undocumented policy engine. HN's m4r71n called hardcoded context rules "a maintenance nightmare" and asked for a DSL.

entries.name: Human-Gated Autonomy
entries.summary: Human-Gated Autonomy puts people at decisions whose consequences are hard to reverse, while permissions and sandboxes handle routine work inside the boundary.
entries.whenToUse:
Use it whenever an agent will run long enough that you would not read every prompt anyway. That is most real work: multi-file features, migrations, unattended runs, and anything parallel. Gating at the plan is cheapest when "you're uncertain about the approach, when the change modifies multiple files, or when you're unfamiliar with the code being modified" (Claude Code best practices). Gating at merge is mandatory when the action is irreversible or leaves your machine: push, deploy, delete, send, pay. The [Bounded Autonomy](https://aipatternbook.com/bounded-autonomy) examples show the shape: code generation and tests run autonomously, pull request drafting notifies, merging to main requires approval, production deploy is human-only, yielding "85% autonomous actions" with review time in minutes.

Use it especially for multi-agent setups. When one lead spawns many workers, per-action prompts "bubble up to the lead" and multiply; the [agent teams documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams) advises pre-approving common operations before spawning. The yolo-cage author's motivation was exactly this: "decision fatigue is a thing" once several agents are running, and a sandboxed agent with prompts off is safer than an exhausted human clicking yes.

Use it when you can make the autonomous region observable: checkpoints (`/rewind` restores code and conversation), git, test output, hooks that log. The gate only works if what arrives at it is inspectable.
entries.whenNotToUse:
Do not skip the per-action prompts on an unsandboxed machine with production credentials in the environment. The [nah thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47343927) has kate23_human's point that "read-only access to a repo can leak quite a bit depending on what's in the workspace" and dns_snek's bypass examples (overwrite source files, inject into `npm test`, use `PAGER` to spawn a shell); the consensus was "a truly adversarial agent needs a sandbox. It's a different threat model." Prompt-injected or misaligned agents are not stopped by an approval policy that trusts the agent's description of its own action.

Do not use plan gates for one-line changes. The documentation says so directly ("if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan"). And do not mistake a gate for a review: the [Human in the Loop](https://aipatternbook.com/human-in-the-loop) entry warns that "oversight without genuine engagement breeds rubber-stamping." Claude Code's agent-teams design shows how easily a gate becomes automatic: a teammate's plan approval request is granted "in the lead's session as soon as the request arrives, without the lead reviewing it."

Finally, do not bypass and then sit at the keyboard anyway. Bubblyworld's comment on Claude Composer, "Am I the only person who just runs claude code in yolo mode? The cost of configuring rules is worse than the cost of just telling Claude Code 'yes,'" is the honest description of what most people do with Manual mode, which is why the sandbox-plus-gates design exists.
entries.drawbacks:
Rubber-stamping at the gate. Approval fatigue moves rather than disappears. If the merge gate receives twenty pull requests a day, it degrades the same way per-tool prompts did. The Gas Town threads document the endpoint: throughput of "4000 lines of code per hour" with commenters asking who reads it.

Gates that bypass themselves. Auto mode falls back to prompting after repeated classifier blocks in interactive sessions, but in `-p` runs "the action doesn't run and Claude keeps working," so an unattended agent can route around a blocked action by trying alternatives. Cursor and Claude Code both describe agents removing obstacles to make tests pass. mceachen on HN: "There's a strong chance it will remove your web service auth filter chain to make an integration test pass."

Boundaries stated in chat are soft. The Claude Code documentation says a spoken boundary "can be lost if context compaction removes the message that stated it. For a hard guarantee, add a deny rule instead."

Bypass mode is still routinely used on host machines. The Docker-wrapper HN thread's verdict was dvanhggier's "More safe, but not completely safe. Maybe that's good enough?"; binwiederhier's "I think convenience wins." Anthropic's own list of what the classifier blocks includes "launching an autonomous agent loop that runs without human approval or a sandbox," an acknowledgement of how common it is. Claude Code refuses bypass as root and requires a one-time accept-responsibility dialog, but a container without network isolation still has your tokens in it.

Consistency objections. In the yolo-cage thread, one commenter argued the gate placement is incoherent: "if I didn't trust a human developer to run shell commands on the webserver... I wouldn't trust them to push code." Gating merge but not shell assumes review catches what the shell could do, which is only true if review is real.

Approval policies drift and need maintenance. The aipatternbook Approval Policy page lists calibration burden, policy drift between projects, and multi-agent scaling as ongoing costs. Bounded Autonomy adds that miscalibrated tiers "defeat the purpose" and that tiers cannot anticipate novel failure modes.

Delegation chains. Subagents and teammates inherit the lead's permission mode ("If the lead runs with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, all teammates do too"), so one bypass at the top removes every gate below it. The [Delegation Chain](https://aipatternbook.com/delegation-chain) antipattern describes 2–4-link chains producing credential exposure and production incidents "that exceed human authorization."

Note on sources: Reddit debates on YOLO mode were searched for but reddit.com was blocked for fetching in this session; the debates cited are from Hacker News. No YouTube video specifically about permission-mode design was identified in the searches run.

entries.name: Initializer Agent
entries.summary: A one-time agent run that builds the scaffolding every later run depends on: a launch script, a machine-readable feature list, a progress file, and a first commit. It writes no features itself.
entries.whenToUse: Use it before any unattended multi-session run: overnight [[Ralph Loop]] work, a [[Parallel Worktree Swarm]] where N agents need identical starting conditions, or a [[Task Queue Consumer]] setup that needs the queue to exist. Use it on a greenfield project, where there is no existing script or task list to inherit. Use it when several agents will run concurrently and inconsistent local setup would produce inconsistent results.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it in a mature repository that already has a start command, a test command, and an issue tracker. The initializer would re-derive things that exist, and may derive them differently. Do not use it for a single short task. Do not let the initializer write feature code. Once it does, its structural choices stop being reviewable in isolation, which was the whole benefit. And do not skip reviewing its output, because everything downstream inherits its mistakes silently.
entries.drawbacks: Its errors are systematic. A wrong `init.sh` breaks the entry smoke test for every later session. An incomplete feature list means the run ends believing it is done. An over-granular one means it never ends. The initializer runs once and unattended, so nobody notices until session five. The feature list is also a reward-hacking surface: an agent that can edit feature descriptions can make the remaining work disappear. That is why the harness forbids editing anything but the `passes` field (see [[Reward Hacking Guardrails]]). Finally, the pattern assumes greenfield. Pointed at an existing repository, it tends to produce a parallel, slightly wrong copy of conventions that were already there.

entries.name: Intent Compilation
entries.summary: Treat the specification as a source language, not a prompt. Write it in a structured, declarative form and compile it deterministically into code and tests. The unresolved problem is that the compiler is a language model, and a compiler has to be deterministic.
entries.whenToUse: Use it where the domain is narrow enough that a declarative specification really is complete: workflow definitions, data transformations, API surfaces, state machines, infrastructure. Deterministic generation from a specification already works there, usually under a different name. Use it when the same specification must serve both humans and machines, which is the family's genuine contribution. Use the deterministic-test-generation idea specifically, even without the code half. Tests generated mechanically from a specification are independent of the implementation in a way hand-written tests are not.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for open-ended application logic, where a specification complete enough to compile is longer and harder to write than the code. Do not use it where requirements change frequently, since recompilation churns everything downstream. Do not adopt it on the strength of the vision. The determinism requirement the proposals themselves state is not currently met by model-based generation. And be wary of the endpoint: a specification language expressive enough to compile arbitrary software is a programming language, and it will be a worse one than the ones that exist.
entries.drawbacks: The central unresolved problem is the determinism requirement colliding with the mechanism. Model-based generation is not deterministic, so today's compilable specs are compilable in aspiration. The expressiveness ceiling is the second problem: strict enough to compile means a programming language, and a new one with no ecosystem. Model-driven development's history is the third, and it is not a small objection. The approach has been tried at scale, and the failure was rigidity rather than tooling. [[Tessl]]'s independent assessment names the specific risk of the LLM version: you take on generated code's constraints without gaining reproducibility. And escape hatches break the model entirely, because the first hand-edit means the specification is no longer the source.

entries.name: Intentional Compaction
entries.summary: After each verified phase, fold the current status back into the plan file. Don't let it pile up in the conversation. The plan becomes a living document, and that makes the work resumable.
entries.whenToUse: Use it on phased work where each phase has a verification step. The technique was designed for that shape. Use it when the plan is the handoff medium, as in [[Research Plan Implement]] and [[Fresh-Agent Chaining]]. Use it before any deliberate [[Context Reset]], so the reset is safe. Use it when you want one file to answer both what is left and what happened, not two.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it on unverified work. The source states that condition, and it is what makes the artifact trustworthy. Do not use it when history matters more than current state. In an investigation, rejected hypotheses are the valuable output. Use an append-only [[Progress File]] there, because rewriting in place loses exactly those. Do not use it on unplanned or exploratory work, where there is no phase boundary. And do not let it replace commits. The plan says what was intended and done. Git says what changed.
entries.drawbacks: Rewriting in place loses history. The loss is usually a rejected approach, which the next agent will now retry. The step is manual, so it can be skipped, and the skip is silent. Nothing notices the plan is three phases stale until an agent reads it and acts on the wrong state. Folding status into a plan the agent may also edit lets it quietly revise the remaining work. That is the [[Test Ratchet]] problem applied to plans. And nobody audits what you chose to keep.

entries.name: Interactive Steering
entries.summary: Interactive Steering is the short feedback loop around an agent’s turn: interrupt a wrong direction early, queue precise context, and restart after repeated corrections.
entries.whenToUse: Use it in interactive sessions where you can watch: unfamiliar code, ambiguous requirements, or early in a project before CLAUDE.md and hooks have absorbed your preferences. Use it in the first few minutes of any long task, when a wrong turn is cheapest to catch ("Correct Claude as soon as you notice it going off track"). Also use it when the agent starts reading hundreds of files ("the infinite exploration") or editing the wrong area, or when you have a fact that saves it a detour ("the config is in `infra/`, not `config/`").
entries.whenNotToUse: Skip it on unattended and looped runs. There, replace steering with verification ([[Verification Loop]], [[Hooks and Guardrails]]) and gates ([[Human-Gated Autonomy]]). Skip it when it means micromanaging every step: Shrivu Shankar found that "Blocking an agent mid-plan confuses or even 'frustrates' it" and prefers gating at submit time ([sshh.io](https://blog.sshh.io/p/how-i-use-every-claude-code-feature)). Also skip it after two failed corrections on the same point. More steering is the wrong move. Restart.
entries.drawbacks:
- **No flow state for the human.** "I haven't been able to enter flow state like I can when I hand write code... it feels like a bicycle that just brakes abruptly every couple minutes. I stop, wait, review, prompt again" (Ask HN, 212 points, [HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48771515)).
- **Correction spirals.** Each correction adds failed-approach tokens. The documentation's two-strikes rule exists because the spiral degrades results.
- **Attention does not scale.** "I don't understand how you can have any meaningful supervising role over 10 things at once given the limits of human working memory" (tmerr on Cherny's parallel-session setup, [HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46470017)). Parallel agents push steering into plans and reviews.
- **Queued messages are not checkpointed.** Rewinding to the turn start discards work done before your note arrived.
- **Interrupting mid-edit can leave half-applied changes.** Check the diff after an Escape.
- **Steering hides missing guardrails.** If you always catch it by hand, you never write the hook or the rule.

entries.name: Interview-to-Spec
entries.summary: Before planning, have the agent interview you with structured questions until the hard parts are covered, then write a self-contained spec. Implement it in a fresh session.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for anything big enough that you would otherwise write a long prompt and hope. Use it when you have not thought the feature through yet. The pattern is good at that case. The questions do work a plan cannot, because a plan assumes the requirements are settled. Use it when several stakeholders disagree, so the interview surfaces that before code does. Use it as the front half of [[Spec-Driven Development]] when the spec would otherwise be written by someone guessing.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for small, clear tasks. The interview is longer than the work. Do not use it when requirements are fixed and already written down. Hand over the document. Do not use it when you cannot answer the questions. An interview answered with "you decide" produces a spec that records the agent's assumptions under your name. That is worse than no spec. And do not carry the interview transcript into implementation. The spec is the artifact. The transcript is exhaust.
entries.drawbacks: Interviews expand. Without the "don't ask obvious questions" constraint, an agent asks fifteen questions where four would do, and the pattern becomes a time sink. It also depends entirely on the human. Answers of "whatever you think" turn the interview into a formality that launders the agent's guesses into an approved document. The spec can be wrong in ways the interview cannot catch, since neither party has tried the change yet. And a spec that is not self-contained yields a fresh session that is confidently missing context. That is worse than a session that knows it is missing context.

entries.name: Issue-Tracker-as-Memory
entries.summary: Replace the markdown task list with a real issue tracker built for agents: a dependency graph in a versioned database, where `ready` returns work with no open blockers and finishing something unblocks whatever waited on it.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when dependencies are real and you keep answering "what can I start" by hand. Use it on long-horizon work spanning many sessions, the case the project names. Use it with multiple agents. A queryable ready set lets workers self-schedule without a coordinator ([[Task Queue Consumer]], [[Agent Teams]]). Use it when a markdown task list has already failed you. The symptoms are agents starting blocked work, redoing finished work, or quietly rewriting the list.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it when a checklist is enough, which is most single-session work. Do not use it beside an existing human tracker unless one of them is authoritative. Two task sources are worse than an unqueryable one. Do not adopt it without understanding the storage model, since the file that looks like the data is not the data. And weigh the dependency. An embedded database in your repository is a real commitment to one project's format.
entries.drawbacks: Dependency edges have to come from somewhere. A wrong agent-inferred edge either blocks work that was never blocked or fails to block work that was. [[Task Master]] has the same weakness, and it is just as invisible. An embedded database is harder to inspect, diff, and repair by hand than a markdown file. That matters most when something has gone wrong. The JSONL export invites the wrong assumption about where the data lives. It duplicates any human tracker. And the evidence base is a single project's README.

entries.name: K9 Audit
entries.summary: A hash-chained ledger. For every agent action it records what the agent was supposed to do, what it did, and how far apart those were. It is deterministic, not model-judged, and tamper-evident by construction.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for unattended or long-running agent operation, where nobody watched and the transcript is all that remains. Use it where you will be asked to account for what an agent did: regulated environments, shared infrastructure, anything customer-facing. Use it after an incident, when the question is "what was it told to do at that point" and the alternative is reconstructing it from a transcript. Use it alongside enforcement, not instead of it. Recording an action does not prevent it.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it as a control. It observes and alerts, and the documented example is explicitly non-blocking. A run that needs stopping needs a guard ([[Command Classifier Guard]]) or a hook. Do not use it for interactive sessions you are watching, where the transcript is enough and the ledger is overhead. The intent contract is not free. You must specify it per action, and a ledger with an empty or generic intent field records nothing useful. Weigh the dependency too: this is a young single-maintainer project.
entries.drawbacks: It records; it does not prevent. A high-severity deviation that alerts while execution continues helps only if someone reads the alerts. The intent contract is the load-bearing field and the hardest to fill. Specifying expected behavior per action is real work, and a vague contract makes the deviation score meaningless. Deviation scoring is a heuristic with unevaluated calibration, so 0.9 means whatever the implementation decided it means. A local ledger is tamper-evident only against the process writing it, not against someone with filesystem access. The evidence is one project's README plus a Show HN.

entries.name: Kiro Spec Workflow
entries.summary: Kiro Spec Workflow turns a prompt into requirements, design, and dependency-ordered tasks, with review gates and synchronization checks connecting the documents to code.
entries.whenToUse: Kiro's workflow suits features large enough to need a design but small enough to fit one spec folder, in teams that already think in user stories and acceptance criteria. It is the natural choice for AWS-centric shops, and for developers who want the gates to be IDE buttons, not slash commands they must remember. It shines on under-specified problems. HN user sqrtc used it on "quite a gnarly date time parsing problem" and found "it forced me to stop and think more clearly about the problem I was trying to solve and in the end left my jaw on the floor as I saw it work through the task list" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44634469)). Semaphor wrote that "the multistep process with manual refinement options after every step just works so much better for keeping LLMs in line." Steering files with file-match inclusion fit monorepos, where different directories follow different conventions.
entries.whenNotToUse: Not for small bugs. Böckeler asked Kiro to fix a small bug. The result: "the requirements document turned this small bug into 4 'user stories' with a total of 16 acceptance criteria, including gems like 'As a developer, I want the transformation function to handle edge cases gracefully'". An HN commenter summarised it as "Kiro, your new corporate project manager" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45610996)). Kiro later added Bugfix specs and Quick Spec, partly in response. It is also a poor fit if you refuse to change editors ("I don't want to be jumping an editor/IDE every 6 months", [HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44560662)). It is a poor fit if you need the workflow to be model-agnostic and scriptable outside Kiro's UI. The CLI narrows that gap but does not close it.
entries.drawbacks: Over-specification is the signature failure. The "sledgehammer to crack a nut" phrase that spread through spec-driven discussions came from Böckeler's Kiro bug-fix experiment. HN user hatmanstack reported that "Kiro's spec-driven approach... generated massive task lists (12+ tasks with 4+ sub-tasks each). The workflow was decent but it deleted code unpredictably and wouldn't revert changes" and concluded it was "so much simpler to just iterate without the puzzle box of tasks" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45610996)). Model dependence is another. Semaphor noted that with Sonnet 3.7 instead of 4.0 "it went way off the rails of kiro's tasks structure every time" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44634469)). Cost and platform lock-in drew the most anger. Critics attacked the August 2025 pricing change, throttling, and waitlists. Several HN commenters argued that everything Kiro's specs do "can also be done with Claude Code" with plan mode and a Markdown file. Böckeler's structural critique stands. Kiro is spec-first. Sync Files exists, but nothing guides you in keeping a spec authoritative across many later changes. So `requirements.md` tends to become a historical document, not a living one.

entries.name: LLM-as-Judge
entries.summary: A model grades an artifact against a rubric and returns a score. No revision loop is attached. It is useful where nothing executable exists. It is demonstrably biased by surface properties that have nothing to do with correctness.
entries.whenToUse: Use it where no executable check exists and the property is subjective: documentation quality, adherence to a written style guide, whether a commit message describes the change, whether an explanation answers the question. Use it for triage and prioritization, not acceptance. Flagging the twenty diffs most worth a human's attention is a good use of a noisy signal. Use it comparatively, as a selector among candidates, where relative ordering is all you need ([[Best-of-N Sampling]]). Use it as one input among several, never the only one.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it as a correctness oracle. Tests, type checks, and builds answer that question, and the bias study shows a judge does not. Do not use it as a merge gate, for the same reason. Do not use it uncalibrated. A rubric never checked against human labels produces numbers with no known relationship to anything. Do not use it where the same model produced the artifact, because shared blind spots stay invisible. Do not build a loop that optimizes against a judge score. That is a reward signal, and it will be hacked ([[Reward Hacking Guardrails]]).
entries.drawbacks: The measured failure is surface bias: six bias types, with formatting and naming inflating or deflating scores on semantically equivalent code, and the effect surviving test-case generation. The broader judge literature documents position and verbosity effects well. Self-preference is a live risk when the judge and the producer share a model family. Scores carry false precision. A 7.4 reads like a measurement and is closer to an impression, and threshold gates built on it inherit that. A judge used as an optimization target stops measuring the thing and starts measuring what is easy to produce.

entries.name: Loop Engineering
entries.summary: Not a loop—a taxonomy of them. Classify a loop by what triggers it and what stops it. The four resulting shapes (turn-based, goal-based, time-based, proactive) each have a different correct use.
entries.whenToUse: Use the taxonomy when choosing how to run something. Most people make that decision implicitly and badly. Ask three short questions. Is a human present? Is there a verifiable exit condition? Is there an event to wait on? A human and no verifiable exit gives you turn-based. A human and a verifiable exit gives you goal-based. No human and a clock gives you time-based. No human and an event stream gives you proactive. Use it also to review an existing setup. If you cannot state a loop's trigger and exit in one sentence each, you do not control it.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not reach for a heavier loop shape than the work needs. A proactive loop for a task you do twice a month is infrastructure you will maintain forever. Do not use a time-based loop where an event exists to wait on. Do not use a goal-based loop when the goal is not verifiable, since the evaluator will approximate. Do not run a proactive loop without the permission posture it requires. It is the only shape with no human present at any point, so [[Permission Tiers]] and [[Sandboxed Execution]] are preconditions, not refinements.
entries.drawbacks: It is a vendor taxonomy built around one product's commands. The shapes map onto `/goal`, `/loop`, and `/schedule` more neatly than onto anything else, and the boundaries blur in practice—a goal-based loop with a long cap is a proactive loop with extra steps. Classification can also substitute for design. Knowing a loop is time-based says nothing about whether its interval is right or its work is idempotent. The taxonomy says little about failure, which is where loops actually break. Nothing in it covers what a loop does when it cannot make progress. That is [[Circuit Breaker]] territory. The higher shapes also need safety machinery the taxonomy does not supply.

entries.name: Memory Bank
entries.summary: Memory Bank writes down the state a fresh agent cannot cheaply infer: current focus, decisions, constraints, and unfinished work. Keep it small enough to read at startup.
entries.whenToUse: Use it on multi-session projects where the same agent returns to the same codebase for days or weeks, especially with tools that do not persist memory themselves. It shines when the code cannot express the project state: which approach was tried and rejected, what the current sprint is, which tests are known-flaky, which decisions were made in conversation. It is also the standard escape hatch for context exhaustion: dump state, `/clear`, resume.
entries.whenNotToUse: Skip it for short, one-off tasks. Reading six files before every task is pure overhead. Do not duplicate what the code already expresses (architecture, file layout). Claude Code's auto memory skips it, and the AGENTS.md study found repository overviews unhelpful. Do not use a memory bank for hard rules. Use a [[Context File]] or hooks. Do not substitute it for git history or an issue tracker when those exist and the agent can read them.
entries.drawbacks:
- **Token tax on every task.** Reading all six Cline files at the start of every task, plus rewriting them, is a fixed cost that dominates small tasks. Claude Code caps the auto-loaded index at 200 lines / 25KB for this reason.
- **Drift and staleness.** Agent-written notes can be wrong, and the next session trusts a wrong note. One HN commenter said that after compaction "the memory of even the current session feels so much dumber", which motivates external memory tools ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46426624)). The same thread has users saying "you really don't need any of this crap. you just need Claude Code and CLAUDE.MD".
- **Summaries lose edge cases.** The maker of ensue-skill argued "summaries often miss edge cases and long sessions drift". That critiques memory-by-summary in general.
- **Tool sprawl and overwhelm.** "Is anyone else just completely overwhelmed with the number of things you need for claude code? Agents, sub agents, skills, claud.md, agents.md, rules, hooks, etc." (JoshGlazebrook, HN).
- **Privacy / exfiltration when memory is hosted.** Hosted memory services drew immediate "I'd prefer not to send proprietary code to third-party servers" pushback on HN; local files avoid this.
- **Not shared across machines.** Claude Code auto memory "is machine-local... Files are not shared across machines or cloud environments", unlike a checked-in memory bank.
- **Context rot still applies.** Loading a large memory bank recreates the long-context degradation documented by Chroma (see [[Context Compaction]]).

entries.name: Merge Queue
entries.summary: Parallel agents produce branches. One serializing integrator merges them in order, one at a time, and runs the checks after each merge. Generate in parallel. Integrate in series.
entries.whenToUse: Use it whenever more than two agents change the same repository: [[Parallel Worktree Swarm]], [[Agent Teams]] doing parallel implementation, or a [[Task Queue Consumer]] with several workers. Use it when the test suite is slow enough that you cannot afford to discover integration failures after the fact. Use it when branches are independent in intent but touch overlapping code. That is the common case, and the one where per-branch green is most misleading.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it when workers already produce disjoint artifacts—separate services, separate packages with no shared interface. There a queue is pure latency. Do not use it when the check suite is too slow to run per merge, because the queue becomes the constraint on the whole system. Fix the suite first, or batch merges and accept coarser attribution. Do not let the integrator fix branches. Do not use it as a substitute for review: landing something because the checks passed is [[Dark Factory]] reasoning, and it is only safe under that pattern's preconditions.
entries.drawbacks: The queue is a bottleneck by construction. Its throughput is one full check run per branch, so a slow suite caps the whole system. In a long queue, each branch is validated against a base that has moved since it was written, so rejection rates climb with queue depth—the classic merge-train problem. An agentic integrator with authority to resolve conflicts can silently produce code neither worker wrote and nobody reviewed. That failure mode is unique to the agentic version. And a queue with a weak check suite just serializes the arrival of defects. The pattern guarantees ordering, not quality.

entries.name: Multi-Agent Debate
entries.summary: Multi-Agent Debate makes disagreement an input to selection or localization. It earns its cost only when perspectives differ, rounds are bounded, and a check can arbitrate.
entries.whenToUse: Use debate where the artifact is short and the decision is discrete: choosing among candidate patches, deciding which module a bug lives in, resolving a design question with real trade-offs, or reviewing a plan before expensive execution. Give agents genuinely different perspectives (a security reviewer, a performance reviewer, a maintainer), not N copies of the same prompt. The empirical study's forceful-agreement failure is worst when agents share a prior. Keep rounds to two. Always finish with a judge that can consult an external check.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it to generate code. The 2503.12029 study found debate produced translated code that passed fewer tests than the single-model baseline, and cost an order of magnitude more calls. Do not use it as a substitute for tests: agents can unanimously agree on a wrong answer. Do not run many rounds, because ending divergence grows with round count. Do not use it interactively. Latency is N × R model calls per decision.
entries.drawbacks: Cost: thousands of calls per benchmark set in the empirical study, with early termination only halving it. Divergence: agents talk themselves out of correct answers. Sycophantic convergence: agents adopt the majority view regardless of correctness. Homogeneity: N instances of one model share blind spots, so debate can add confidence without adding information. Task sensitivity: the same paper found MAD helpful for summarization and harmful for translation, so results on one task type do not transfer.

entries.name: Multi-Agent RPI
entries.summary: Spec Kit split across PM and developer agents. Read-only probing hooks ground each phase in repository evidence before it produces its artifact. Reported gains are small but statistically significant.
entries.whenToUse: Use the grounding idea on any spec-driven workflow. That is the transferable part: a phase that reads the repository before writing about it describes the repository, not a plausible version of it. Use the role split when specification and implementation benefit from different framing. Use it in brownfield codebases. Ungrounded specifications drift furthest from reality there, and a plan that assumes the wrong architecture costs the most.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not adopt it expecting large gains. The measured effects are a few percent, and the paper says so. Do not use it on greenfield work, where there is no repository to ground against. Do not add probing hooks to phases that do not need repository evidence—the specify phase for a genuinely new feature may not. Weigh the quality metric: the headline improvement is on an LLM-as-judge composite, which [[LLM-as-Judge]] shows is biased by surface properties.
entries.drawbacks: The gains are small: +0.15 on a five-point scale, 1.7% on SWE-bench Lite. The primary quality instrument is an LLM-as-judge composite with known biases, so the headline number is softer than its significance test suggests. Probing hooks add latency and tokens to every phase. Two roles cost more than one. And a probe returns whatever it finds. Grounding in a misleading part of the repository produces a confidently wrong specification—grounded is not the same as correct.

entries.name: Multi-Model Cross-Check
entries.summary: A second model gets a clean view of the diff and the contract. The goal is to expose blind spots, not to collect a pile of opinions.
entries.whenToUse: Consider a second model for a consequential change when you can name defect classes the current reviewer misses and can supply the contracts. Concurrency and recovery behavior are good candidates to evaluate. Missing requirements call for domain input. Another model cannot settle behavior nobody specified.
entries.whenNotToUse: Skip it when another review is worth less than its triage and execution cost, when you cannot supply the relevant requirements, or when a second provider cannot receive the code. Do not treat agreement as acceptance. Different models can agree because they lack the same domain fact.
entries.drawbacks:
- **Cost multiplies**: Each review round is another full-context call. Debate rounds multiply it again.
- **Over-reporting and over-engineering**: Speculative findings can provoke needless abstractions, defensive branches, and tests for unreachable cases. Verify reachability and requirement impact before changing the implementation.
- **Limited outcome evidence**: Larger vendor evaluations exist, but human triage, precision, and escaped defects are still only partly measured. Do not generalize one model pair to all tools or languages.
- **Shared blind spots**: Independent models may miss the same behavioral requirement. The residual misses in S22 belong to one evaluation mode. They do not describe the debate mode's result.
- **Coordination friction**: Different vendors have different tool conventions, rate limits, and refusal behaviors. Orchestration tools exist because the manual loop is tedious.
- **Human still decides**: HN's kybernetikos: "the bottleneck has shifted even more dramatically to human code understanding vs code generation"; more findings do not reduce the reading load; they can increase it ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48771515)).

entries.name: Multi-Reviewer Fan-Out
entries.summary: Several reviewers run in parallel, each looking for a different class of issue. A verification step filters false positives, and a synthesizer deduplicates and ranks what survives. One reviewer serializes and truncates. A fan-out does not.
entries.whenToUse: Use it on changes with several independent risk dimensions: anything touching authentication, anything with a performance profile, anything that spans layers. Use it when a single review pass keeps missing a category you care about, a sign that attention is being spent unevenly. Use it when review is the bottleneck and human attention is scarce. Use it for high-stakes merges where a missed defect costs more than several review passes.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it on small diffs. One reviewer covers the whole surface, and the fan-out is pure cost—review cost scales with pull request size, and a fan-out multiplies it. Do not use it without a verification stage. Unverified parallel reviewers produce noise that trains people to ignore review output. Do not use it as a merge gate. The documented design keeps the check neutral, and a probabilistic reviewer blocking merges is worse. Do not fan out on dimensions that are not independent. Overlapping reviewers mostly produce duplicates for the deduplicator to remove.
entries.drawbacks: Cost is the plain one: N reviewers plus verification plus synthesis. The managed service documents an average of $15–25 per review and roughly twenty minutes of wall clock. False-positive volume is the structural one, and it compounds. Every reviewer is incentivized to find something, so the verification stage is not optional. Correlated blind spots survive fan-out entirely. Reviewers from the same model family miss the same things in parallel, which is what [[Multi-Model Cross-Check]] addresses. Dimension choice bounds coverage, so anything nobody assigned a reviewer goes unreviewed. And an uncapped nit stream ends in review fatigue, which is why the documented customization surface includes a nit cap.

entries.name: OpenSpec
entries.summary: Keep the current behavior in living specs, describe one change as a delta, implement it, verify it, then archive the delta back into the source of truth.
entries.whenToUse: OpenSpec suits existing codebases where behaviour must be documented incrementally and several people or agents change the same domains at once. The delta format keeps reviews small. The archive step keeps the specs honest. It is also the pick for teams who found Spec Kit or BMAD too ceremonial but still want requirements written before code. In the HN GSD thread gbrindisi wrote "I like openspec, it lets you tune the workflow to your liking and doesn't get in the way. I started with all the standard spec flow and as I got more confident and opinionated I simplified it to my liking," and alasano agreed that GSD and Superpowers "are way too opinionated" by comparison ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47417804)).
entries.whenNotToUse: For a brand-new project with no existing behaviour, deltas against empty specs add little over a plain design doc. Spec Kit's constitution and research steps may serve better. OpenSpec does not manage context, subagents, or verification beyond `/opsx:verify`. Long or complex implementations still need the discipline of [[GSD]]-style fresh contexts or [[Superpowers]]-style TDD. And if nobody archives, the specs stop being true. The method depends on running the closing step every time.
entries.drawbacks: Specs and code can still diverge if `/opsx:apply` implements something other than the delta and `/opsx:verify` is skipped. The tool checks structure, not semantics. Domain organisation is manual. On large systems a spec per domain can grow into the same "markdown nobody reads" that HN commenters complain about for all SDD tools (gsadaka: BDD "documents the features as code rather than verbose markdown files no one will read", [HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45610996)). Given/When/Then scenarios are only as testable as someone's willingness to turn them into tests. OpenSpec does not generate tests. Independent experience reports are thinner than for Spec Kit or GSD. Most coverage is tutorial videos. I found no dedicated critical write-up, no arXiv paper on OpenSpec itself, and no HN thread specifically about it with substantial discussion.

entries.name: Orchestrator-Workers
entries.summary: One lead agent owns decomposition and synthesis. Workers handle narrow, isolated investigations. The lead picks the next wave from what it learns.
entries.whenToUse:
Use it when you cannot know the subtasks until you look at the input, and when each subtask's raw material would drown the main conversation. The Claude Code [best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices) guide names the canonical case: research. "When Claude researches a codebase it reads lots of files, all of which consume your context. Subagents run in separate context windows and report back summaries." The [subagents blog post](https://claude.com/blog/subagents-in-claude-code) adds parallel independent work ("three subagents working simultaneously generally finish the task in less time"), fresh-perspective review, verification before commit, and pipeline stages with clear handoffs.

It also fits breadth-first problems, where you want several hypotheses explored at once and then compared. The agent-teams documentation's "investigate with competing hypotheses" example spawns five teammates to disprove each other, because "a single agent tends to find one plausible explanation and stop looking." It also shapes cost. A strong orchestrator can route grunt work to cheaper models (Claude Code's `model: haiku` frontmatter, Cognition's "smart friend" inversion where a small model escalates to a large one).

The Substack piece [The Orchestrator's Dilemma](https://responseawareness.substack.com/p/claude-code-subagents-the-orchestrators) argues for a stricter variant on complex multi-domain work. Keep the main agent in "pure orchestration mode" so implementation tokens never bury the architectural plan. Redundant file reads are the price of a coherent plan.
entries.whenNotToUse:
Anthropic says coding is a poor fit for the full research-style version: "most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research, and LLM agents are not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents in real time." The subagents blog lists the concrete anti-cases: sequential dependent work, where step two needs step one's full output; parallel edits to the same file; small tasks where overhead dominates; too many specialist agents, which makes automatic delegation unreliable; and anything where workers need to talk to each other, because "subagents report back but can't communicate with each other."

Cognition's [Don't Build Multi-Agents](https://cognition.com/blog/dont-build-multi-agents) shows the failure in one example. Asked to build Flappy Bird, one worker builds a Super Mario-styled background while another draws a bird that does not match. The synthesizing agent inherits contradictions it cannot reconcile. Its two principles, "share context, and share full agent traces, not just individual messages" and "actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results," are what an orchestrator-workers split violates by design. If the workers' outputs must agree on style, naming, or architecture, and the workers cannot see each other's decisions, do not parallelize the writes.
entries.drawbacks:
Token cost is the loudest complaint. Anthropic's own figure is 15× chat usage. A widely upvoted [HN comment thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48883796) opens with "I once gave Claude Code a pretty big task, and it immediately launched 7 sub agents which burned through my budget." Others report spawn counts of 102, 171 and 415 agents on a single task, and monthly budgets gone in minutes. Commenters note that each subagent re-processes a ~30k-token system prompt and re-reads files the parent already read. They also note that prefix caching does not help across parallel workers. Eric Cheng's [dev.to write-up](https://dev.to/onlineeric/claude-code-sub-agents-burn-out-your-tokens-4cd8) measured a 300-file refactor. Parallel subagents finished in 15 minutes instead of 30 but hit the Pro quota twice as fast, "speed kills (your quota)."

Unreliable delegation is the second. In the [HN launch thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44686726) for Claude Code subagents, pjm331 reported asking for a review via a defined agent. Claude "went off and did it by itself without using the agent." oc1 summarized: "Most of the time they aren't used when it would be appropriate. What's the point of this agents and standards when you can't make them reliably used." The [agent teams documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams) still carries a troubleshooting entry for the lead "implementing tasks itself instead of waiting for teammates."

Synthesis loss and orchestrator context saturation are structural. The [aipatternbook page](https://aipatternbook.com/orchestrator-workers) lists these problems: orchestrator context saturation as worker outputs pile up, information lost when summarizing worker reports, awkward handling of partial failures, cost overruns from speculative dispatch, and a trust hierarchy in which the orchestrator's authority flows to workers nobody approved. That last point is the "delegation chain" antipattern. Subagents inherit parent permissions. Claude Code's auto-mode classifier now checks a subagent's task description before it starts, each action while it runs, and its full action history when it returns ([permission modes documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes)).

The academic critique is [Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657) (Cemri, Pan, Yang et al., UC Berkeley, March 2025). The authors annotated 150 expert-reviewed traces (1,600+ in the dataset) from seven frameworks, including MetaGPT, ChatDev and AutoGen. From them they built the MAST taxonomy of 14 failure modes in three categories: specification issues (41.8%, including step repetition at 17.1% and failing to follow task requirements at 11.0%), inter-agent misalignment (36.9%, including reasoning-action mismatch at 14.0% and proceeding on wrong assumptions instead of asking at 11.7%), and task verification (21.3%: premature termination, missing or incorrect verification). ChatDev scored only 33.3% correctness on their ProgramDev benchmark of tasks like Tic-Tac-Toe. They conclude that these failures need system-design fixes, not just bigger models.

Finally, humans cannot see what is happening. In the [Agent orchestration for the timid](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46746681) HN thread, a recurring worry was that orchestration "overwhelms everyone's ability to keep track of what it's doing." In the agent-teams thread the consensus line was "fancy orchestration is mostly a waste, validation is the bottleneck."

entries.name: Parallel Worktree Swarm
entries.summary: Give each agent its own worktree and branch. Integrate the results through ordinary Git review. Isolation keeps simultaneous edits from tangling one working tree.
entries.whenToUse:
The pattern works when the work already splits along clean file boundaries. The Claude Code [agent teams documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams) list the good cases: new modules or features where "teammates can each own a separate piece without stepping on each other," cross-layer changes where frontend, backend and tests each have an owner, and mechanical migrations. The [/batch guidance](https://readysolutions.ai/blog/2026-05-04-claude-code-batch-when-to-use/) narrows that to "repetitive, pattern-based changes" such as a lodash-to-native migration or class-to-function component conversions, "work that would justify a codemod if you had two free days." Per-unit review there is mechanical and bounded.

Jonas Braadbaart's [Managing parallel coding agents (without going insane)](https://metacircuits.substack.com/p/managing-parallel-coding-agents-without) reports roughly 14,000 lines across 62 files in about an hour, a 2–3× speedup over sequential agent work. That came only after he "first needed to create a reference software architecture" so that agents worked on "completely different parts of the system." That is the tell. If you can write down module ownership before starting, the swarm will probably merge cleanly.

Best-of-N fits hard, self-contained bugs or design questions, where attempts vary widely and judging is cheaper than solving. Cursor's guidance is that it pays off "for complex problems where different models employ distinct strategies"; the Claude Code documentation frame the debugging version as "teammates test different theories in parallel and converge on the answer faster."
entries.whenNotToUse:
Do not swarm coupled work. `/batch` "cannot handle coupled refactors where unit B needs utilities unit A creates." The agent-teams documentation is blunt: "for sequential tasks, same-file edits, or work with many dependencies, a single session or subagents are more effective." Worktrees isolate only the filesystem. The same article warns that "agents still share the same Postgres, [Redis](https://redis.io/), and queue topology," so a migration run by one agent breaks another's tests. If your project needs a database, a dev server on a fixed port, or a heavy `node_modules` per checkout, plan for that before multiplying.

Do not swarm when you cannot review the output. In the Gas Town HN thread, lifetimerubyist wrote, "If babysitting 30 claude agents is the future of professional programming I want zero part of it," and qcnguy read it as "Gas Town sounds fun if you are accountable to nobody." The [paddo.dev analysis](https://paddo.dev/blog/gastown-two-kinds-of-multi-agent/) credits the architecture (external state, worktree isolation, parallel execution) but notes that real deployments showed "$100/hour token burn rates" and "dangerous behaviors like auto-merging failing tests," and concludes that a focused single agent with a verification loop "remains optimal for most developers." Do not swarm on a subscription plan you need for the rest of the month. Eric Cheng measured that parallelism drains quota in proportion to concurrency ([dev.to](https://dev.to/onlineeric/claude-code-sub-agents-burn-out-your-tokens-4cd8)).
entries.drawbacks:
Cost covers all workers, coordination, review, and repairs. It need not scale linearly with worker count. The `/batch` article documents one developer whose daily spend rose "122-fold" (about $12 to $1,504) between February and March 2026 after moving to concurrent sessions. Yegge needed a third Claude account within weeks of launching Gas Town to avoid throttling. munchler on HN: "With dozens of agents running at a time, it must cost $1000's."

Merge conflicts are deferred, not eliminated. Braadbaart hit "endless merge conflicts" until he front-loaded an architecture doc. The agent-teams documentation says simply "two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites. Break the work so each teammate owns a different set of files." HN commenters on Gas Town reported that the git-backed Beads tracker itself produced merge conflicts that destroyed human work. The v1.0 thread noted Beads "required constant 'doctor' repairs."

Environment drift: each worktree is a fresh checkout with no `.env`, no installed dependencies, and no built artifacts. Claude Code added `.worktreeinclude` and Cursor added `worktrees.json` because agents kept failing on missing env files. Git LFS content shows up as pointer files in Claude-created worktrees, because the tool deliberately skips repository-local filter drivers.

Shared services are the silent killer. Databases, caches, ports, and queues are not per-worktree, so parallel test runs interfere in ways that look like flaky tests.

Quality drift across agents: without a shared style decision, N agents produce N conventions. This is Cognition's "conflicting implicit decisions" problem again. The [24 simultaneous agents](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47099597) write-up mitigated it by having agents "communicate through the codebase" via governance documentation defining module ownership and enforced test ratios.

Review bottleneck: throughput moves to whoever reads the pull requests. The Gas Town v1.0 thread summed up that lines-per-hour "is a poor metric; value depends on production quality and review burden." The agent-teams HN thread converged on "validation is the bottleneck."

Best-of-N without a judge is just N× the bill. Kim et al. argue that "effective test-time scaling for agents fundamentally depends on representation quality and intelligent selection mechanisms rather than raw attempt multiplication."

Note on sources: I tried to search Reddit for worktree conflict threads, but the search and fetch tools were blocked for reddit.com in this session. The discussions cited here are from HN and blogs.
