entries.name: Permission Classifier
entries.summary: A second, smaller model judges each proposed action. The action runs, goes to a human, or is blocked. The classifier fills the autonomous region that permission tiers leave undefined. It is also an attack surface, with a published false-negative rate.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when the action space is too varied for static rules, which describes most shell access. Use it to cut prompts without cutting decisions—the classifier makes the same decisions, faster. Use it in multi-agent runs, where it is the only practical way to police messages and actions across several workers. Use the input-side probe whenever the agent reads untrusted content: web pages, issues, pull request comments, tool results from third parties.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it as the sole safety layer. Do not use it for tier-4 actions—production deploys, secret access, infrastructure deletion. The correct policy there is refusal, not classification, because a classifier that can approve can be persuaded. Do not use it without a sandbox. A classifier reduces the rate of bad actions. A sandbox reduces their consequences, and only the sandbox is a bound. And do not use it where a deterministic rule would do the job. A regex cannot be talked into anything.
entries.drawbacks: It misses things, and the rate is published, not hypothetical. The aipatternbook page cites a disclosed "17% false-negative rate for the production classifier," roughly one dangerous action in six going undetected. That is survivable as one layer among several. It is unacceptable as the only one. The classifier is also a concentrated target—"a successful attack on the classifier bypasses the entire safety layer in a way no individual approval would." Compromising it once is worth more to an attacker than defeating any number of individual prompts. Calibration is a two-sided trap: "a too-conservative classifier reproduces approval fatigue under a new name; a too-permissive one provides false comfort." And the pattern shifts oversight from an accountable human to an opaque model, which makes drift hard to notice. The same page stresses that human oversight remains necessary to catch it.

entries.name: Permission Tiers
entries.summary: Sort every action an agent can take into a few tiers by consequence and reversibility. Attach a fixed policy to each tier. Approval becomes a property of the action, not a judgment call made under fatigue.
entries.whenToUse: Use it as soon as more than one agent is running. Per-action prompts from several workers bubble up to one human and multiply. Use it wherever the same policy should apply across people. A tier table is reviewable and a habit is not. Use it when actions differ in consequence, which is almost always. A uniform prompt policy cannot express that. Use it when you want to widen autonomy over time and need a defensible record of what widened and why.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for a short interactive session where you watch every step. The table is overhead you will not recoup. Do not use it as a substitute for a sandbox. Tiers govern intent, not blast radius. An agent in tier 1 on a production machine is still on a production machine. Do not build more than about four tiers. Classification cost rises and the boundaries stop being obvious. And do not set the tiers once and forget them—a stale table no longer matches the risks.
entries.drawbacks: Miscalibration defeats the pattern in both directions. Tiers set too tight reproduce the fatigue they were meant to remove. Tiers set too loose grant blanket permission under a governance-sounding name. The scheme also cannot anticipate novel actions. Anything not in the table falls through to a default, and a permissive default is where the real risk lives. Tier promotion tends to be a ratchet. Things move up when they are annoying and rarely move back down, so autonomy drifts wider than anyone decided. And tiers are inherited. As [[Delegation Chain]] documents, a subagent typically receives its parent's permission mode. A tier assigned at the top silently applies several links down, where nobody evaluated it.

entries.name: Plan Mode
entries.summary: A runtime mode where the agent may read and explore but may not edit until a human approves its plan. It is [[Plan-and-Execute]] with the separation enforced by the tool, not the prompt.
entries.whenToUse: The documentation's criteria are the right ones: use it "when you're uncertain about the approach, when the change modifies multiple files, or when you're unfamiliar with the code being modified." Surrounding practice adds two more. Use it when the work touches something whose blast radius you cannot fully see. Use it before delegating, so the workers receive the plan you approved, not an interpretation of it.
entries.whenNotToUse: Skip it for one-sentence diffs. Skip it in unattended or headless runs. Nobody is there to approve, and the mode becomes an extra round trip. Use a written specification and a verification gate instead ([[Spec-Driven Development]], [[Verification Loop]]). Skip it for exploratory work where the plan would be fiction. A plan written before you know what is there is a commitment you will pay to undo. And do not treat it as a security boundary. It blocks source edits, not every side effect. A read-only mode is not a sandbox.
entries.drawbacks: It has a real cost, and the documentation names it outright. On small tasks the overhead exceeds the benefit. Plans are optimistic. An agent that has not tried the change does not know what it will hit. Approving a plan is not approving an outcome, and treating approval as a guarantee is the most common misreading. Approval fatigue applies here as everywhere. A human who approves every plan unread has bought a delay, not a gate. And plan mode restricts source edits, not all action. Do not mistake it for [[Sandboxed Execution]].

entries.name: Plan-and-Execute
entries.summary: Plan-and-execute separates deciding what to do from carrying it out. The plan is a hypothesis that execution can revise when the repository disagrees.
entries.whenToUse:
Use it when the task has a stable structure you can know up front: multi-file features, migrations of the "for each X do Y" shape, refactors where edit order matters, or any task where a wrong first move is expensive. Anthropic's guidance: "Planning is most useful when you're uncertain about the approach, when the change modifies multiple files, or when you're unfamiliar with the code being modified." The Codex knowledge-base article draws the line at roughly three or more files and any ambiguous requirement ("make the checkout flow faster"). The aipatternbook entry says the pattern "pays off around 15-20 steps and dominates above 50."

Use it when you want a human checkpoint before edits. The plan is the cheapest place to catch a misunderstanding. A bad plan step costs one line of markdown to fix. A bad implementation of it costs a diff.

Use it when execution can be parallel or cheap. A DAG plan lets independent steps fan out to worktrees or subagents ([[Parallel Worktree Swarm]]), and a lean executor model can run the steps a big planner model specified.
entries.whenNotToUse: Skip it for small, well-scoped changes. Anthropic: "If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan." The Codex article warns that on simple tasks plan mode can "double cost and halve throughput for no safety benefit." Skip it when the environment is the source of truth and every observation reshuffles the next step, such as an unknown bug you can only find by probing. The aipatternbook rule is "Pick ReAct when each step's outcome substantially changes what the next step should be." Also skip it, or keep the plan deliberately loose, when you are too confused to write one. People raise the same objection against [[Spec-Driven Development]].
entries.drawbacks:
**Brittle plans and Frankenstein replans.** If early observations invalidate the plan, "the executor flounders and re-planning becomes dominant work." Deciding whether to patch or discard produces "Frankenstein plans" or lost work ([aipatternbook](https://aipatternbook.com/plan-and-execute)). Debugging becomes global: a failure at step 7 may trace back to a planning assumption, not the step.

**Giant plans nobody wants to read.** On HN, user deaux complained that in plan mode "Claude would write up a giant p[lan]" and any edit meant regenerating the whole thing. Replies pointed to Plannotator and inline plan comments as workarounds ([HN 47624807](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47624807)). People level the same "wall of markdown" complaint at spec-kit.

**The agent ignores the plan.** Plan adherence is advisory unless enforced. On HN, user dota_fanatic's TODO.md-driven workflow worked "better than 50/50". User turnsout noted Claude "is not great about moving cards when it's done with a task" ([HN 45416803](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45416803)). Cursor's best-practices guide and the Codex article both warn against treating an approved plan as immutable. The agent should adapt when it hits an unexpected constraint. So "did it follow the plan?" is not a clean acceptance test.

**Plan mode is a permission boundary, not a thinking boundary.** In Claude Code, plan mode blocks source edits, but reads and read-only commands still run. With auto mode enabled, other shell commands route to a classifier ([What plan mode actually blocks](https://dev.to/rulestack/claude-code-plan-mode-what-it-actually-blocks-what-still-runs-and-what-approving-switches-you-22m3)). In Codex the read-only constraint "operates at the prompt level only—there's no runtime sandbox preventing mutations." Don't confuse planning with safety.

**Overhead on small tasks.** Planner cost is not amortized under a handful of steps. Anthropic and the Codex article both say so. Some practitioners drop the mode: HN user jspdown "stopped using it and instead moved to a workflow where I simply ask it to write the plan in a file. It's much easier to edit and improve this way."

**Serial execution by default.** Vanilla plan-and-execute and ReWOO run steps sequentially; parallelism needs a DAG planner (LangChain post).

entries.name: Plan-Then-Execute for Security
entries.summary: Fix the plan before the agent reads any untrusted content. Injected text can then influence values inside a predefined execution graph. It cannot redefine the task or invent new actions.
entries.whenToUse: Use it whenever an agent reads content it did not author: web pages, issues, pull request comments, emails, third-party tool results, scraped documents. Use it for anything with side effects reachable from that content. A browsing agent that can also send, purchase, or deploy is the canonical risk. Use it in unattended runs, where a redirected agent has time to act on the redirection. Use it when the task decomposes into a programmatic plan. The paper's WebArena measurement suggests that happens more often than expected.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for exploratory work where the next step must depend on what was just found. A fixed plan is the wrong structure there and will fail rather than fail safe. Do not use it as the only injection defense. It bounds blast radius and does not prevent injection, so input probes, tool-call classification, and sandboxing still apply ([[Permission Classifier]], [[Sandboxed Execution]]). Do not assume it covers the 20% of tasks the paper found not completable programmatically. And do not confuse it with [[Plan Mode]], which gates on human approval and does nothing about untrusted content.
entries.drawbacks: It gives up runtime adaptivity, the property agents are valued for. The paper's own measurement leaves a fifth of tasks outside it. Values and branches remain attacker-influenceable, so a plan with broad branches concedes most of the benefit. "If the page says X, do Y" is a node an attacker can steer into. A plan fixed before reading anything is a plan made without information. That trades a security property for a quality cost. And the security case is argued architecturally. No measured reduction in attack success accompanies it in the abstract, so the size of the benefit is unquantified.

entries.name: Planner-Generator-Evaluator
entries.summary: Three roles, not two. One expands intent into a specification. One implements. A third, separate from the implementer, decides whether the work is done. The separation exists because agents confidently praise their own output.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for long autonomous runs where nobody watches each step. That is where confident self-praise does the most damage. Use it when "done" is behavioral, not textual—an application that must actually work—since the evaluator's job is to exercise it. Use it when you have already tried asking one agent to check its own work and found the reports unreliable. Use the sprint-contract step whenever review keeps expanding into preferences.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for short tasks. Three roles on a one-file change is three times the cost for no benefit. Do not use it when a deterministic check settles the question. If the test suite decides, use [[Verification Loop]] and skip the evaluator, which is a model and therefore fallible. Do not skip the contract step and expect the evaluator to be fair. And do not assume the separation solves generosity: the source says external evaluators remain generous, only more tunable.
entries.drawbacks: Three roles is three contexts and three bills. The evaluator is still a model and still generous, so the pattern reduces a bias but does not remove it. A spec with too much implementation detail cascades errors downstream. That is why the planner is told to stay ambitious and abstract, and getting that level right is hard. Contract negotiation is overhead on every sprint. Recursive planners, as in Cursor's design, can generate more work than the workers can absorb. And the source attributes much of the system's behavior to prompting, not structure. Adopting the diagram without the prompts may reproduce little of the benefit.

entries.name: Progress File
entries.summary: One append-only file on disk records what was done, what was tried and failed, and what comes next. The agent reads it first and updates it last, so a fresh context can pick up where the last one stopped.
entries.whenToUse: Use it any time work spans more than one context window: overnight runs, multi-day features, anything driven by [[Ralph Loop]] or [[Fresh-Agent Chaining]] where each iteration starts blind. Use it when several sessions or agents touch the same work and you need one narrative, not N disconnected transcripts. Use it when you are debugging something hard and the search space is large enough that repeating a failed hypothesis is expensive.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for a single-session task. The overhead buys nothing, and the file goes stale the moment you stop maintaining it. Do not use it as a substitute for commits. Git already records what changed, and a progress file that duplicates the diff is noise. Do not use it as the plan. A file that mixes intent and history leaves it unclear which lines are still true. And do not let it grow unbounded without a rotation strategy, or the read-at-startup step will consume the context you were trying to protect.
entries.drawbacks: The file rots. Agents under-write it (nothing appended because "nothing notable happened") and over-write it (every trivial edit logged until the file is longer than the code). Both make it useless. The second is worse because it burns context on every read. Agents also lie to it, recording a feature as complete when the test never ran. So a progress file should never be the completion oracle; see [[Smoke Test on Entry]] and [[Verification Loop]] for the checks that should outrank it. If the file is editable, an agent stuck on a hard problem may quietly delete the record of its failed attempts and then repeat them. And an unrotated file eventually costs more to read than it saves.

entries.name: Progressive Disclosure
entries.summary: Keep a one-line description of every capability in context. Load the full content only when it is used. The index is cheap. The contents are not.
entries.whenToUse: Use it whenever installed capability exceeds what any single session needs. That is the normal state of a well-equipped environment. Use it for MCP servers in particular, because their schemas are verbose and numerous, and most sessions touch none of them. Use it for large reference material—style guides, API documentation, runbooks—where a pointer plus a fetch beats inlining. Use it when you want to add capability without paying for it on every request.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not defer something the agent needs on essentially every task. A retrieval round trip every time costs more than paying for the tokens once, and prompt caching already makes stable content cheap after the first request. Do not defer safety-critical constraints. A rule that loads only when relevant will not load when the agent fails to notice it is relevant—see [[Constraint Pinning]] for the opposite discipline. And do not rely on it when the descriptions are poor, since the pattern degrades to "capability the agent never finds."
entries.drawbacks: Discovery failure is the dominant one. A vague description means the capability is never selected, and the failure is silent because nothing errors. Loading at the moment of use costs latency and tokens, which is noticeable when several capabilities are needed in sequence. Deferral is not universal. The documentation notes a fallback to upfront loading on unsupported models and certain platforms, so a setup that relies on deferral for its context budget can quietly lose it. And the pattern is wrong for constraints, where the rule must be present even when the agent has not thought to look for it.

entries.name: Prompt-as-Program
entries.summary: The prompt is a maintained source file, not a message. You watch the agent fail, add a "sign" at the point of failure, and commit. No prompt is perfect. Some have been tuned against observed behavior.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for any loop that runs more than a handful of times. That is where signs add up to something valuable. Use it for [[Ralph Loop]] and [[Fresh-Agent Chaining]], since every iteration starts from the same prompt and one unfixed failure mode repeats indefinitely. Use it when the same correction keeps being needed. That repetition is a sign waiting to be written. Use it when several people run the same workflow, so the tuning is shared and not re-derived.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for one-off tasks. A prompt file is overhead there. Do not use it in place of deterministic controls. A sign is advisory. Anything you cannot afford to have ignored belongs in a hook or a deny rule ([[Hooks and Guardrails]]). Do not let the file grow unbounded. A long prompt dilutes, which [[Context File]] documents directly. A sign that is never read is worse than none, because it creates false confidence. And do not tune without observing. Instructions added on speculation often change nothing.
entries.drawbacks: Signs accumulate, and a growing prompt dilutes itself. The rule added in week one competes with the forty added since. The author's own "less is more" warning cuts against adding one more sign. Nothing prunes the file, because removing a sign means declaring a failure mode extinct, and nobody can verify that. The practice requires watching. That costs human time, which is what an unattended loop was meant to save. Signs are advisory and can be ignored, particularly after compaction ([[Constraint Pinning]]). And tuning against observed failures is overfitting: the prompt fits the situations you happened to watch.

entries.name: PRP Context Engineering
entries.summary: A PRP turns a feature request into a compact packet: requirements, repository examples, known traps, and executable checks. It pays off when it cuts discovery during implementation.
entries.whenToUse: PRPs work best for well-bounded features in a codebase with established patterns and an executable test suite. You can point the agent at the example to copy, the documentation to read, and the commands that define success. It suits teams that want a repeatable, reviewable artifact per feature, without a persona pipeline or phase gates. It also suits anyone whose agent failures were mostly missing context rather than bad reasoning. The layered validation gates also make it one of the more honest "autonomous" methods. The loop cannot claim success without green checks.
entries.whenNotToUse: Skip it when nothing is executable to validate against (design work, UI polish, exploratory refactors). The validation loop has nothing to grip, and a PRP degrades into a long prompt. A good PRP takes real effort. For a small change, the research step costs more than the change. PRPs are also per-feature and disposable. They do not keep a living description of the system the way [[OpenSpec]] specs do, and they do not carry state between sessions the way [[Cline Memory Bank]] does. Over-stuffed PRPs hit the problem every long context hits. Anthropic's context-engineering guidance and the BMAD documentation's "extra context is a cost" both argue for curation over completeness. "Include ALL necessary documentation" is easy to misread as "include everything."
entries.drawbacks: A generated PRP can be confidently wrong. The same model does the research, so stale URLs, invented "gotchas", and mismatched examples flow into implementation. Validation loops can be gamed in the usual ways (weakening tests, special-casing). `/prp-ralph` removes the human from the loop entirely and inherits the runaway-cost risk of [[Ralph Loop]]. Long PRPs eat a large share of the window before implementation starts. Authorship confusion between the coleam00 template and Widing's original has produced fragmented forks with different command names (`/generate-prp` vs `/prp-plan`), so tutorials disagree. I found no independent evaluation and no arXiv paper. The evidence base is creator videos, HN's general context-engineering threads, and star counts.

entries.name: Ralph Loop
entries.summary: A Ralph loop gives an agent the current task state, lets it act, and checks an external condition. Then it starts another bounded iteration. It stops when the condition passes or the budget ends.
entries.whenToUse: Ralph shines on greenfield projects with a written spec and mechanical verification. Huntley is explicit that it targets "approximately 90% completion" of a new codebase and that "there's no way in heck would I use Ralph in an existing code base." It suits batch mechanical work with a machine-checkable finish line. That includes migrations (Chris Tate at Vercel used it for a Jest-to-Vitest migration with explicit iteration, token and spend limits, per [Tessl](https://tessl.io/blog/unpacking-the-unpossible-logic-of-ralph-wiggumstyle-ai-coding)), test coverage pushes, porting, and "keep going until the tests pass" bugs. One HN commenter reported an integration-test loop that ran "unattended for 24 hours before solving the bug" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46682325)). It also works well as an overnight or "AFK" mode once you have tuned the prompt interactively. Matt Pocock frames this as progressing from human-in-the-loop to AFK ([11 Tips](https://www.aihero.dev/tips-for-ai-coding-with-ralph-wiggum)).
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it when a command cannot verify "done". The plugin README lists "human judgment calls, one-shot operations, unclear success criteria, production debugging" as anti-uses. Do not point it at a mature production codebase with implicit conventions. The Geocodio team warns against exactly this, because rapid generation "creates security/bug surface area" ([Geocodio](https://www.geocod.io/code-and-coordinates/2026-01-27-ralph-loops)). Do not run it where the agent can touch irreversible external systems. Paul Iusztin's [Ralph Loops](https://www.decodingai.com/p/ralph-loops) piece relays Alexey Grigorev's story of an agent running `terraform destroy` on production and deleting two and a half years of data. And do not run it on a $20/month plan. Sustained use needs the $100+ tier ([Kinney](https://stevekinney.com/writing/the-ralph-loop)).
entries.drawbacks:
**Runaway cost.** Every source warns about it. A 50-iteration pass on a large codebase can cost $50–100+ ([paddo.dev](https://paddo.dev/blog/ralph-wiggum-autonomous-loops/)). A Geocodio colleague "exhausted TWO Claude Max 20x subscriptions" ($400/month each) within days. Sean K's [dev.to post](https://dev.to/sean8/i-accidentally-made-claude-ask-itself-the-same-question-1966-times-1c5h) describes the plugin's configuration being written with `max_iterations: 0` (which means unlimited). After that, "Claude attempted this task 1,966 times without producing a single asset" and hijacked every later message until he deleted `.claude/ralph-loop.local.md`.

**Non-convergence.** "For every overnight success, loops fail to converge and waste credits" ([paddo.dev](https://paddo.dev/blog/ralph-wiggum-autonomous-loops/)). Huntley himself: "You'll wake up to a broken codebase... from time to time." Recovery is `git reset` plus a different prompt.

**Reward hacking and false completion.** The stop-hook variant's exit condition is a string the model emits. paddo.dev raises a concern that the hook's language ("do not lie to exit") may make a false completion claim the only path out. Lukas Grigis calls this the referee problem: "an agent grading its own homework gives itself an A every time" ([lukasgrigis.dev](https://lukasgrigis.dev/blog/ralph-loop/)). The fix is a separate evaluator—see [[Evaluator-Optimizer]] and [[Fresh-Context Reviewer]].

**Lost reasoning.** Files preserve artifacts, not deliberation. A later iteration can undo a deliberate earlier decision, because "files are a good place to keep state and a bad place to keep reasoning" ([dev.to/sangampandey](https://dev.to/sangampandey/ralph-loops-are-not-about-throwing-away-context-3m34)).

**Cache economics.** The naive one-liner rebuilds the prompt each iteration. If the prefix is not byte-identical, prompt caching never hits and "you pay full token price on every loop" (same source).

**Duplicate implementations.** Non-deterministic code search can lead an iteration to conclude a feature is missing and re-implement it. Huntley's prompt therefore insists "search codebase (don't assume not implemented) using subagents."

**Quality critiques.** On HN, commenters wrote "Just look at the code quality produced by these loops... It's complete garbage" and "vibe coding with extra steps." Others complained that Huntley's actual PROMPT.md is paywalled, which makes the system hard to reason about ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46682325)). Consensus there: it works for small greenfield projects and is questionable for production.

**Plugin-specific.** Dex Horthy found the official plugin "opaque" and reported it "dies in cryptic ways unless you have `--dangerously-skip-permissions`" ([HumanLayer](https://www.humanlayer.dev/blog/brief-history-of-ralph)). The plugin accumulates context, so Huntley's warning applies: "At some point you get compacted. Compaction is the devil" ([Tessl](https://tessl.io/blog/unpacking-the-unpossible-logic-of-ralph-wiggumstyle-ai-coding)).

entries.name: RalphMAD
entries.summary: Plan with [[BMAD Method]] interactively, then hand the resulting stories to a [[Ralph Loop]] that implements them autonomously, one story per iteration, test-first, committing as it goes.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when you already use BMAD and find its implementation phase slow. That is the complaint it answers. Use it when work decomposes cleanly into stories with acceptance criteria. The loop's quality depends entirely on that decomposition. Use it for overnight or unattended implementation of a plan you have already reviewed. Use the seam idea more widely: any planning methodology that produces discrete stories can feed any loop that consumes a task list.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it if you do not already want BMAD. You inherit its ceremony in full. Do not use it when the stories are vague. Given a vague story, an autonomous loop does confident work on the wrong thing and commits it. Do not use it without reviewing what lands. Plan approval is the only gate in the run, and a commit per story is a boundary, not a review. And be honest about maturity: this is a small wrapper around two other projects, with the dependency risk that implies.
entries.drawbacks: It inherits both parents' weaknesses: BMAD's ceremony and Ralph's dependence on the quality of external state. Story decomposition is the single point of failure. A poorly split story becomes a poorly implemented commit with no one watching. It wraps two independently evolving projects, so an upstream change breaks the seam. Fresh context per story means cross-story context is lost, which matters when stories interact. And the evidence is one README for a small project.

entries.name: ReAct Loop
entries.summary: A ReAct-style agent chooses an action, runs a tool, reads the result, and chooses again. It is useful when the next step depends on what you discover. I would pair the loop with an external success check and a bounded failure path. A final answer tells you the agent stopped. It does not tell you the task succeeded.
entries.whenToUse:
Use the bare loop when each observation changes the next useful action. Examples: tracing an unfamiliar call path, reproducing a bug, inspecting a failing command. For a small, well-defined change, I would let the agent inspect and act without a separate planning document.

It also fits inside larger workflows. [[Plan-and-Execute]] can run a short tool-use loop for each step. [[Orchestrator-Workers]] can give each worker its own loop. The outer pattern decides what task and context each invocation receives.
entries.whenNotToUse:
If you already know the transformation across hundreds of files, a script or fixed pipeline may be easier to verify than hundreds of model decisions. If the task spans sessions, persist requirements and progress. Do not expect the conversation alone to carry them.

I would not run an open-ended repair loop without a check and an explicit attempt or cost limit. Two repeated failures should trigger a new diagnosis, not a third spelling of the same patch. The [Claude Code best-practices guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices) recommends early course correction and concrete verification signals.

Untrusted tool output is another boundary. [Web Agents Should Adopt the Plan-Then-Execute Paradigm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14290) studies a plan-first alternative for web agents. That bears on prompt injection. It does not establish that a written plan alone secures a coding agent. Tool permissions and isolation still belong in the harness.
entries.drawbacks:
Context growth can make the important constraint harder to retain. In the [version 2 context-rot study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17937v2), one code-audit task passed 8 of 10 clean-context runs and 3 of 10 runs in each long-context condition. A second task passed in both settings. The authors do not claim a universal length threshold. I would test the actual workload before prescribing a context size.

Repeated actions can also hide a stalled diagnosis. Preserve the failed command, its output, and what changed between attempts. If the same proposed fix fails twice, stop and reconsider the reproduction. [[Shift-Worker Handoff]] helps when another session must pick up the investigation.

Cost grows with repeated model calls and tool output. Compaction and caching cut some overhead. Neither makes an unbounded task a good idea. Use the harness's budget controls and report a budget stop as incomplete work.

Errors compound when later edits assume an earlier change was correct. Check intermediate behavior and preserve recoverable states with [[Checkpoint and Rollback]]. A reviewer can challenge the interpretation. The original requirement and the test evidence should decide whether the repair holds.

Finally, a repository file or web page can contain instructions meant to redirect the agent. Treat retrieved content as data. [[Sandboxed Execution]] and [[Hooks and Guardrails]] cover execution boundaries that a reasoning loop cannot enforce alone.

entries.name: Reflexion
entries.summary: Reflexion stores an agent's verbal critique of a failed attempt and feeds that lesson into the next attempt. The memory helps only when it changes the next action.
entries.whenToUse: Use Reflexion when you have a cheap, trustworthy evaluator and the first attempt often fails for reasons the model can state. Examples: a failing test with a clear assertion message, a build error, a lint violation, a benchmark that regressed. It makes a retry loop *smarter than a retry*. You do not resend the same prompt. You send the prompt plus "last time you forgot to handle the empty list." It also works as a cross-session habit. If your agent keeps making the same project-specific mistake (wrong test runner, wrong import style), one reflection written to `CLAUDE.md` or a learnings file prevents the whole class of failure.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it where the only judge is the model itself. Without an external signal, Huang et al. show the loop can wander and get worse. Do not use it when failures are non-deterministic or environmental (flaky network, flaky tests). The reflection will confidently blame the wrong cause and poison later attempts. Do not let the reflection buffer grow without bound. The MindStudio guide warns that a learnings file past roughly 80-100 entries becomes "worse than no file at all" because it crowds out useful context.
entries.drawbacks: Reflections can be wrong. The model explains the failure with a plausible story. If the story is wrong, the next attempt goes the wrong way. This is the mechanism behind the degradation Huang et al. observed. Reflection adds a full extra LLM call per failure. The Hugging Face overview flags this as the main efficiency cost and suggests that future systems "trigger reflection only when needed." Persistent learnings files bloat and go stale. Entries true in March are wrong in June, and nothing expires them, so practitioners must schedule consolidation passes. Finally, "reflection" as a prompt phrase is now so common that practitioners report over-generic output ("be more careful next time") that carries no information. For this reason the dev.to write-up adds a "META" section that teaches Claude to write rules precisely. It reports no quantitative results.

entries.name: Repository Map Context
entries.summary: A repository map gives the agent a compact index of files, symbols, and relationships. The agent gets it before it spends context reading implementation.
entries.whenToUse: Use a repository map when three things hold. The codebase is large enough that "read everything" is impossible or wasteful. The agent repeatedly touches the wrong file or reinvents a helper that already exists. The code is statically analyzable: tree-sitter has a grammar and symbols mean what they say. A map works best at the start of a task, before the agent has any files in context. It also works for cross-cutting changes, where knowing which files reference a symbol is the whole problem (CodePlan's package-migration case).
entries.whenNotToUse: Skip it for small repositories (the AgentPatterns write-up suggests under roughly 20 files, where reading source is cheaper). Skip it for heavily metaprogrammed or dynamically dispatched code, where the AST does not reflect runtime structure. Skip it for repositories that change faster than the map is rebuilt. Skip it when the whole relevant subtree fits comfortably in context. The map is orientation, not truth. An agent that treats it as complete will miss files ranked out of the budget.
entries.drawbacks: Silent failure is the one most reported. An HN user wrote that Aider "has never successfully created a repository map, regardless of whether the codebase is [Python](https://www.python.org/), JS, or TS." Maintainers pointed at untracked files, encoding issues, and the `/map` and `--show-repository-map` commands as diagnostics ([HN 42185733](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42185733)). Ranking bias is another. PageRank favors widely referenced utilities, so the map fills with `utils.py` while the obscure file holding the bug is cut. Staleness bites in fast-moving branches. And the map has no bodies by design, so it can mislead the agent about behavior: a signature looks right, but the body does something else.

entries.name: Research Plan Implement
aliases: Advanced Context Engineering for Coding Agents
entries.summary: Research, planning, and implementation form a relay. First learn what the repository and sources say. Then write an executable plan. Then make and verify the change.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for changes in unfamiliar or large codebases where a wrong approach costs a lot. Examples: cross-cutting features, removals that touch many files, bug fixes in code you do not know. The goose team's worked example is a 10-phase removal spanning 32 files. It took 52 minutes (9 research, 4 planning, 39 implementation) and drew zero review comments on the pull request. Use it when you want to review something smaller than the diff. RPI answers "code review is the bottleneck." Use it whenever a task will not fit in one context window, because the artifacts are the resume points.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for small changes in well-understood code. The aipatternbook entry says plain plan mode suffices there, and three review cycles are pure overhead. Do not expect it to solve an intractable problem. Horthy reports failed attempts (removing a dependency from parquet-java) and writes that "There are big hard problems you cannot just prompt your way through in 7 hours." Do not run it unattended. The leverage comes from a human reading the research and plan. If nobody will read them, you have a slower [[Plan-and-Execute]].
entries.drawbacks:
**Overhead.** Three artifacts and three review points per task. The aipatternbook entry lists "three review cycles add significant overhead" and "not cost-effective for small changes." The same complaint applies to [[Spec-Driven Development]], and the two patterns produce similar volumes of markdown.

**Artifact quality is the whole game.** Phases communicate only through documents, so "conversational nuance is lost between phases" and the plan is only as good as the research it read. A research document that quietly includes a wrong assumption is the failure the no-opinions rule tries to prevent. The rule does not eliminate it.

**Instruction drift during implementation.** The implementer should flag deviations, not improvise, but plan adherence is advisory. The context-rot study of skills in long tool-using trajectories found that small omissions still break artifacts even when a requirements list stays over 92% covered. It also found that a detailed external checklist beat generic self-checking 10/10 to 5/10 ([arXiv 2607.17937](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17937)). That is the case for explicit, mechanical per-phase verification steps in the plan.

**It doesn't fix maintainability on its own.** HumanLayer's own "Why Software Factories Fail" concedes that models are not rewarded for maintainable design. It says removing human review "leads to production incidents and degraded codebases within months." RPI moves review upstream. It does not remove it.

**Limited independent evidence.** The pattern's author and a tool vendor's tutorial self-report the headline results: the 300k-line Rust fix, 35k lines in 7 hours, and the 32-file removal with zero review comments. Searches for HN or Reddit threads debating RPI returned nothing beyond secondary coverage. The pattern is widely copied but little critiqued in public.

entries.name: Reversa
entries.summary: Spec-driven development pointed backwards. A multi-agent pipeline reads a legacy system and produces traceable operational specifications. It marks each claim with a confidence level and records the gaps it could not resolve.
entries.whenToUse: Use it on legacy systems facing modernization. That is the case it was built for. Use it before letting agents work on an undocumented codebase. An agent with no specification will infer one silently and act on it. This pipeline makes the same inference explicit and reviewable. Use it when the people who knew the rules are gone and the code is the only source left. Use the gap-preservation discipline anywhere you extract requirements from an existing system, whatever the tooling.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it on greenfield work, where forward spec-driven development applies. Do not treat its output as authoritative. The claims are inferred, and the confidence markings exist because some of them are wrong. Do not skip the human validation the gaps call for. Skipping it discards the framework's main safeguard. Do not assume the COBOL-to-Go result transfers to your stack. It is one exploratory case study.
entries.drawbacks: Every claim is an inference from code, and code encodes bugs as faithfully as intentions. An extracted specification will document a defect as a requirement. That is the classic hazard of reverse engineering. The framework's mechanisms surface it but cannot solve it. The model assigns the confidence markings, and the [[LLM-as-Judge]] literature finds that kind of calibration unreliable. Five hundred claims is a large review burden, and the work must happen for the output to be trustworthy. The evidence is one exploratory case study by the framework's own authors.

entries.name: Reward Hacking Guardrails
entries.summary: These defenses keep an agent from satisfying the check instead of the task. Freeze the tests. Hold some out. Cap the achievable score, so a perfect one is evidence of cheating. Monitor test edits. Enforce all of it with hooks, not instructions.
entries.whenToUse: Use it any time a check is also a target. That means every test-driven agent loop. Use it whenever the agent has write access to the files that judge it. That is the default, and it should change. Use it in unattended runs, where nobody notices a deleted test until much later. Use it in benchmark or evaluation settings, where the incentive to game is strongest and the result is a number everyone quotes. Use the capping idea whenever you are measuring agents rather than shipping their work.
entries.whenNotToUse: Never leave the oracle unprotected when it decides anything. But keep the defense in proportion. A solo interactive session where you read every diff does not need held-out suites. Elaborate defenses around a check nobody relies on are wasted effort. Holding out tests also costs feedback quality, because an agent that cannot see why it failed iterates worse. Make the split deliberate, not maximal. Capping is an evaluation technique. It does not belong in a production suite where you want everything green.
entries.drawbacks: Each defense has a cost and buys one specific thing. Frozen tests mean genuinely wrong tests cannot be fixed inside the loop. That produces stuck runs that look like agent failure. Held-out tests degrade the feedback signal, so the agent iterates blind against the part that matters most. Capping is unnatural in production and applies only where you control the evaluation. Monitoring catches direct edits and misses indirect ones: a configuration change that excludes a directory, a rewritten fixture, a conditional that makes an assertion vacuous. None of this addresses the deepest version of the problem. There, the code passes every test and still does the wrong thing, because the specification was the weak link, not the oracle.

entries.name: Role Pipeline
entries.summary: A role pipeline gives each phase a narrow job—research, plan, implement, review, verify—and hands explicit artifacts between phases.
entries.whenToUse:
Use it when the stages need different capabilities. Planning benefits from read-only tools and a strong model. Implementation needs write access. Review benefits from a fresh context that never saw the implementer's rationalizations. Testing needs to run things and perhaps write only under `tests/`. Claude Code's best-practices guide gives the two-session form. A Writer session implements a rate limiter. A Reviewer session is asked to "look for edge cases, race conditions, and consistency with our existing middleware patterns." The review is fed back to the writer. The reviewer and tester stages exist to close the guide's "trust-then-verify gap" failure pattern.

Use it when you want permissions to encode policy. A reviewer with no Edit tool cannot "fix" a finding by weakening the assertion. A planner with no Bash cannot start implementing early. A tester restricted to `Edit(tests/**)` cannot make tests pass by editing production code. Per-role tool scoping prevents the [aipatternbook Delegation Chain](https://aipatternbook.com/delegation-chain) antipattern: "blanket tool access: all agents get identical toolsets regardless of actual tasks."

Use it when the work is long enough that context rot would blur the plan. Handing a written plan to a fresh implementer follows the Claude Code advice to write a spec, then "start a fresh session to execute it."
entries.whenNotToUse:
Do not use it for small, well-scoped changes. The Claude Code documentation says plan mode "adds overhead" and that "if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan." A four-stage pipeline for a typo fix costs four times the tokens for no benefit. Zenflow's founders saw the same in their own experiments: "heavy multi-step processes often multiply errors rather than fix them. Massive, complex prompt templates look good on paper but fail in practice."

Do not use it as a substitute for verification. MAST's data ([Cemri et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v2)) is instructive. "Disobey role specification" was only 0.5% of failures. "No or incomplete verification" (6.8%), "incorrect verification" (6.7%), and "premature termination" (7.8%) together were over a fifth. ChatDev, the archetypal role pipeline, achieved only 33.3% correctness on simple ProgramDev tasks. Agents stay in character fine. The pipeline fails when the tester stage is decorative.

Do not build long chains of pure-persona stages. If your "architect," "PM," and "analyst" have the same tools, the same model, and the same context, you have one agent with three hats and three times the latency.
entries.drawbacks:
Persona theater. Zheng et al. found that personas do not improve performance. The label in the system prompt buys nothing by itself. Only differences in context, tools, and model do. Paddo.dev makes the practitioner version of the point: BMAD-style chains simulate "human coordination friction through phase gates and role confusion."

Handoff loss. Each stage sees an artifact, not the transcript, so anything not written down is gone. Cognition's original objection ("share full agent traces, not just individual messages") critiques role pipelines directly. MAST's "loss of conversation history" (3.3%) and "proceeding with wrong assumptions instead of seeking clarification" (11.7%) are the measured symptoms. ChatDev's "communicative dehallucination," where the assistant role asks before acting, exists to patch exactly this.

Reviewer over-reporting. The Claude Code best-practices callout: "Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering: extra abstraction layers, defensive code, and tests for cases that can't happen." Unbounded review-fix loops converge on bloat, not correctness.

Cost and latency grow linearly with stages, and each stage re-reads the codebase. Per-stage system prompts and file reads are the same token multiplier HN users complained about for subagents generally ([thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48883796)).

Rubber-stamp testers. If the tester can edit production code, or the implementer also writes the tests, the pipeline collapses into self-grading. MAST's verification failures are the evidence.

Automatic role selection is unreliable. From the Claude Code subagents [HN thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44686726): "Most of the time they aren't used when it would be appropriate." Pipelines that rely on the model choosing to invoke the reviewer will skip the reviewer. Invoke stages explicitly, or script them.

entries.name: Roo Boomerang Orchestrator
entries.summary: Boomerang tasks let a parent agent delegate a focused child task, receive a result, and continue with the returned context. The parent stays responsible for the overall outcome.
entries.whenToUse: Boomerang fits multi-part features in an IDE where you want a visible plan and small, bounded changes. HN's phn found that Orchestrator mode "'chews' the tasks I give it to then spoon feed into sub-tasks in 'Code' mode, leaving less room to stray from very focused 'bite-sized' changes... since it doesn't change a lot at a time." So it stays steerable ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46529815)). It is also the easiest way to mix models by role: a strong reasoning model for Architect and Orchestrator, a cheap fast one for Code. jjmarr recommends it when you want the agent to "do tons of requirements analysis before starting work" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44071050)).
entries.whenNotToUse: Small changes do not need an orchestrator. shostack noted "the forcing function of needing to think through technical and business considerations... up front... can be tedious if you are the type that likes to jump in and hack at it" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44684572)). Context passes only through summaries. Tasks with tightly coupled subparts lose information at each boundary, and a single Code-mode session may do better. Roo Code is discontinued as a product, so new adopters should look at Kilo Code or at the same pattern in Claude Code subagents.
entries.drawbacks: Summaries are lossy. The orchestrator can proceed on a rosy report from a child that did not finish. Nothing verifies a subtask's claim unless a Debug or test subtask is added. The orchestrator model writes the briefs and can omit constraints the user gave earlier, since children do not see the conversation. Approval fatigue is real when a feature explodes into many subtasks, and auto-approving removes the safety the pattern relies on. Sequential subtasks make it slow compared with parallel worktree approaches. The product was discontinued in April 2026. The methodology lives on in forks and in other tools' subagent features.

entries.name: RooFlow
entries.summary: A memory bank plus five specialized modes for the Roo Code extension, with prompts written in YAML rather than Markdown to cut token consumption.
entries.whenToUse: As a tool, it is hard to recommend. The extension it extends is discontinued. Two things in it are worth taking elsewhere. First, the five-file split by volatility is a better default than a single memory file. Stable context can be re-read without being rewritten, and the split works with any agent. Second, the decision log—architectural decisions with their rationale—is the file most teams lack. It is the one that most often stops an agent from undoing a deliberate choice.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not adopt it as a tool. The host extension shut down in April 2026. Even while it ran, the extension's maintainers explicitly did not endorse the bundle, which was built on a feature they named "Footgun". Do not take the YAML claim on faith. No figure accompanies it, and prompt formatting is exactly the kind of micro-optimization that fails to reproduce. Do not use five memory files where two would do. That is the standing critique of memory-bank schemes recorded under [[Memory Bank]]: reading them all at session start costs the context they were meant to protect.
entries.drawbacks: The host product is discontinued, which is decisive for adoption. The host never endorsed the bundle. Replacing an extension's system prompts through an experimental escape hatch is a supportability problem even when the host is alive. Five files read at session start is a real context cost. The scheme is also the most prone to the failure where maintaining the memory bank displaces the work. The YAML efficiency claim is unmeasured. It is a community bundle over an extension, so it inherits two dependencies, not one. And the files, like all agent-maintained memory, drift when nobody checks them. Nothing here detects drift.

entries.name: Sandboxed Execution
entries.summary: Put the agent behind a filesystem and network boundary that fits the task. Keep credentials and valuable host state outside it.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for any unattended or loop-style run ([[Ralph Loop]], [[Task Queue Consumer]], CI fan-out with `claude -p`). Use it for any session on a repository you do not fully trust (prompt injection via README, issues, or dependencies). Use it when a team wants engineers to work without permission prompts but with a policy floor (managed settings inside the image, `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode`). Use it for many parallel agents ([[Parallel Worktree Swarm]]) that each need their own environment. Use it when you cannot afford to leak credentials. Keep them out of the sandbox entirely and use short-lived, repository-scoped tokens.
entries.whenNotToUse: Skip it when the task needs the host's real environment (GUI apps, hardware, host-only services) and replicating that costs more than the risk. Skip it for quick interactive edits where prompts are not painful. Never use it as a substitute for judgment on trusted-but-destructive operations. The sandbox does not stop the agent from running `DROP TABLE` on a database whose credentials you mounted, or from force-pushing to a remote it can reach. Anthropic's own warning: "dev containers do not prevent a malicious project from exfiltrating anything accessible inside the container, including the Claude Code credentials stored in ~/.claude."
entries.drawbacks:
- **Not a full security boundary.** Docker shares the host kernel; HN's matheusmoreira built a VM-based tool because "sharing a kernel with untrusted software is too dangerous". Anthropic: "no system is completely immune to all attacks."
- **Credentials inside the box are fair game.** `~/.claude` tokens, mounted cloud creds, `.env` files: anything readable can leak if the network allowlist is loose. Bind-mounting the workspace means the agent "can still modify any file in the bind-mounted workspace, which appears directly on your host".
- **Hooks weaken under bypass.** With `--dangerously-skip-permissions` hooks fire asynchronously, so a PreToolUse blocker can lose the race ([nah, HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47343927)).
- **Friction and lock-in.** Docker Sandboxes require login; several HN commenters rejected it on that basis ("Requires login. Garbage."). Devcontainers need Docker, VS Code or a compatible IDE, and the firewall needs extra capabilities that "might as well run these processes in a VM" (avtar on HN).
- **False sense of safety.** "Sure, but all projects are version controlled? You only mount the project dir so you can only lose your current changes" (tjoff) is true only if you commit often and mount nothing else. See [[Checkpoint and Rollback]].
- **Auto mode is closer to bypass than to review.** One HN commenter noted "the new auto mode is closer in spirit to --dangerously-skip-permissions than it is to the current system"; a classifier is a probabilistic guard.
- **Real losses happen anyway.** The production-database deletion thread shows that a sandbox does nothing if the agent holds production credentials.

entries.name: Screenshot Feedback Loop
entries.summary: For visual work, a screenshot is a test artifact. Render the page, inspect the image and console, make a bounded correction, and repeat against a concrete target.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for front-end or UI work where correctness is visual: layout, responsive behavior, design fidelity, visual regressions. Use it to debug runtime errors the test suite does not catch (console errors on load, hydration mismatches). Use it when implementing from a Figma mock or a competitor's screenshot. Use it for unattended UI tasks, where the screenshot loop is the only verification available. Use it for mobile and desktop work via simulator/emulator MCPs.
entries.whenNotToUse: Skip it for backend or library code with a real test suite. Tests are cheaper and deterministic. Skip it for pixel-perfect requirements the model cannot judge reliably (subtle spacing, color accuracy). Use visual-regression tooling with numeric thresholds instead. Skip it for long autonomous loops with unbounded screenshots, which bloat context and cost. Skip it for sensitive apps. Screenshots and GIF recordings capture "everything visible in the browser, including account details on logged-in pages".
entries.drawbacks:
- **Context cost.** Browser tools add tokens even when idle ("Enabling Chrome by default in the CLI increases context usage since browser tools are always loaded"); the Playwright MCP's schema and screenshots are heavy. That motivated the skill-based and CLI-based alternatives.
- **The model is not a great judge.** "Taking screenshots and recording is not quite the same as 'seeing'... If the tool can identify issues and improvements... that's I think useful" (zkmon on HN); ProofShot's author leaves pass/fail to the human on purpose.
- **Flaky infrastructure.** Chrome extension service workers go idle ("Receiving end does not exist"), modal dialogs block commands, connections drop in long sessions.
- **Iteration without convergence.** Without a concrete target ("this mock", "no console errors"), the agent can loop on subjective improvements. Bound the iterations.
- **Tool sprawl and NIH.** The ProofShot thread devolved into "What does this do that playwright-cli doesn't?" Pick one capture path per project.
- **Privacy.** Shared recordings and screenshots of logged-in pages leak data.

entries.name: Self-Refinement
entries.summary: Self-refinement alternates generation, critique, and revision in one model context. It improves an artifact when the feedback is specific. Execution checks or an independent reviewer beat self-agreement.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when the output is judged on qualities the model spots well on a second read: naming, structure, missing docstrings, obvious edge cases, style-guide conformance, prose clarity in commit messages. Use it as a cheap pre-filter before an expensive external check. Use it when no grounded signal exists (design documentation, plans, migration strategies). Expect modest gains there. Ask for critique along *specific* dimensions, not "is this good?".
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not rely on it for correctness. If tests exist, run them. If they do not, write one. Do not run many rounds in one context. The paper's gains come mostly from the first one or two iterations, and Anthropic advises clearing context after repeated corrections. Do not make it the only reviewer for security-sensitive or agentic-safety checks. Use a fresh-context reviewer.
entries.drawbacks: The main failure is confident agreement with a wrong draft. Huang et al. show accuracy can drop after self-correction on reasoning tasks. A second failure is oscillation. The critic finds a nit, the refiner fixes it and introduces another, and the loop burns tokens without converging. A third is over-engineering. A critic told to find problems will find them, and Anthropic's documentation warns that "chasing every finding leads to over-engineering: extra abstraction layers, defensive code, and tests for cases that can't happen." Cost grows linearly with rounds, and each round re-reads the full history.

entries.name: Shift-Worker Handoff
entries.summary: A shift-worker handoff makes a long task resumable. It records the current state, decisions, failures, verification evidence, and next bounded action. An honest failed checkpoint is useful. A clean-looking but unverified handoff is not.
entries.whenToUse: Use it whenever a project will outlive one context window: multi-day builds, scientific or numerical work with long verification cycles, anything you want to check on from your phone rather than babysit. Use it when a human must be able to read the state of the work at any point. People can read the progress file and feature list. They cannot read a raw transcript. It also suits work where earlier failed approaches are expensive to rediscover. The cosmology team's changelog existed so sessions would not repeat gauge-convention mistakes. Reach for it when auto-compaction is losing your decisions. The handoff plugin exists because compaction summaries drop things.
entries.whenNotToUse: Skip it for work that fits in one session. The initializer overhead and ceremony are pure cost. Skip it when tasks are truly independent and parallel with no shared narrative. That is a [[Task Queue Consumer]] problem, and HN critics pointed out Anthropic was "attempting to reinvent a project tracker" with JSON files when tools like Plane already exist ([HN, `_boffin_`](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46081704)). Do not expect the handoff to substitute for understanding: "You can't outsource to the LLM" the architectural comprehension needed to build the system (`roughly`, same thread).
entries.drawbacks:
*Handoffs lie.* Anthropic found Claude "performed poorly on feature verification without explicit instruction" and marked features passing that were not. The fix was forcing browser-based end-to-end testing. Even then, Puppeteer could not see native alert modals, so modal-dependent features stayed buggier.

*Progress file rot.* HN commenters on the Ralph history thread flagged "context rot from growing implementation documents" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46682325)). A progress file appended to for weeks becomes its own context problem. The arXiv study [Filesystem-Based Memory for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26637) (Zhou et al., July 2026) found that organized memory stores "roughly halve retrieval cost where material is large," yet agents "struggle to maintain organization over time". The memory bank decays unless something curates it.

*Constraints lose their scope.* A summary can omit a boundary or turn a temporary conclusion into a permanent rule. The older [Governance Decay lead](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22528) concerns policy retention, not a controlled comparison of coding handoff files. Its figures are not used here as a handoff effect size. Preserve consequential constraints with their authority and rationale. Then verify that the incoming worker can retrieve them.

*Artifacts survive, reasoning doesn't.* A handoff records what was done, rarely why. Later shifts may undo deliberate decisions ([dev.to/sangampandey](https://dev.to/sangampandey/ralph-loops-are-not-about-throwing-away-context-3m34)). Addy Osmani calls the analogous risk "alignment drift": goals lose fidelity through repeated summarization.

*Domain blindness across shifts.* The cosmology agent "made elementary mistakes (gauge convention errors) that domain experts would catch instantly" and spent hours on bugs a cosmologist would recognize. No handoff file supplies expertise the model lacks. The final solver was explicitly "not production-grade."

*Cost of the long tail.* `roughly` on HN: the first 70% is easy, but the last 30% needs "multi-agent judge setups, external memory, context management" at "several hundred dollars per run" without guarantees.

entries.name: Skill Library
entries.summary: A skill library packages discoverable instructions with optional scripts, templates, and references. Progressive loading gives the agent specialist behavior without putting every workflow in every context.
entries.whenToUse: Use a skill library when the same multi-step procedure recurs across sessions or repositories: release checklists, migration recipes, "how we write a database migration here," PDF or spreadsheet handling, deploy steps, a fixed code-review rubric. It is also the right home for anything Anthropic's CLAUDE.md guidance says to keep *out* of CLAUDE.md: "for domain knowledge or workflows that are only relevant sometimes, use skills instead," because skills load on demand, not every turn. A team can also use skills to encode process so the agent follows it the same way for everyone.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not put project-wide, always-relevant rules in a skill. That is CLAUDE.md's job. Do not let the agent auto-generate skills from single successes without verification. Voyager stores only programs that pass self-verification, and a procedural memory of unverified shortcuts makes bad habits permanent. Do not install skills from untrusted sources. They execute code. Do not expect skills to fix a capability the model lacks. They encode *how*, not *whether*.
entries.drawbacks: Skill rot: a procedure written for last quarter's build system silently misleads, and nothing expires it. Triggering errors: with many skills, the description scan can pick the wrong one or none. Practitioners report tuning descriptions like search keywords. Security: a skill is arbitrary code and instructions. Anthropic's post warns of exfiltration risk and recommends auditing dependencies and network calls. Over-proceduralization: encoding every habit as a skill can make the agent rigid on tasks that needed judgment. Curation is real work. Voyager's library was self-verified against a game, but a coding skill needs a human or a test to certify it before it is stored.

entries.name: Slash Command Workflow
entries.summary: A slash command gives a repeatable workflow a named entry point, arguments, and an explicit permission boundary. It is a task interface whose implementation you can inspect.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for procedures you run more than a few times a week: catching up on a branch, preparing a pull request, triaging an issue, running a migration checklist, the team's TDD ritual ("My Agent Skill for Test-Driven Development", HN 251 points). Use it for domain knowledge that only some tasks need (a payments API's conventions, a game engine's idioms) and that would be dead weight in CLAUDE.md. Use it for anything with bundled scripts or references (schemas, style guides, fixtures) that the agent should consult, not reconstruct. Use it for team standards you want shared across Claude Code and Codex from one folder.
entries.whenNotToUse: Shrivu Shankar's rule: "if you have a long list of complex, custom slash commands, you've created an anti-pattern." He keeps only `/catchup` and `/pr` ([sshh.io](https://blog.sshh.io/p/how-i-use-every-claude-code-feature)). Anson Biggs adds that asking the agent to write a skill for something it is bad at "is identical to thinking blocks." Skills earn their place only for "Remembering a novel problem, and avoiding repetition" ([notes.ansonbiggs.com](https://notes.ansonbiggs.com/youre-probably-using-agent-skills-wrong/)). One-line facts belong in CLAUDE.md. Hard rules belong in hooks. Things the model already does well need no skill.
entries.drawbacks:
- *Supply-chain risk.* Skills execute in your environment. Malicious skills have already been distributed (HN, Jan 2026). Willison: "we really need to figure out how best to sandbox these environments such that attacks such as prompt injections are limited to an acceptable amount of damage."
- *Auto-invocation surprises.* A skill the model judges "relevant" can fire when you did not want it, even one with side effects. Hence the manual-only flag.
- *Truncation after compaction* drops everything past 5k tokens of a skill body.
- *Bloat by another name.* Large skill collections bring back the CLAUDE.md problem one layer down. SkillsBench found smaller bundles beat larger ones.
- *Self-written skills are low value.* Agents "can't create valuable procedural knowledge without first understanding the gaps in their own capabilities" (Biggs); the ETH AGENTS.md study found LLM-generated context files slightly hurt.
- *Fragmentation and overwhelm.* "Agents, sub agents, skills, claud.md, agents.md, rules, hooks, etc." (HN); adastra22 noted that per-tool sections in CLAUDE.md are "largely a waste of tokens these days. Use the skills feature". That is true, but it adds another mechanism to learn.

entries.name: Smoke Test on Entry
entries.summary: Every session starts the application and runs an end-to-end check before it touches new work. The check catches breakage the previous session did not know it caused.
entries.whenToUse: Use it in any run where sessions hand off: overnight loops, [[Shift-Worker Handoff]] setups, [[Fresh-Agent Chaining]], anything driven by a queue. Use it when the application has meaningful startup behavior—migrations, environment variables, service dependencies—because cross-session breakage concentrates there. Use it when several agents work in parallel and merge into a shared branch, since no single worktree shows integration damage.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it when the check is slow enough to dominate the session. A ten-minute entry check on a twenty-minute task is a bad trade, and the agent will start skipping it. Do not use it in place of the full suite before merge. It is a liveness check, not a correctness check. Do not use it for pure library work with no runnable application, where the unit suite already is the end-to-end path. Do not let a flaky entry check stand. An agent that learns the check fails randomly will learn to ignore it.
entries.drawbacks: The check can itself be wrong. A smoke test that only confirms the process started will pass on an application that returns 500 for every request. This is the most common bad implementation: readiness probes that prove the port is open, not that the service can serve. A slow or flaky check gets skipped, and an agent that skips a check silently is worse than no check. The pattern also spends session budget before any value is produced, which matters when the budget is tight. And it says nothing about correctness: an application that starts and serves the wrong content passes.

entries.name: Software Factory
entries.summary: Team-scale agent development in four stages: product requirements, architecture, program design, then vertical slices. Humans keep reviewing. Models optimize for passing tests, and nothing penalizes a decaying codebase.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for team-scale agent work, where several people and agents touch one system. Use it when review is the bottleneck, since the whole argument is about moving attention earlier to cut review volume. Use it when maintainability matters more than throughput: long-lived systems, not prototypes. Use vertical slices regardless. They improve reviewability at no cost.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for solo work on a small codebase, where four planning phases outweigh the work. Do not use it for throwaway prototypes, where you will never pay the maintenance cost. Do not treat the phases as gates needing sign-off. That recreates the ceremony [[Specsmaxxing]] and others react against. And do not expect a measurement: "30 minutes saves hours" is a claim from experience, not a study.
entries.drawbacks: Four planning phases are real overhead. Teams will skip them under pressure, starting with the one that feels most abstract. The central claim is unmeasured. No data supports the thirty-minutes-to-hours trade. The maintainability-erosion argument reasons about incentives. It does not observe decay. Planning can be wrong, and a wrong architecture phase constrains everything after it more than no architecture phase would. It assumes review capacity exists, the very constraint [[Dark Factory]] exists to escape. And "human steering" is not specified, so the prescription only gives a direction.

entries.name: Spec Kit
entries.summary: Spec Kit turns intent into linked Markdown artifacts—specification, plan, tasks, and implementation—through a portable command workflow. The documents organize the work. Tests still establish behavior.
entries.whenToUse: Spec Kit fits moderate greenfield features. The requirements should be unclear enough that writing them down helps, and several agents or people should implement from the same document. HN user 42point2 reported a team using it "on a large-ish feature, with several repos involved... The constitution that's created as the first step is valuable in its own right. Something that can be used for onboarding both engineers and LLMs" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45798473)). It is also the least vendor-locked methodology. The same `specs/` directory works with Copilot, Claude Code, Codex and Gemini. Users report mixing agents: one for specify/plan, another for implement. Delimarsky is explicit that the goal is not one-shot products: "human in the loop is as important as it ever was."
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for small fixes. Böckeler's line, borrowed from her Kiro experience but applied to all three tools, is that it feels "like using a sledgehammer to crack a nut". It is also a poor fit if you are "too confused to write the spec" (the title of a widely shared February 2026 post on HN, [46955747](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46955747)). The clarify step helps, but the workflow assumes intent exists to be captured. Brownfield work is under-served. A common HN complaint is that every tutorial builds a todo app from scratch, with little guidance on "incremental improvements or refactorings to a huge legacy code base" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45610996)).
entries.drawbacks:
Verbosity and review burden are the top complaints. Böckeler wrote she would "rather review code than all these markdown files" and found Spec Kit "particularly verbose and repetitive". A March 2026 write-up titled "SpecKit: Not Impressed" describes reviewing "47 tasks to verify 3 user stories" and a checklist of "around 30 different issues that I needed to clarify" before any code. Then the author found that "no tests were generated and unsurprisingly the application did not work at all". The verdict: "the worst of both worlds: the complexity of code and the lack of verifiability of documentation" ([jaksa.me](https://jaksa.me/blog/2026-03-26-speckit-not-impressed)). On HN, yoaviram let Spec Kit run for ten days on a new codebase. "When it finished, there was still a huge gap. Most tests were failing, and the build was not successful" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45610996)); ctxc "had to dump it eventually when it generated steps that were the equivalent of Tony Stark building a robot from scratch in a cave when 'just screw this bolt on' would have sufficed."

Spec drift is the structural weakness. The same critic found that when corrections were requested "the agent modified just some of the documents and left the others unchanged". Böckeler's judgement that Spec Kit is "spec-first only, not spec-anchored over time" means nothing keeps spec.md true once code diverges. `converge` (added in v1.0) is a partial answer. HN's trjordan put the deeper objection: "There has to be one source of truth. If you want to go all in on specs, you must fully commit to allowing the AI to regenerate the codebase from scratch at any point... a laughable stance with current tools" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45798473)). Macedo's taxonomy paper lists "drift between specification and code, excessive trust in generated artifacts, fragility of community extensions, platform dependence" as recurring risks across the category.

Discipline erosion is subtler. apex_sloth wrote: "The longer I use it, the less code I read myself and just fire quick /implement loops and go do something else." The meta-critique from marmelab's "Spec-Driven Development: The Waterfall Strikes Back" (HN, 225 points, [45935763](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45935763)) is that front-loading complete specifications brings back the failure mode agile was invented to escape.

entries.name: Spec Kitty
entries.summary: Spec-driven development with the missing runtime attached: repository-native mission state, Kanban lanes, a worktree per work package, and an explicit `next -> review -> accept -> merge` loop.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when you like the spec-plan-tasks shape but keep losing track of which tasks are in flight. Use it when several agents implement in parallel and branch collisions keep recurring. Worktree isolation is built in. Use it when you want project state auditable in git, not in a tool's database. Use it when explicit review and accept gates match how your team merges.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for small changes. The full spec-to-merge pipeline is heavy for a one-file fix. Do not use it if you already run a task tracker you like. A repository-native board is a second source of truth, and two boards are worse than one. Do not adopt it for the dashboard alone. Weigh its maturity: it is a small independent project, with the sustainability profile that implies.
entries.drawbacks: Process weight is the obvious cost. The same objection applies to every framework in [[Spec Kit]]'s family: the pipeline has to earn its overhead. Repository-native state means merge conflicts in the state files themselves, an irritating kind to resolve. Worktrees multiply disk usage and dependency installs. The evidence is thin: one project README, no independent evaluation, a small maintainer base. Adopting it is a bet on the project as much as on the method.

entries.name: Spec-Driven Development
entries.summary: Spec-driven development treats the specification as the durable source of intent. Plans, tasks, code, and tests derive from it. The useful question is whether the spec stays aligned after implementation.
entries.whenToUse:
Use it for greenfield or well-bounded features. The requirements should be genuinely known, the cost of building the wrong thing high, and more than one person or agent should need a shared, durable statement of intent. HN user 42point2 found Spec Kit's constitution "valuable for onboarding engineers and LLMs" on a large multi-repository feature ([HN 45798473](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45798473)). In the "still using it?" thread, user waldopat argued "LLMs dramatically reduce the cost of both good documentation and good technical specifications." waldopat also recommended ~750-line documents ([HN 46864948](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46864948)). Diaz et al. make the team-scale case: when agents do the typing, SDD is where accountability and transferability live.

Use it when you want an artifact that survives the session and the tool. RPI research and plan files are per-task and disposable. A spec is meant to be the thing future changes start from. Use the Constitutional or VSDD variants when you need enforceable non-functional constraints (security, style, architecture) on every change.
entries.whenNotToUse:
Do not use it while you are still discovering the problem. The most repeated critique comes from a post titled exactly "Spec driven development doesn't work if you're too confused to write the spec." Its point: writing a precise spec *is* the hard thinking.
