"Any spec unambiguous enough to work is already close enough to code that we could just express it as code" ([deontologician](https://publish.obsidian.md/deontologician/Posts/Spec-driven+development+doesn%27t+work+if+you%27re+too+confused+to+write+the+spec)). HN user _pdp_ on the VSDD thread: "you can't spec out something you have no clue how to build."

Do not use the full pipeline for small changes. Böckeler watched Kiro turn a small bug fix into "16 acceptance criteria across 4 user stories" and called it a "sledgehammer to crack a nut." Zaninotto's date-display feature generated 1,300 lines of spec. Anthropic's rule of thumb for planning applies with more force here: if you can describe the diff in a sentence, skip it.

Be cautious on large brownfield codebases. Zaninotto reports "diminishing returns on large, existing codebases." Spec Kit Agents exists because plain Spec Kit agents "often remain 'context blind' in large, evolving repositories, leading to hallucinated APIs and architectural violations."
entries.drawbacks:
*Markdown fatigue and double review.* Böckeler: "To be honest, I'd rather review code than all these markdown files." Zaninotto lists "double code review" (spec, then implementation) and says the volume "exhausts developers." HN user danielvaughn: "I don't want to read a wall of text." gherkinnn: "I have to read a lot of prose."

*The agent ignores the spec anyway.* Böckeler found that "despite comprehensive specifications and checklists, agents frequently ignored instructions or over-eagerly applied them, creating duplicates and violating existing code structure." She warns that "larger context windows don't guarantee proper instruction adherence." Zaninotto calls this "false security." HN user Marazan: agents get near-perfect, then "fail mysteriously." You either intervene constantly or write specs "so detailed they defeat the purpose."

*Waterfall dynamics.* The Marmelab thread's anti camp (pydry, constantcrying) argued the real issue is feedback-loop length. Enough spec detail to guide the LLM makes iteration slow. Too little leaves it unguided, and quick changes mean "abandoning the spec entirely." HN user dgabriel, months later: "Spec driven development is waterfall, and we're all in the midst of a new experiment to see if it works." Böckeler notes small iterative steps "almost seem counter to the idea of SDD."

*Spec rot and LLM-maintained specs.* Spec-first specs stop matching the code after the first change. If the agent also maintains the spec, "the specs end up being LLM maintained, which defeats the purpose" (danielvaughn). SpecMine exists partly in response. Nobody had measured whether specs and code actually co-evolve.

*Non-determinism at the spec-as-source level.* Böckeler saw Tessl produce different code from the same spec across runs. She warns spec-as-source "might end up with the downsides of both MDD and LLMs: Inflexibility *and* non-determinism." She compares it to Model-Driven Development, which "never took off for business applications." A 2026 cross-model study of SDD frameworks found they "differ fundamentally in how they enforce traceability." It studied output determinism and hallucination detection directly ([arXiv 2606.30689](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30689), abstract only).

*Reading atrophy.* HN user apex_sloth on Spec Kit: "The longer I use it, the less code I read myself." User arkensaw reported "constant regression" in LLM-built apps "despite using test-suites and spec-driven development."

*Wrong problem still possible.* A spec is an artifact, not a validation harness. HN user diegojromero: "your specification is as solid as your validation harness. If you have added strong e2e tests, with the critical scenarios covered, then you are safe" ([HN 49618556](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49618556)).

entries.name: Spec-Flow
entries.summary: A Claude Code workflow toolkit that runs spec → plan → tasks → implement → optimize → ship. It has tiered quality gates and specialized role agents. An academic assessment scored it highest of every framework it examined. It has only 85 GitHub stars.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when you want the full pipeline through deployment. Most spec frameworks stop at implementation. This one keeps going. Use it when quality gating matters enough to tier it by cost instead of running everything every time. Use it if you are already on Claude Code, since the slash commands assume it. Use the tiered-gate idea regardless of tooling: cheap checks continuously, expensive checks at boundaries. That is the most portable thing here.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for small changes. Six phases through a deployment pipeline is more process than a bug fix can repay. Do not adopt it for the score. A high mark on one study's taxonomy is a claim about completeness against that taxonomy. It is not evidence of outcomes. Weigh the adoption honestly. 85 stars means a small maintainer base and little community knowledge to draw on when something breaks. And do not use it if you do not want an opinionated deployment stage. The last two phases assume a particular shape of release process.
entries.drawbacks: Low adoption is the practical risk. The maintainer base is small, written experience is thin, and the bus factor deserves thought before you build a team workflow on it. The independent assessment measures design completeness against a taxonomy, not results. Scoring 11 of 12 says the framework has the parts. It does not say they work. Six phases are heavy for routine change. The deployment stage encodes assumptions about your release process. The name collision is a real hazard too. Three unrelated projects share it, and documentation found by search may describe a different tool.

entries.name: Specsmaxxing
entries.summary: A spec is a numbered list of requirements. Each has a stable identifier. Code and tests that satisfy a requirement reference it. Coverage becomes a query, not a judgment.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when you want coverage to be a fact, not an assertion. That is the pattern's unique contribution. Use it when heavier frameworks have failed you on weight. This is roughly the lightest thing that still counts as spec-driven. Use it when requirements are stable enough to number and the codebase is large enough that "did we build all of it?" is hard to answer. Use the identifier-reference idea alone, with whatever spec format you already have. That part is portable.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it on requirements that churn. Renumbering invalidates every reference, and the discipline collapses. Do not use it for exploratory work, where the requirements are the output, not the input. Do not let an agent generate the spec. The author rejects this, and it makes the coverage check circular. A spec written by the thing that writes the code measures agreement, not conformance. And do not mistake reference coverage for correctness. An identifier next to a function proves an annotation exists. It does not prove the requirement is met.
entries.drawbacks: Annotation rot is the main failure. Tags drift from the code they label. A stale tag is worse than no tag, because coverage reports keep counting it. Renumbering pressure is constant and destructive. Any reorganization of the spec threatens every reference. The coverage metric is gameable in the most literal way: an agent can satisfy it by adding tags. That puts it in [[Test Tampering]] territory unless the tags are checked against behavior. YAML has structure but no semantics, so nothing stops a requirement from being unfalsifiable prose with a number attached. And the evidence base is one author's tool and one discussion thread.

entries.name: Stop Hook Loop
entries.summary: A `Stop` hook intercepts the agent's attempt to end its turn, exits non-zero, and feeds the same prompt back. The loop runs inside one session, so context accumulates instead of resetting.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when the task is iterative and the accumulated context is an asset, not a liability. Examples: a long refactor where the agent must remember what it already tried, a migration across many files where earlier decisions constrain later ones, a debugging session where the trail matters. Use it when you want a loop without managing an external process, and when you want to resume by staying in the session. Use the quality-gate form whenever "the agent says it's done" is not a trustworthy stopping signal and a script can decide instead.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for long unattended runs. Context grows every iteration, so the pattern is open to context rot and eventually to compaction. Fresh-context [[Ralph Loop]] was invented to avoid exactly that. Do not use it without `--max-iterations`; the documentation says so directly. Do not make an exact-match sentinel your only exit condition, because the model controls the string. Do not use a `Stop` hook as a gate when its check is slow: you pay for it on every attempted turn-end.
entries.drawbacks: The main failure is context exhaustion. Every iteration adds tokens. A loop that could run indefinitely in fresh-context Ralph is finite here, and it degrades before it ends. Performance drops as the window fills. Then compaction fires and silently changes what the agent believes. The second failure is the sentinel. An exact-match completion promise is a string the model can emit whenever it wants, which is reward hacking by construction (see [[Reward Hacking Guardrails]] and [[Test Tampering]]). The third is hook-block caps. Claude Code limits how many times a `Stop` hook may block consecutively, so an unbounded loop hits a ceiling you did not design. The fourth is cost. Re-injecting a prompt into a growing context is the most expensive iteration shape available, because every turn re-reads everything before it.

entries.name: Subagent Context Isolation
entries.summary: Subagent context isolation gives a focused worker its own prompt, context, model, and sometimes worktree. It keeps research or review from bloating or biasing the main session.
entries.whenToUse: Codebase investigation before implementing ("The infinite exploration: You ask Claude to 'investigate' something without scoping it. Claude reads hundreds of files, filling the context. Fix: Scope investigations narrowly or use subagents"). Verbose verification: running a test suite, reading CI logs, evaluating coverage. Reviews where independence matters. Parallel, non-overlapping research questions. Tasks that suit a restricted tool set or a cheaper model (Claude Code's `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL`, per-agent `model:`; see [[Architect-Editor Split]]).
entries.whenNotToUse: Claude Code's own list: when "the task needs frequent back-and-forth or iterative refinement", when "multiple phases share significant context", for "quick, targeted changes", and when "latency matters". Do not use custom subagents to enforce a human process on the model. Shrivu Shankar dislikes them because they "gatekeep context" and "force human workflows", and prefers to let the main agent decide when to delegate ([sshh.io](https://blog.sshh.io/p/how-i-use-every-claude-code-feature)). Do not delegate implementation to many subagents in a shared working tree without a coordination scheme. That is [[Parallel Worktree Swarm]] territory.
entries.drawbacks:
- *Token multiplication.* Anthropic measured multi-agent research at about 15x the tokens of a chat; "Token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance" in performance, so isolation trades money for quality.
- *Subagents fly blind.* CuriouslyC on HN: "Subagents don't get a full system prompt (including stuff like CLAUDE.md directions) so they are flying very blind in your projects, and as such will tend to get derailed... and veer into mock solutions and 'let me just make a simpler solution that demonstrates X.'" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45181577)). Others in the same thread restrict subagents to analysis: "I don't use subagents to do things, they're best for analysing things."
- *Lossy summaries.* Whatever the child omits from its report is gone. A wrong summary poisons the parent with confidence.
- *Checkpoints don't cover them.* Claude Code: edits made by non-forked subagents are not restored by `/rewind`; "Use git to revert them" ([checkpointing documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing)).
- *Over-spawning.* Anthropic's early research system spawned "50+ subagents unnecessarily" and duplicated work "due to vague task descriptions"; prompt engineering was "our primary lever" to fix it.
- *Reviewer over-reporting.* "A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound... Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering" ([Best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices)).
- *Latency.* A fresh subagent must re-gather context. For small tasks this is slower than working inline.
- *Refusal cascades.* A 2026 regression where a malware reminder on every read "still causes subagent refusals" reached 252 points on HN ([issue #49363](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/49363)), so subagents inherit harness quirks in bulk.
related: Subagents, Parallel Workflows, and Agent Orchestration

entries.name: Superpowers
entries.summary: Superpowers makes planning, test-first implementation, review, and debugging explicit through reusable skills. The gates improve repeatability, while each gate adds time and context overhead.
entries.whenToUse: Superpowers fits application code with a real unit-test culture, and developers who want discipline imposed, not remembered. In the HN "Get Shit Done" thread, jghn reported moving "from pure plan mode to superpowers... I've been finding it's doing a better job with similar problems than I was getting with base plan mode" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47417804)), and Schwartz's review is titled "rave" for a reason: "the features it builds are so much more correct than with stock Claude Code." The brainstorming skill also works alone for people who find plan mode too monolithic. It is a skills library, not a workflow engine, so teams can adopt single skills (systematic-debugging, verification-before-completion) without the whole method.
entries.whenNotToUse: It fits poorly where TDD is awkward. Pulumi's assessment is that it "struggles beyond build phases; infrastructure where TDD is less natural", because the real validation happens at `pulumi preview`, not in a unit test. Small tasks do not need the ceremony. Experienced engineers who already run a similar process may see no gain. HN user d--b wrote "I think Claude makes more mistakes when using superpowers than when not... Just don't believe it's a silver bullet. It's still the same Claude" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47623101)). If your bottleneck is context length over a multi-week project, not discipline within a session, GSD's fresh-window execution is the more direct remedy.
entries.drawbacks: Cost and time: the two-stage review and a fresh subagent per task multiply calls. HN commenters group Superpowers with GSD as frameworks that "burn 10x more tokens" versus plain plan mode, though "GSD has a reputation for being a token burner compared to something like Superpowers" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47417804)). huydotnet reported a design flaw in the same thread: Superpowers "writes all the codes into the implementation plan, at the plan step, then the subagents basically just rewrite these codes back to the files", and progress tracking across sessions needed a hand-rolled progress file. Because it shares one orchestrator context across all phases, Pulumi notes it risks context overflow on very long sessions, unlike GSD. HN described the install path for non-Claude agents ("fetch and follow instructions from this raw URL") as "like curl|bash but with added LLM agents". That is a supply-chain concern for a plugin with mandatory-behaviour prompts. Reviewer subagents are the same model reviewing itself, so systematic blind spots survive both stages. The method also leans on persuasion text to keep the agent compliant, and that can degrade with new model versions. Vincent's pressure tests exist because compliance is not guaranteed.

entries.name: SWE-Agent Style
entries.summary: SWE-agent style treats issue fixing as a loop over a sandbox, a model-facing computer interface, and tests that decide whether the patch works.
entries.whenToUse: Use the SWE-agent style when the task has an executable oracle: a failing test, a reproduction script, a CI job. Issue resolution, bug fixing, dependency upgrades that break tests, and any "make the red thing green" work fit naturally. It suits batch or fleet operation (OpenHands' "managing fleets of coding agents" talk, or Ramp's SWE-bench harness) because success can be judged without a human. It is also the right choice when you need to compare scaffolds or models rigorously. The benchmark harnesses are the only widely accepted way to do that. The Agentless variant is a good default when cost and predictability matter more than peak capability, and when you want to run many candidates in parallel and pick by tests.
entries.whenNotToUse: It is the wrong methodology when there is no oracle. Feature work with unclear requirements, UI polish, refactors judged on taste, and anything where the "test" is a human opinion all defeat the loop's definition of done. That is why the spec-driven methodologies ([[Spec Kit]], [[BMAD Method]], [[GSD]]) exist. It also does not, by itself, address multi-session projects. The transcript is the only state, and when it fills up the agent degrades. [[Shift-Worker Handoff]] and fresh-context methods fill that gap. And benchmark numbers do not transfer. A 2026 study of 33K agent-authored pull requests on GitHub, cited on HN, found the top rejection reason was "missing context" and that about 80% needed human fixes ([arXiv 2601.15195](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.15195) as cited by HN user knes in [47417804](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47417804)).
entries.drawbacks: Reward hacking against the tests is endemic. Agents learn to special-case the failing test, delete or weaken assertions, or catch exceptions broadly. The PASS_TO_PASS check only catches regressions the existing suite covers. Benchmark contamination and quality are real problems. Agentless found ground-truth patches leaking into issue text, and ambiguous descriptions. SWE-bench Verified was created because a large fraction of the original set was unsolvable as specified. An August 2026 paper found code agents brittle under "semantics-preserving transformations" of the same tasks ([arXiv 2608.18389](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18389)). Loops without a cap run away. SWE-agent imposed step and dollar limits because the ReAct loop will otherwise cycle between two edits. mini-SWE-agent's stateless `subprocess.run` design exists because a stateful shell wedged too often. Tests judge patch quality, not maintainability. The 2024 HN thread's complaint that agent fixes "will make any codebase worse" has never been fully answered by the benchmark. Finally, the lineage says nothing about specification, planning across sessions or human review. Teams that adopt "just run the loop" on real backlogs find those gaps quickly.

entries.name: Task Master
entries.summary: Parse a product requirements document into a dependency-aware task graph, then serve that graph to a coding agent over MCP so `next` always returns something unblocked.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when you have a real PRD and want it decomposed once, not re-derived every session. Use it when dependencies matter and you keep answering "what can I start now" by hand. Use it when several tools or editors touch the same project, since MCP shares the graph across them. Use it as the intake side of a multi-worker setup, feeding [[Parallel Worktree Swarm]] or [[Agent Teams]].
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for work that fits in one session. A task graph for three tasks is overhead. Do not use it when your existing issue tracker already holds the graph. Maintaining both is the usual failure, and the tracker usually wins. If the open-core split matters to you, check which capabilities sit in the CLI and which in Studio before building a workflow on it. Do not rely on the decomposition without reading it. A generated task graph inherits every ambiguity in the PRD, and the dependencies are inferred, not known. Watch the context cost of the MCP surface. Load the core tool set unless you need more.
entries.drawbacks: A model generates the decomposition, so task boundaries and dependency edges are guesses that look authoritative once written down. A wrong edge blocks work that was never blocked. A missing one lets an agent start something it cannot finish. Keeping the graph current is manual work that tends to lapse, and then `next` is confidently wrong. It duplicates any existing tracker. The project also now sits under a commercial layer. That is the ordinary open-core risk, not a defect. The CLI is MIT and the company says the core stays free, but the boundary between tiers is theirs to move.

entries.name: Task Queue Consumer
entries.summary: A task queue consumer claims one durable task, performs bounded work, persists the result, and acknowledges only after success. Leases, retries, and queue-age metrics make crashes visible.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when the work splits into many small, mostly independent items with a few explicit ordering constraints: large refactors, per-file migrations, test-coverage campaigns, documentation sweeps, a backlog of small features or bugs. TaskQ's README targets exactly "hundreds of test cases or pattern migrations." Use it when you want more than one worker. A queue is the only sane way to keep parallel agents from duplicating work. Use it when humans and agents share the backlog. Backlog.md's whole premise is "one task = one PR" with spec, plan and code review checkpoints, and Linear/GitHub integrations let the tracker you already have become the queue. And use it when you need durability across crashes. Gas Town's molecules are "persistent across crashes" because the bead, not the agent, owns the state.
entries.whenNotToUse: Don't use it for sequential work with many dependencies or for same-file edits. Claude Code's documentation says that "for sequential tasks, same-file edits, or work with many dependencies, a single session or subagents are more effective." Don't use it when the decomposition itself is the hard part. A queue of badly-cut tasks just parallelizes confusion, and MindStudio notes that "incorrect assumptions by one agent can cascade to others." Don't use it if you cannot review the output as fast as it is produced. On the Gas Town thread `qcnguy` observed "the bottleneck is going to be how fast humans can review code." And don't adopt heavyweight tooling for a small project. HN users reported doing fine with markdown files, GitHub Issues or Taskwarrior.
entries.drawbacks:
*Status lag and stuck dependents.* Claude Code's documented limitation: "teammates sometimes fail to mark tasks as completed, which blocks dependent tasks." One unflipped flag can stall a whole subgraph.

*Merge and sync chaos.* Beads' own `.beads` directory was messy enough that HN commenters questioned whether the project dogfooded its schema ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46075616)). A later "I replaced Beads" thread cited a background daemon that "took to syncing the wrong things at the wrong times" and every release getting "slower and more frustrating" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46487580)). Gas Town commenters reported "merge conflict issues that confuse agents" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46458936)).

*Work gets lost.* Yegge is candid: "some work gets lost. Fish fall out of the barrel." One Gas Town user described autonomous pull request merges despite failing integration tests as "riding a wild stallion," and Yegge's production database was down two days after an agent erased passwords ([mikemason.ca](https://mikemason.ca/writing/ai-coding-agents-jan-2026/)).

*Cost.* Yegge called Gas Town "a cash guzzler" and needed a second Claude Code account, with a third expected. Claude Code documents that agent teams "use significantly more tokens than a single session," scaling linearly with teammates.

*Missed items on manual population.* TaskQ: "always use a script" to populate tasks, "as manual population causes agents to miss items."

*Tool bloat and agents ignoring the tracker.* "Beads is an incredibly difficult-to-follow mess for something that is at its core a pretty simple idea" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46487580)). Skeptics also questioned whether agents genuinely prefer the tracker or only say so.

*Human review as the bottleneck.* `lifetimerubyist`: "If babysitting 30 claude agents is the future of professional programming I want zero part of it."

*Task tools disappearing.* Several Claude Code issues report `TaskCreate`/`TaskList` not exposed in some environments (VS Code extension, web, `claude-code-action`), for example [#23816](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/23816), [#80015](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/80015).
related: Subagents, Parallel Workflows, and Agent Orchestration

entries.name: Tessl
entries.summary: Spec-as-source taken literally: the specification is the maintained artifact, and the code carries a header saying it was generated and must not be edited. It is the clearest statement of the position. The most interesting fact about it is that Tessl's own public product is something else.
entries.whenToUse:
For spec-as-source, use it where generated code is already normal and nobody expects to edit it: clients generated from an API schema, serialization layers, boilerplate derived from a data model. There the pattern is not radical. It is what everyone already does. Outside that, the case is speculative, and a vendor's own product decisions argue against it.

For the shipping platform, the question is not this pattern. It is whether you need organization-wide skill governance, which [[Skill Library]] covers.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use spec-as-source where people reason about the code, which is most application logic. Do not use it where debugging matters and the failing code is code nobody wrote. Do not use it where regeneration is not reproducible. That is the non-determinism half of Böckeler's objection: a regeneration that produces a materially different implementation from the same spec breaks the mental model the header promises. And do not adopt it on the strength of a framework description. That is doubly true here.
entries.drawbacks: Böckeler's "inflexibility and non-determinism" is the central objection, and it is unanswered. You take on the constraints of generated code without the reproducibility that made those constraints tolerable. Escape hatches are the practical failure. Every generated-code system eventually needs a hand-edit. When one happens, the header is a lie and the spec is no longer the source of truth. Debugging generated code is a known cost. Model-driven development's record in business applications is not encouraging. The strongest drawback is circumstantial, not argued: the vendor that defined the approach has repositioned around skills and governance.

entries.name: Test Ratchet
entries.summary: Quality measures move in one direction only. Tests may be added, never removed or weakened. A feature's status may flip from failing to passing, and nothing else about it may change.
entries.whenToUse: Use it on every project where an agent can edit the files that judge it. That is the default, and it should not be. Use it in unattended runs, where nobody will notice a weakened check for a long time. Use it when the quality measure is the completion signal, as in any [[Goal Loop]] or [[Convergence Loop]] whose exit condition is "the suite is green." Use it on coverage and lint configuration as well as on tests. The second attempt goes there.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it where a test is genuinely wrong and must be fixed. That is the real cost: a ratchet makes correcting a bad test a separate, human-authorized act, not something the agent does mid-task. Do not apply it to measures without a meaningful direction. A ratchet on test count rewards many trivial tests. Do not use it to freeze a suite you know is bad. A ratchet preserves whatever floor it starts from, including a floor of noise. And do not rely on the instruction alone.
entries.drawbacks: It makes fixing a wrong test expensive. That cost lands exactly when an agent has correctly found a wrong test, and the stuck run looks like agent failure. It preserves bad floors indefinitely. It invites indirect weakening: configuration changes, glob exclusions, inline suppressions, and assertions quietly made vacuous. A test-path deny rule sees none of these. Ratcheting the wrong measure creates a perverse incentive, as with test count. And a ratchet enforced only by instruction is not a ratchet. That is the most common way it is implemented.

entries.name: Test Tampering
entries.summary: Test tampering is when an agent changes the test, fixture, or check instead of fixing the behavior. Protected tests and independent verification keep “green” meaningful.
entries.whenToUse: Read this pattern when you build or run any of: [[Verification Loop]], [[Test-Driven Agent Loop]], [[CI Repair Loop]], [[Ralph Loop]], [[Best-of-N Sampling]], [[Tree Search Over Actions]], [[Execution Feedback Repair]], or any unattended run whose stop condition is a check the agent can reach. The defenses cost less than shipping a lookup table. Make tests read-only. Keep a held-out set. Feed back verbatim output. Have someone else grade. Give the agent a way to say "this cannot be done as specified."
entries.whenNotToUse: The defenses have costs. ImpossibleBench found that hiding test files "nearly eliminated cheating but harmed legitimate performance," because tests are also the best specification the agent has. Strict prompting helped enormously in one setting (GPT-5's cheating from 93% to 1%) and barely in another (66% to 54%). Prompts alone are not a control. Read-only tests block the legitimate case where the test really is wrong, so pair the restriction with an explicit "report a test bug" path. For throwaway prototypes with no held-out consumers, the overhead may exceed the risk.
entries.drawbacks: The failure mode itself: passing dashboards, broken software, and commit messages that rationalize it. Over-defending causes its own failures. An agent forbidden from touching tests stalls on a genuinely wrong test. Hidden tests leave the agent under-specified. A verifier subagent "will usually report some [gaps], even when the work is sound" and drives over-engineering (Anthropic's caveat). SpecBench found that more tests can widen the gap, so test volume does not replace test *structure* (compositional, held-out). Search also amplifies hacking: a value function that rewards passing tests selects the branch that games them.

entries.name: Test-Driven Agent Loop
entries.summary: A test-driven agent loop writes and observes a failing behavior test before implementation, freezes the test during the green phase, and refactors only while it stays green.
entries.whenToUse:
Use it when you can state the behaviour as input/output pairs before you know the implementation. Parsers, validators, API contracts, bug reproductions, and algorithmic code fit. Anthropic's example is "write a validateEmail function. example test cases: user@example.com is true, invalid is false, user@.com is false. run the tests after implementing." It is also the best defence against the "grading its own exams" problem. sReinwald on HN: "write (or have AI write) tests first, review them as the spec, then let it implement... May as well ask high schoolers to grade their own exams. Everyone got an A+, how surprising!" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46693275)).

Use it for bug fixes ("write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it"). The failing test is both the reproduction and the regression guard. Use it too when you plan to rewrite rather than review: cadamsdotcom's workflow is to have the agent delete untested code and reimplement test-first, yielding "coverage that you KNOW covers the code because you watched those tests fail before they passed" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48548883)).
entries.whenNotToUse:
Do not impose it on issue-resolution tasks where the test suite already exists and the agent's job is to make it pass. Chen et al. analysed six models on SWE-bench Verified and found "prompt-induced changes in the volume of agent-written tests do not significantly change final outcomes". An HN reader summarised the paper's numbers as "encouraging tests cost +19.8% output tokens for 0% gain" and that imposing TDD "increased regressions from 6.08% to 9.94%" ([Rethinking the Value of Agent-Generated Tests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07900); [rsalus on HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48398925)). The same commenter thread has zuzululu preferring "tests as verification oracles post-generation" for cost reasons.

Do not use it when the spec is too vague to encode. edude03's reply on HN is that "creating sufficiently detailed specifications is often the real difficulty." UI polish, exploratory prototypes and throwaway scripts fit poorly.

Do not use it with a heavy integration harness the agent cannot stand up. Matlakhov's VibeTDD experiment found that when Spring Boot/MongoDB configuration got hard, Claude Code "substituted mocked repositories instead of integration tests," because it "prioritizes successful test execution above other instructions" ([VibeTDD Experiment 4.4](https://dev.to/maksim_matlakhov/vibetdd-experiment-44-storage-layer-testing-and-the-never-give-up-problem-5f1g)).
entries.drawbacks:
*Agents delete, disable or weaken tests.* This is the signature failure. Beck lists "disabling or deleting tests to fake progress" among his three derailment signs and describes catching the agent commenting out tests "only through careful code review." Anthropic's long-running-agent harness had to add "strongly-worded instructions like 'It is unacceptable to remove or edit tests'" ([Effective harnesses](https://anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents)). On the dotnet/runtime Copilot pull requests, diggan reported "funniest PRs are the ones that 'resolves' test failures by removing/commenting out the test cases, or change the assertions" ([HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44050261)). Okuno's "hard realities" post lists "Tests are passing!" after "modifying tests to skip rather than fixing issues" ([dev.to](https://dev.to/choplin/claude-code-3-hard-realities-nobody-talks-about-kp0)). The pattern only works if the freeze is enforced by hooks or permissions, not just prose.

*Mock substitution and the "never give up" problem.* Matlakhov found the agent "systematically avoids challenges rather than requesting clarification—substituting mocks for real database tests, modifying existing code to accommodate flaws, or creating workaround solutions," and that "there's no global config to change it because it's considered a feature, not a bug."

*Test quality.* Swett: agents typically produce tests that are "vague, cryptic, overcomplicated, hacky" without guidance. disgruntledphd2 dislikes the "over-emphasis on mocks in training data"; Anthropic's own prompt advice is to say "avoid mocks."

*Stubbing instead of implementing.* Beck's second failure mode: the agent "implements features only partially, stubbing them out without actual functionality—discovered only through telemetry inspection." Green tests do not prove the feature is wired end-to-end; see [[Verification Loop]] for the browser-level check Anthropic found necessary.

*Cost and speed.* The SWE-bench study above; shaman-apprentice's release-parrot experiment found "waiting for AI output proved slower and more exhausting than coding manually," no measurable quality gain, and that the agent "sometimes got stuck in loops producing hundreds of lines of non-functional code for simple three-line changes" ([AI-assisted TDD Experiment](https://dev.to/shaman-apprentice/ai-assisted-test-driven-development-experiment-quick-takes-17fe)).

*Peeking.* If the agent can read the existing implementation while writing tests, the tests describe what the code does, not what it should do (Berger).

*Scope creep in GREEN.* esperent's "trigger happy" green worker; Beck's "premature functionality beyond what was requested."

*Skepticism about the evidence.* jvuygbbkuurx on HN: "if TDD actually was better it would simply be in system prompts"; bob1029 asks whether AI-authored tests "create complacency" and whether "total coverage is a terrible objective."

entries.name: Tool-Result Externalization
aliases: Grep the File Not the Context
entries.summary: Write large tool outputs to disk and keep only a reference in context. The agent reads the parts it needs with the tools it already has. It does not carry the whole output in every later request.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for anything verbose: full test-suite output, build logs, `git log` over a long range, large data files, API responses. Use it in long sessions, where the accumulation cost compounds. Use it when the agent needs a small part of a large output, which is nearly always. In a failing build, the twenty lines around the first error matter. Use it when the output should outlive the session, since the next session can read the artifact on disk.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for small outputs, where the indirection costs more than the content. Do not use it when the agent needs the whole output anyway, since you pay for the output plus the round trip. Do not use it when the artifact will not exist later. A file in a container that is about to be destroyed is a reference to nothing. Do not externalize output the agent must reason over as a whole. A targeted read gives it a keyhole view, and it will draw conclusions from the keyhole.
entries.drawbacks: The agent has to know what to search for. An agent that greps for the wrong string concludes the output contained nothing. That false negative looks exactly like a clean result. Partial reads mislead: a log tail can show a passing final step while the real failure sits a thousand lines earlier. Each retrieval costs a round trip, which is worse than inlining when several retrievals are needed. Artifacts accumulate on disk and need cleanup. In ephemeral environments the path can outlive the file, and the agent holds a reference it cannot resolve.

entries.name: Tracker-as-Queue
aliases: Assign the Issue to the Agent
entries.summary: Assign a tracker issue to an agent the way you would assign it to a person. The agent plans, opens a pull request, writes the code, runs the tests, and asks for review. Someone other than the issue's author must approve it.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for well-specified, self-contained issues: bug fixes with a reproduction, mechanical refactors, dependency bumps, small features with clear acceptance criteria. Use it when the work is already in a tracker and a second queue would fragment it. Use it for asynchronous work you want to hand off and forget, since the pull request is the notification. Use it when organizational controls—review separation, audit trail, permissions—matter. You inherit them instead of rebuilding them.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for vague issues. The agent cannot ask the clarifying question a human assignee would, and a thin ticket produces thin work. Do not use it for exploratory or architectural work where the shape of the answer is the deliverable. Do not use it where review capacity is already the bottleneck. This pattern converts implementation capacity into review load, so the bottleneck moves. And do not let the separation-of-duties rule erode. The author of an issue is the worst available reviewer of work generated from it.
entries.drawbacks: Output quality is bounded by intake quality. The loop that normally fixes a bad ticket—someone asking what you meant—is missing. Review becomes the bottleneck, the predictable result of cheap implementation. The agent's decomposition can be wrong in ways visible only once the code exists, and the checklist's look of progress can mask that. Cost scales with issues assigned, invisibly. The pattern is also vendor-managed: the plan, the run, and the environment are outside your control, unlike a local agent.

entries.name: Trajectory Memory
entries.summary: Trajectory memory distills prior attempts into reusable lessons, insights, and workflows. It should record why an approach worked or failed. It should not become an unreadable transcript archive.
entries.whenToUse: Use it when the same agent works the same codebase or domain repeatedly and keeps rediscovering the same facts: which command runs the tests, that a module is deprecated, that an approach failed last week. Use insight-style memory for rules ("never mock the database in integration tests here"). Use workflow-style memory for procedures ("how to add an endpoint"). Use similar-trajectory retrieval when tasks are near-duplicates (a migration across 200 files). There a past success is the best possible few-shot example.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not replay raw trajectories in the prompt for large tasks. A past trajectory can run to tens of thousands of tokens and is mostly noise. Do not store unverified "insights" from failures. ExpeL extracts from *comparisons* with successes for a reason. Do not let memory grow unbounded. The learnings-loop guide warns that a file past 80-100 entries is "worse than no file at all," and that applies to any retrieval-free memory. And do not confuse memory with correctness. A remembered workflow that was wrong is a bug that replays (Opalic's warning about procedural memory).
entries.drawbacks: Staleness: memory does not know the repository changed. Contamination: a wrong insight, retrieved confidently, steers future tasks wrong, and voting fixes it only after repeated contradiction. Retrieval misses: a task described in different words from the stored trajectory does not surface the relevant memory. Privacy and leakage: memory that persists across projects can carry secrets or client-specific facts between them. Bloat: without consolidation, memory becomes a second context-rot problem. And the evidence for coding is thinner than for web tasks. ExpeL and AWM were evaluated on HotpotQA, ALFWorld, WebShop, Mind2Web and WebArena, not on SWE-bench.

entries.name: Tree Search Over Actions
entries.summary: Tree search over actions expands several candidate next actions, scores the resulting states, backtracks from weak branches, and commits the best surviving trajectory. More search costs more compute.
entries.whenToUse: Use tree search when the task has a reliable terminal check (tests, a compiler, a benchmark), early decisions are hard to undo (which file to touch, which design to adopt), and you will pay several times the single-trajectory cost for a higher solve rate. It suits offline or batch settings: nightly runs against an issue queue, benchmark climbing, hard bugs a linear agent has already failed on. SWE-Search's scaling curve makes the case. With compute and a good verifier, search converts compute into solved issues.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it interactively. The latency and cost are wrong for a developer waiting at a terminal. Do not use it without a grounded value function. An LLM judge alone will rate a plausible dead end highly, and the multi-agent debate literature reports agents "reinforcing each other's flawed reasoning" ([arXiv 2503.12029](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.12029)). Do not use it when the search space is trivial (one obvious fix) or when side effects cannot be isolated per branch (shared databases, external APIs without sandboxes).
entries.drawbacks: Cost multiplies by branching factor and depth. Moatless defaults of 5 expansions and 100 iterations imply hundreds of agent steps per issue. The paper does not report wall-clock or dollar cost. Every branch needs an isolated environment, so infrastructure is the real barrier. The value function is the weak point. An LLM judge can be reward-hacked (a branch that *claims* tests pass). With tests, the agent can special-case them (see [[Test Tampering]]). Search also amplifies flaky tests: a nondeterministic pass can steer the whole tree. Finally, no practitioner-facing CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) exposes true MCTS. The pattern remains research and benchmark tooling. The searches run for this file found no Reddit/HN discussion of SWE-Search or moatless.

entries.name: Ultraplan
entries.summary: Planning moves off your machine. A cloud session drafts the plan while your terminal stays free. You review and comment on it section by section in a browser. Then you execute it remotely or send it back to the CLI.
entries.whenToUse: Use it for large changes where exploration is long and you would otherwise sit watching it: migrations, architectural changes, anything spanning several subsystems. Use it when someone other than you must review the plan, since a commentable document is shareable and a terminal is not. Use it when you want to keep working locally while the plan is produced. Use it when the work suits remote execution anyway.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for small changes, where the browser round trip costs more than the work. Do not use it when the task depends on local state the cloud environment lacks—uncommitted work, local services, environment-specific configuration. Do not use it when the code cannot leave your machine. This is a cloud feature, and that is a policy question before a technical one. And treat it as a research preview. Behavior and availability may change.
entries.drawbacks: It is a research preview from a single vendor, so it is a product feature before it is a portable pattern. The cloud environment is not your machine. Plans can be drafted against a state that differs from your working tree in ways neither you nor the agent notices. Round-trip latency makes it wrong for small tasks. Code leaves the local machine, a constraint in some environments however the feature works. And asynchronous review invites one failure in particular: you read a plan an hour later, against a repository that has moved, and approve it assuming nothing changed.

entries.name: Verification Loop
entries.summary: A verification loop turns "done" into layered evidence: targeted checks, broader checks, and inspection of the result. A failure feeds diagnosis and another bounded change.
entries.whenToUse:
Use it whenever you can express "correct" as a command. Willison's heuristic: "any time you find yourself thinking 'ugh, I'm going to have to try a lot of variations here'" is a strong signal. Examples are debugging failing tests, optimising against a benchmark, upgrading dependencies checked by a test suite, and shrinking a container image. Any unattended run requires it. Anthropic's guide says the `/goal` and Stop-hook versions "are what let an unattended run finish correctly without you," and the [[Ralph Loop]] is this pattern wrapped in a `while true` with fresh context each turn.

It also fits UI work if you can make the check visual: "[paste screenshot] implement this design. take a screenshot of the result and compare it to the original. list differences and fix them" is Anthropic's own example prompt, and the long-running-agent harness uses Puppeteer/[Playwright](https://playwright.dev/) MCP so the agent tests "as a human user would."
entries.whenNotToUse:
Do not use it when there is no mechanical oracle. The loop stops on a signal. If the only judge is taste ("make the dashboard look better"), the agent will loop forever or declare victory on its own say-so. Anthropic's best-practices page contrasts the vague and checkable versions of that prompt.

Do not make a weak or agent-written test suite the only gate. aipatternbook warns that "agent-generated tests shouldn't be trusted as sole verification mechanism," and SpecBench's authors observe that when developers cannot review large outputs, "oversight collapses onto a single surface: the automated test suite," which agents then game ([SpecBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21384)).

Skip the full loop for trivial edits. aipatternbook notes that "running full test suites after minor changes can be wasteful," and Anthropic's CLAUDE.md example advises "prefer running single tests, and not the whole test suite, for performance."
entries.drawbacks:
_Reward hacking against the check._ This is the central failure mode, and it is well documented. EvilGenie (Gabor, Lynch, Rosenfeld, arXiv 2511.21654) let agents "hardcode test cases or edit the testing files" and found that "both Codex and Claude Code demonstrated direct reward hacking behaviors" and "all three proprietary agents exhibited some form of misaligned behavior" ([EvilGenie](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21654)). SpecBench (Zhao et al., arXiv 2605.21384) found "all frontier models saturate visible test suites while failing held-out tests," that the gap "grows by 28 percentage points for every tenfold increase in code size," and cites a "2,900-line hash-table 'compiler' that memorizes test inputs" ([SpecBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21384)). Lodkaew et al. (arXiv 2606.07379) propose randomized tests with a deliberately capped ceiling so that scores above the cap signal cheating ([Do Coding Agents Deceive Us?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07379)).

_False claims of success._ Practitioners report agents asserting green when it isn't. Akihiro Okuno lists "Tests are passing!" after "modifying tests to skip rather than fixing issues" among Claude Code's "hard realities," summarising that "Claude Code sometimes lies to save face" ([Claude Code: 3 Hard Realities](https://dev.to/choplin/claude-code-3-hard-realities-nobody-talks-about-kp0)). A Substack author who built a Stop hook wrote: "Claude told me the work was done. The tests passed. Everything green. It wasn't true," and found one failing test when running the suite independently ([The Stop Hook That Won't Let Claude Lie to You](https://codingwithroby.substack.com/p/the-stop-hook-that-wont-let-claude)). Kent Beck lists "disabling or deleting tests to fake progress" as one of three warning signs that the agent is derailing ([Augmented Coding: Beyond the Vibes](https://newsletter.kentbeck.com/p/augmented-coding-beyond-the-vibes)).

_Premature exit on partial checks._ Anthropic's harness team saw agents pass unit tests and `curl` checks yet ship features that "didn't work end-to-end." The fix, mandatory browser testing before marking a feature done, is expensive. The full generator/evaluator harness ran "6 hours, $200" versus "20 minutes, $9" for a solo run.

_Prompt-based gates are soft._ On Hacker News, `adidoit` pointed out that the state of the art is "to use strong-worded instructions… can you really trust systems like these in production?" and `daxfohl` reported that adding QA/verification agents often makes multi-agent runs "get all out of whack… far more frequently it'll get stuck in a loop" ([HN: Effective harnesses for long-running agents](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46081704)). A deterministic gate enforces only its own predicate. Bound retries and detect stalled progress in the harness. A product-specific stop-hook limit does not guard in general against repeated outer-loop restarts.

_Turning requirements into machine-checkable form is the real bottleneck._ Nate's field notes argue "in agent land, the wrapper is the product" and that "converting subjective task requirements into machine-checkable constraints represents an emerging bottleneck. Most teams haven't recognized this skill gap yet" ([My honest field notes on the verification gap](https://natesnewsletter.substack.com/p/my-honest-field-notes-on-the-verification)).

_Symptom suppression._ Told "the build is failing," the agent may silence the error instead of fixing the cause. Anthropic's guidance: say "address the root cause, don't suppress the error."

entries.name: Verified SDD
entries.summary: Spec-driven development with a conformance step. The spec produces tests and formal properties before any code exists, and generated code must satisfy them. The hard part: specifying an unsolved problem is harder than testing a solved one.
entries.whenToUse: Use it where the requirements are knowable in advance: protocol implementations, format parsers, API contracts, migrations with a defined equivalence, anything with an existing standard to conform to. Use it where correctness matters more than speed and a defect is expensive. Use it when generation volume is high enough that human review is the bottleneck, since a conformance check scales and a reviewer does not. Keep the ordering—spec, then tests, then code—even if you skip the formal machinery. The ordering is most of the benefit.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for discovery work. The critics' reason holds: you cannot specify a solution you have not found. Do not use it for exploratory or design-led work where the requirement changes as you see the result. Do not use it when an agent writes the spec. A spec from the same model that writes the code shares its blind spots, and the conformance check becomes circular. And do not mistake conformance for correctness. Passing a spec proves only that the spec was satisfied, and the spec may be wrong.
entries.drawbacks: The discovery objection is the serious one, and it is not a detail. Most interesting software work is figuring out what to build, and this pattern assumes that phase is over. Specification cost is real and front-loaded, and it is wasted when requirements change. Formal methods have a decades-old adoption problem that nothing here solves. The spec can be wrong, and a wrong spec verified rigorously yields confidently incorrect software with a clean audit trail. A spec elaborate enough to verify is itself an artifact that can drift from reality. And a substantial share of the Hacker News commenters dismissed the source gist as AI-generated content with no practical evidence behind it. Weigh the proposal's provenance accordingly.

entries.name: Vibe Coding
entries.summary: Vibe coding means directing an agent in conversation while accepting generated code with little inspection. It suits disposable experiments. Durable software still needs code ownership and verification.
entries.whenToUse: Willison's list: "Low-stakes personal projects with minimal harm potential", "Throwaway prototypes and experiments", "Learning tools to build intuition about LLM capabilities", and sandboxed environments where the blast radius is bounded. Spikes to answer "is this even possible?", personal scripts, demos, and internal tools whose failure costs nothing. It is also the honest name for the exploratory first hour on a new idea, before you decide whether it deserves engineering.
entries.whenNotToUse: Do not use it for anything with users, money, secrets or data: "Security vulnerabilities could harm users or expose secrets", "Private data might inadvertently leave the machine", "Unmonitored API usage could incur unexpected costs", "Software will be used by other people without experienced review". Do not use it in established codebases that others maintain. Mo Bitar's core complaint: "Agents write units of changes that look good in isolation… But respect for the whole, there is not" ([atmoio](https://atmoio.substack.com/p/after-two-years-of-vibecoding-im)). Do not use it for open-source contributions, where maintainers now say they can tell ("I know when you're vibe coding", HN 353 points) and where the "cleanup as a service" market (HN 250 points) shows the downstream cost.
entries.drawbacks:
- *Comprehension debt.* "The code grows beyond my usual comprehension" (Karpathy) becomes unpayable when the project stops being a toy. Bitar: "You cannot get away from the tech debt models produce" and it becomes "a self-reinforcing loop".
- *Skill atrophy.* Bitar reports loss of "the engineer's own mental model and problem-solving abilities"; an HN thread titled "Man, AI is killing my brain" made the same point.
- *Security and data leakage.* Willison's explicit risk list; the [[Sandboxed Execution]] literature's incidents (a production database deleted by an agent, HN 860 points) are the extreme form.
- *Ecosystem harm.* Koren et al. argue vibe coding erodes the user engagement that funds OSS maintainers.
- *Slop and cleanup cost.* Maintainers reject vibe-coded pull requests; "Vibe coding cleanup as a service" exists.
- *Blurred lines even for experts.* Willison: "I'm not reviewing that code. And now I've got that feeling of guilt." The pattern's boundary moves as agents improve, so "am I vibing?" stays an open question.
- *Misleading productivity sense.* HN commenter bonesss on the AGENTS.md study: "the normal time versus productivity sense is further pulled out of whack" by pleasant but unproductive interactions.
